advisories.summary: Forge: ASN.1 resource exhaustion via BIT STRING decoding in asn1.fromDer
advisories.description:
### Summary
`asn1.fromDer()` decodes the contents of BIT STRINGs as ASN.1 by default. That decode ignored the `maxDepth` recursion limit (an incomplete fix of CVE-2025-66031) and also decoded nested BIT STRINGs, keeping a full copy of the decoded contents at each level, so small crafted DER or PEM inputs (certificates, keys, PKCS structures) use excessive CPU time and memory and can abort the Node.js process. Fixed in node-forge 1.4.1.

### Details
`asn1.fromDer()` attempts by default to decode the contents of primitive BIT STRINGs as ASN.1 (`decodeBitStrings`, default `true`). Two flaws in that decode in `lib/asn1.js` allow resource exhaustion:

1. `_fromDer()` started the BIT STRING decode with a new options object, `{strict: true, decodeBitStrings: true}`, that did not include `maxDepth`. Inside that decode the depth check compared against `undefined` and never triggered, so the recursion limit added for CVE-2025-66031 (GHSA-554w-wpv2-vw27) was not enforced for anything below a decoded BIT STRING. Both the global `asn1.maxDepth` (default 256) and the per-call `maxDepth` option were ignored there. Errors in this speculative decode, including stack overflows, are caught and the contents kept as raw bytes, so deep nesting is parsed instead of rejected. This is an incomplete fix of CVE-2025-66031.
2. BIT STRINGs nested inside decoded BIT STRING contents were decoded as well, and `asn1.create()` gives each decoded BIT STRING a deep copy of its decoded contents (`obj.original`, used by `toDer()` to detect changes). Memory use therefore grows quadratically with the nesting depth, even within the default depth limit.

No specification is violated; the parser lacks a resource limit.

The fix passes `maxDepth` to the BIT STRING decode, and decodes BIT STRING contents with `decodeBitStrings: false`, so only one level of BIT STRING contents is decoded. Contents that would exceed the limit, and BIT STRINGs inside decoded BIT STRING contents, are kept as undecoded BIT STRING values; `toDer()` writes their original bytes. Common structures such as SubjectPublicKeyInfo only use one level. Code that relied on nested decoding can decode the inner value explicitly with `asn1.fromDer()`.

#### Patches
Fixed in node-forge 1.4.1. The `maxDepth` limit now applies to ASN.1 decoded from BIT STRING contents, and only one level of BIT STRING contents is decoded.

#### Workarounds
Code that calls `forge.asn1.fromDer()` directly and does not need encapsulated BIT STRING contents de

advisories.description:
### Summary

- **Verified version:** zip `9.0.0-pre3`
- **Affected versions:** `7.2.0` and later
- **Precondition:** The attacker knows (or can guess) the absolute path of the extraction destination

The validation applied to symlinks is purely lexical.
As a result, an attacker can write arbitrary files outside the extraction directory through a symlink.
Exploitation requires the attacker to know (or guess) the absolute path of the destination, but this is realistic in practice: CI workspaces, `/opt/app`, a fixed Downloads path, and so on.

> **Impact extends further on Windows (verified on real hardware for both the separate-drive and UNC-share cases)**:  
> Because `simplified_components` discards the `Prefix` component, paths like `D:\<same tail as dest>` or a UNC path `\\attacker\share\<same tail>` pass the `starts_with` check.  
> As a result, `outpath.push` gets replaced onto a different drive/remote share, so **a single symlink is enough — no intermediate symlink chain is required**.  
> That said, creating a symlink on Windows requires `SeCreateSymbolicLinkPrivilege` (administrator rights or Developer Mode enabled).
> **Real-hardware verification (Windows 10 VM (19045.2604), `tests/poc_win.rs`)**:  
> With the extraction target set to a temporary directory under `C:`, both of the following paths returned `Ok(())` from `extract()` and successfully wrote outside the extraction target.

advisories.summary: Addressable: Regular Expression Denial of Service in templates with certain exploded expressions
advisories.description:
### Impact

Within the URI template implementation in Addressable, templates using the `*` (explode) modifier with the `/`, `.`, `;`, `?` or `&` operators (e.g., `{/segments*}`, `{.ext*}`, `{;params*}`, `{?query*}`) generate regular expressions vulnerable to catastrophic backtracking. When `Template#match` or `Template#extract` is called with a maliciously crafted URI that starts with the operator's leading character, matching takes exponential time, leading to uncontrolled resource consumption and denial of service. An input under 60 bytes is enough to occupy a thread for minutes.

GHSA-h27x-rffw-24p4 (CVE-2026-35611) reported this pattern as fully remediated in 2.9.0. The 2.9.0 fix only made the joiner between exploded members mandatory for templates without an operator, and its regression specs used inputs that never start with the operator's leading character, so the vulnerable part of the expression was never reached. This issue was originally reported in #364 by @ebenoist in 2019 but insufficiently investigated.

Users of the URI parsing capabilities in Addressable but not the URI template matching capabilities are unaffected. Users who only call `Template#expand` are unaffected.

### Affected Versions

This vulnerability affects Addressable >= 2.3.0 (note: 2.3.0 and 2.3.1 were yanked; the earliest installable release is 2.3.2), including 2.9.0. It is fixed in 2.9.1.

The vulnerability is only exploitable on Ruby implementations whose regular expression engine backtracks without memoization: MRI Ruby < 3.2 and JRuby. MRI Ruby 3.2 and later are not affected: their regular expression engine memoizes backtracking, so these patterns still match in linear time. TruffleRuby 40.0 is not affected either. Earlier TruffleRuby versions were not tested.

This has been confirmed on the following runtimes with Addressable 2.9.0:

| Runtime | Status |
|---------|--------|
| MRI Ruby 2.7 | Vulnerable |
| MRI Ruby 3.1 | Vulnerable |
| MRI Ruby 3.2 | Not affected |
| MRI Ruby 3.3 | Not affected |
| MRI Ruby 3.4 | Not affected |
| MRI Ruby 4.0 | Not affected |
| JRuby 9.4 | Vulnerable |
| TruffleRuby 40.0 | Not affected |

- Upgrade to MRI Ruby 3.2 or later, if the consuming application does not use JRuby.
- Avoid matching user-supplied input on unpatched versions of the library against templates that use the `*` modifier with the `/`, `.`, `;`, `?` or `&` operators.

advisories.summary: Nuxt dev server serves files from a parent directory with a stray lockfile or workspace file
advisories.description:
### Summary

Nuxt can pick a parent directory that does not declare a workspace as its default `workspaceDir`: the farthest directory with a lockfile when the project is not inside a git repository, or the farthest directory with a `pnpm-workspace.yaml` or `deno.json` file, even one that only holds settings. The Vite dev server allows `/_nuxt/@fs/` requests for any file under `workspaceDir`. A stray lockfile or settings file in a parent directory, such as the home directory, therefore lets anyone who can reach the dev server read files in that directory and everything below it.

### Impact

This affects the development server only; production builds are not affected. All of the following have to hold:

- A parent directory contains either:
  - a lockfile (`package-lock.json`, `pnpm-lock.yaml`, `yarn.lock`, `bun.lock` and similar), while the project is not inside a git repository and has no workspace file (`pnpm-workspace.yaml`, `turbo.json`, `lerna.json` and similar) above it. Running `npm install` once in the home directory is enough to create one there.
  - a `pnpm-workspace.yaml` without a `packages` list (for example one that only holds pnpm settings such as `onlyBuiltDependencies`), or a `deno.json` or `deno.jsonc` without a `workspace` field. This applies even if the project is inside a git repository.
- The dev server is reachable from the network (`nuxt dev --host`, `nuxt dev --tunnel`, a published container port, or a proxy onto the dev port). The default localhost bind limits this to local processes, which can usually read the same files directly.

For example, with `~/package-lock.json` and a project at `~/projects/app` that has no `.git` directory, `nuxt dev --host` serves `GET /_nuxt/@fs/<home>/.ssh/id_ed25519` with status 200. Any file in the home directory that is not covered by Vite's `server.fs.deny` list can be read this way, including SSH keys, cloud credentials and the Nuxt DevTools auth token in `~/.nuxt/devtools/dev-auth-token.txt`.

No browser is involved: a plain HTTP client is enough. A web page on another origin cannot read the response, and DNS rebinding is rejected by Vite's host check.

Projects whose parent directories contain none of these files are not affected, nor are projects inside a git repository whose only lockfile is their own. Nuxt 3.5.0 and later are affected.

### Patches

Fixed in `@nuxt/schema` 4.6.4, which `nuxt` 4.6.4 depends on. A parent directory now only becomes the default `workspaceDir` if it declares a w

advisories.summary: Action Pack: Possible sensitive session information leak in Active Storage proxy mode
advisories.description:
### Impact
When `ActionDispatch::Cookies` reads a signed or encrypted cookie that was written under a rotated secret (`config.action_dispatch.cookies_rotations`) or in the format that a `:hybrid` cookie serializer migrates from, it writes the cookie back to the response in the current format, and that write ignores `request.session_options[:skip]`. `ActiveStorage::DisableSession` relies on that option to keep the session cookie off the public, immutable responses of the Active Storage proxy controllers, but those controllers still load the session, so a request carrying an old-format session cookie could receive the rewritten session cookie in `Set-Cookie` on a cacheable response. A shared cache that stores such a response together with its `Set-Cookie` header could then serve one user's session to later requesters of the same URL, or serve an attacker's session to other users.

Applications are affected when they serve Active Storage files through the proxy controllers, have a cookie rotation or a `:hybrid` serializer migration configured, and run behind a cache that stores `Set-Cookie` on public responses. This is a path around the fix for [CVE-2024-26144](https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-8h22-8cf7-hq6g).

### Details
In the fixed releases, a response that skips the session leaves an old-format signed or encrypted cookie unchanged, and the next request that does not skip the session upgrades it. An application that skips the session on every request no longer upgrades its signed or encrypted cookies. Cookies that the application sets explicitly are still written. See the Action Pack CHANGELOG.

advisories.summary: Loofah allowed_uri? treats data:text/html as safe text/plain
advisories.description:
## Summary

`Loofah::HTML5::Scrub.allowed_uri?` returns `true` for a `data:` URI whose mediatype is written with the HTML5 named character reference `/` in place of the solidus. Loofah reads that mediatype as malformed and falls back to the allowed `text/plain`, while a browser decodes the reference and reads the same URI as `text/html`.

## Details

`allowed_uri?` decodes HTML entities with `CGI.unescapeHTML`, which handles numeric character references but not HTML5 named character references. `/` therefore survives normalization, so the mediatype carries no `/`, fails the MIME grammar, and falls back to the allowed `text/plain` under the WHATWG rule for a malformed mediatype.

`:`, `/`, `	` and `
` are the only named character references in the HTML5 table that decode to characters that change how a URI parses (U+003A, U+002F, U+0009 and U+000A; there is no named reference for U+000D), so this closes the set.

Loofah's default `sanitize()` path is **not** affected, because Nokogiri decodes the entity during parsing before Loofah evaluates the URI. This issue affects only callers of the public `allowed_uri?` string-level helper that pass it HTML-encoded strings.

## Impact

Applications that validate a user-controlled URL with `Loofah::HTML5::Scrub.allowed_uri?` and then render the approved value into an `href` or another browser-interpreted URI attribute may be vulnerable to cross-site scripting. `Rails::HTML::Sanitizer.allowed_uri?` re-exports the same helper.

## Mitigation

Upgrade to Loofah >= 2.25.3.

## Credit

Responsibly reported by GitHub user @ngpestelos.

advisories.summary: qbee-agent: Docker Compose build context Zip Slip writes outside context directory
advisories.description:
## Summary

`qbee-agent` contains a Zip Slip vulnerability in `app/utils/tar.go`. The tar extractor checks whether an entry remains inside the destination directory with:

```go
strings.HasPrefix(targetPath, destdirClean)
```

This does not enforce a path separator boundary. If the destination directory is `/tmp/.../context`, a tar entry such as `../context-outside/payload.txt` cleans to `/tmp/.../context-outside/payload.txt` and still passes the prefix check. qbee-agent then creates the outside directory and writes the payload outside the intended extraction root.

The issue is reachable through the Docker Compose build context path when `UseContext` is enabled.

## Details

Code references below were verified against `qbee-io/qbee-agent` commit:

- `1d8bdbb7422adb4ca563d3114cbe2817d6ba3581`

Affected repository:

- `qbee-io/qbee-agent`

Affected files:

- `app/utils/tar.go`
- Docker Compose context path in `app/configuration/bundle_docker_compose.go`

The vulnerable extraction code:

- `app/utils/tar.go:89-93`

```go
targetPath := filepath.Clean(filepath.Join(destPath, header.Name))
destdirClean := filepath.Clean(destPath)

if !strings.HasPrefix(targetPath, destdirClean) {
    return fmt.Errorf("tar entry %s is outside of destination directory %s", targetPath, destdirClean)
}
```

The file is then created at the accepted `targetPath`:

- `app/utils/tar.go:96-109`

```go
case tar.TypeDir:
    if err := os.MkdirAll(targetPath, 0755); err != nil {
        return err
    }
case tar.TypeReg:
    targetFile, err := os.Create(targetPath)
```

Docker Compose build contexts reach this extractor:

- `app/configuration/bundle_docker_compose.go:238-270`

The context archive is downloaded and then unpacked into the compose project context directory with `utils.UnpackTar`.

Archive source and role evidence:

- `app/configuration/compose.go:14` defines the Docker Compose build context as the remote configuration field `Context string`.
- `app/configuration/compose.go:26` enables this path with `UseContext`.
- `app/configuration/file_manager.go:240-246` and `app/configuration/file_manager.go:281-287` show that context sources are resolved either from `file://` local files or from the Qbee file-manager API.
- Qbee's Docker Compose documentation lists "Build Context" as a Docker Compose configuration option: https://docs.qbee.io/configuration-docker-compose.html
- Qbee's RBAC documentation separates `configuration:manage` from `files:manage`, and maps "Configure -> Modify

advisories.summary: pyLoad: Server-Side Request Forgery via Download Link Submission Enables Cloud Metadata Exfiltration
advisories.description: ## Summary PyLoad's download engine accepts arbitrary URLs without validation, enabling Server-Side Request Forgery (SSRF) attacks. An authenticated attacker can exploit this to access internal network services and exfiltrate cloud provider metadata. On DigitalOcean droplets, this exposes sensitive infrastructure data including droplet ID, network configuration, region, authentication keys, and SSH keys configured in user-data/cloud-init. ## Details The vulnerability exists in PyLoad's download package functionality (`/api/addPackage` endpoint), which directly passes user-supplied URLs to the download engine without validating the destination. The affected code in `src/pyload/webui/app/blueprints/api_blueprint.py`: ```python @bp.route("/addPackage", methods=["POST"], endpoint="add_package") @login_required def add_package(): name = flask.request.form["add_name"] links = flask.request.form["add_links"].split("\n") # ... validation omitted ... api.add_package(name, links, dest) # No URL validation ``` The download engine in `src/pyload/core/managers/download.py` accepts any URL scheme and initiates HTTP requests to arbitrary destinations, including internal network addresses and cloud metadata endpoints. ## Proof of Concept **Live Demo Instance:** http://143.244.141.81:8000 **Credentials:** `pyload` / `pyload` - Login into the pyload application - Navigate to package tab and enter the package name and fill the Link section with the following URL ``` http://169.254.169.254/metadata/v1.json ``` - Now navigate to Files section and download the link. - It was observed that we are able to Read the Digital Ocean Metadata The downloaded `v1.json` file contains sensitive cloud infrastructure data: - **Droplet ID**: Unique identifier for the instance - **Network Configuration**: Public/private IP addresses, VPC topology - **Authentication Keys**: Cloud provider auth tokens - **SSH Keys**: Public keys configured in droplet metadata - **Region and Datacenter**: Infrastructure location ## Impact **Vulnerability Type:** Server-Side Request Forgery

advisories.summary: Action Pack: Possible DoS vulnerability in Action Controller Live streaming
advisories.description:
### Impact
`ActionController::Live::Buffer#close` pushes its end-of-stream marker onto the response's bounded queue while it holds the buffer's monitor. When the client has stopped reading and the queue is full, the push blocks, and `Buffer#abort`, which runs when the client disconnects or a write times out, waits indefinitely for the same monitor. Each such response could permanently hold a web server thread and its `ActionController::Live` thread, possibly resulting in a DoS vulnerability through thread exhaustion.

Applications that stream responses with `ActionController::Live`, including `send_stream`, are affected. Applications that serve large files through Active Storage proxy mode are exposed to unauthenticated clients.

### Releases

### Credit

advisories.summary: Addressable: Denial of service in URI path normalization
advisories.description:
### Impact

`Addressable::URI.normalize_path` takes time quadratic in the number of nested dot segments in a path (e.g., `"/" + "a/" * n + "../" * n`, which for n = 3 is `/a/a/a/../../../`), because it removes one dot segment per pass over the whole path. `URI#normalize`, `URI#normalized_path`, `URI#==`, `URI#===` and `URI#join` all call it. Normalizing, comparing or joining a URI taken from user input can result in uncontrolled resource consumption, leading to denial of service. On 2.9.0, normalizing a 34 KB path takes about 3.5 seconds on MRI Ruby 4.0, and the cost grows with the square of the path length.

This affects every Ruby implementation, including MRI Ruby 3.2 and later. `URI.parse` by itself is unaffected, as is code that never normalizes, compares, or joins URIs from untrusted sources.

### Affected Versions

This vulnerability affects all versions of Addressable prior to 2.9.1. It is fixed in 2.9.1.

### Workarounds

- Limit the length of URIs taken from user input before calling `normalize`, `==` or `join` on them. Web servers often limit request lines to about 8 KB, which keeps the cost to about 150 milliseconds per call on typical hardware, but URIs from other sources (request bodies, headers such as `Location`, stored data) may not be limited.
- Reject paths with many dot segments before normalizing them.

### Credits

Reported by Matthew Mongeau (@halogenandtoast), Ruby Central Gem Security, who also suggested the single-pass approach used in the fix.

### For more information

If there are any questions or comments about this advisory:
* [Open an issue](https://github.com/sporkmonger/addressable/issues)

advisories.summary: Loofah allowed_uri? treats javascript&#x3a alert(1) as safe
advisories.description:
## Summary

`Loofah::HTML5::Scrub.allowed_uri?` returns `true` for a `javascript:` or `vbscript:` URI whose scheme is split by a numeric character reference without a trailing semicolon, followed by a character that `allowed_uri?` strips, such as a space or tab. A browser ends the reference at that character and reads `javascript&#x3a alert(1)` as `javascript: alert(1)`.

## Details

`allowed_uri?` strips control characters and whitespace before it decodes numeric character references. Removing the character that ends a semicolon-less reference lets the reference run on into the following text, so `&#x3a alert` decodes as `&#x3aa` (U+03AA) instead of a colon, and no scheme is detected. The same applies to decimal references and to references that encode a scheme letter, as in `&#x6a\tavascript:alert(1)`.

Loofah's default `sanitize()` path is **not** affected, because Nokogiri decodes the entity during parsing before Loofah evaluates the URI. This issue affects only callers of the public `allowed_uri?` string-level helper that pass it HTML-encoded strings.

## Impact

Applications that validate a user-controlled URL with `Loofah::HTML5::Scrub.allowed_uri?` and then render the approved value into an `href` or another browser-interpreted URI attribute may be vulnerable to cross-site scripting. `Rails::HTML::Sanitizer.allowed_uri?` re-exports the same helper.

## Mitigation

Upgrade to Loofah >= 2.25.3.

## Credit

Responsibly reported by GitHub user @manus-pi.

advisories.summary: pgEdge RAG Server discloses part of the configured provider credential through API error messages
advisories.description:
### Impact

An unauthenticated remote caller could read part of the operator's configured LLM provider API key.

The query API relayed the text of a provider error straight to the caller. That text carried the upstream provider's own message, and providers characteristically quote a partially masked form of the credential they rejected when authentication fails — so a failing provider call published a fragment of the operator's key. A caller who can reach the endpoint can cause such a failure and read the result.

**Who is affected:** any deployment of pgEdge RAG Server at `1.0.0` or earlier, including all alpha and beta pre-releases, whose query endpoint was reachable by an untrusted party. The endpoint carries no authentication in the affected versions.

The disclosed material authenticates to a **third-party provider account** rather than to pgEdge software, which is why the severity carries Scope: Changed.

`v1.0.0:internal/server/handlers.go:121` relayed `err.Error()` to the client when pipeline execution failed. `parseError` in
`v1.0.0:internal/llm/openai/client.go` produced that error by two routes, and both disclose:

```go
var errResp ErrorResponse
if err := json.Unmarshal(body, &errResp); err != nil {
    return fmt.Errorf("API error (status %d): %s", resp.StatusCode, string(body))
}
return fmt.Errorf("API error (status %d): %s", resp.StatusCode, errResp.Error.Message)
```

The first branch interpolates the entire unparsed response body. The second returns the provider's own message, which for OpenAI quotes the `sk-proj-` prefix and the final four characters of the submitted key.

### Patches

**Fixed in `2.0.0`. Upgrade to `2.0.0` or later.**

The fix adds `internal/safeerr` and stops provider error text reaching API clients.

**Upgrading does not undo the disclosure, and this needs action beyond upgrading. Rotate any LLM provider credential that was configured on an affected version while the endpoint was reachable by an untrusted caller**, particularly if that provider was rejecting the key at the time. A fragment already disclosed stays disclosed.

### Workarounds

Place the server behind a proxy that rewrites 5xx response bodies, or terminate provider errors before they reach the API surface. Keeping provider credentials valid, so that no authentication failure is produced, also avoids the disclosure in practice.

None of these removes the underlying defect, and none is a substitute for upgrading.

advisories.description:
## Summary

The traversal fix for CVE-2026-33344 was implemented as HTTP middleware installed only in the chi handler chain, but the MCP service calls the same API method in process, so arbitrary YAML file read is reachable again through the MCP tool surface with a viewer-role key. Read-only, limited to .yaml/.yml targets. Confirmed at HEAD f6c039f (post v2.10.7).

## The defect

The fix for CVE-2026-33344 is a reflection-based HTTP middleware (internal/frontend/.../api.go, roughly lines 553-597) that inspects a request field named FileName and rejects anything that is not a plain name. It is installed in exactly one place: the chi strict-handler chain (api.go around line 419).

The MCP service does not go through that chain. internal/service/mcp/server.go calls the API method directly as an in-process Go call:

```go
func (svc *Service) getDAGSpec(ctx context.Context, name string) (map[string]any, error) {   // line 307
    resp, err := svc.api.GetDAGSpec(ctx, daguapi.GetDAGSpecRequestObject{
        FileName: daguapi.DAGFileName(name),                                                 // line 309
    })
```

No HTTP request is constructed, so no middleware executes, and the underlying resolver is still uncontained:

```go
func (store *Storage) locateDAG(nameOrPath string) (string, error) {                 // line 1041
    if strings.Contains(nameOrPath, string(filepath.Separator)) {                    // line 1042
        foundPath, err := findDAGFile(nameOrPath)
        if err == nil {
            return foundPath, nil                                                    // line 1045, no containment check
        }
    }
```

An absolute path contains a separator, so it takes the first branch and is returned as-is, with no check that it falls under store.baseDir or any entry in store.searchPaths.

Verified end to end using the project's own conformance/mcptest harness against a real running HTTP server, not by source reading:

```
dagu_read {"target":"dag_spec","name":"/abs/outside/secret.yaml"}
-> HTTP 200, full file contents returned in data.spec
```

advisories.description:
### Summary

A non-admin user who can update their own shares can reassign a share's creator (`user_created`), `role`, `item`, and `collection` fields after the share is created. The update is authorized against the row as it existed before the change, and the resulting row is never revalidated, so these fields can be set to values the user would not be permitted to assign when creating a share. By reassigning both `user_created` and `role` to an administrator the share's effective permissions get elevated.

This is a server-side authorization gap in the share update path. It does not by itself produce an administrator token. It re-opens a previously patched privilege-escalation surface on the effective permissions of a share.

### Prerequisites

- An authenticated non-admin account that holds update permission on `directus_shares`. This is not part of the baseline app-access grant, which is read-only on a user's own shares, but it is part of the recommended defaults permission template for `directus_shares` that instances commonly apply so the share feature is usable.
- An item the account is allowed to share.
- Knowledge of an administrator user and role identifier to assign. In the reported case these were read from a relation on the shareable item using ordinary read permissions.

### Details

The recommended default permission for updating `directus_shares` selects rows where the caller is the creator and permits writes to the full field set, including the creator, role, item, and collection. The ownership filter is evaluated only against the row as it exists before the update, so an owned share passes the check. The merged row is never re-checked to decide whether the caller may assign the new values.

Two guards that are enforced when a share is created are absent on update. On create, the creator is forced to the acting user, and a share-access check is run against the target item to confirm the caller is allowed to share it. On update, the supplied creator value is stored as given and no equivalent share-access check is run against the new item or collection, so both the creator and the shared target can be repointed to values the caller was never authorized to set. The read-only marking on the creator field in the schema is a Data Studio UI hint and does not constrain writes through the API.

advisories.summary: mail-parser: Uncaught `OverflowError` / `OSError` on an out-of-range `Received` date
advisories.description:
### Impact

A `Received` header whose trailing date carries an out-of-range year, or a timezone offset
large enough to push the timestamp past the int64 epoch range, raises an exception that is
**outside the `MailParser*` hierarchy**. A caller that catches only mail-parser exceptions
does not catch it, and the parse of the entire message is aborted — the same class of issue
as [GHSA-24mq-4vc6-2prf](https://github.com/SpamScope/mail-parser/security/advisories/GHSA-24mq-4vc6-2prf),
which this survives (it is not a duplicate; 24mq is fixed in 4.6.2 and this reproduces on 4.6.2).

All entry points are affected: `parse_from_string()`, `parse_from_bytes()`, `parse_from_file()`,
`parse_from_file_obj()` and the `mail-parser` CLI. The header is fully attacker-controlled and
a single line is enough, so any pipeline that parses untrusted mail can be made to lose the
message — and, if one worker handles a queue, to drop the batch.

```python
import mailparser

raw = ("Received: from x ([1.2.3.4]) by mx.victim.com; "
       "Tue, 7 Mar 292277026596 14:29:24 +0000\r\n\r\nbody\r\n")
mailparser.parse_from_string(raw).mail_json
# <= 4.6.2 -> OverflowError: signed integer is greater than maximum
# 4.6.3    -> parses; the unusable hop date is reported as "date_utc": null
```

**Root cause.** `receiveds_format()` in `src/mailparser/utils.py` guarded the date conversion
with `except (TypeError, ValueError)`, but `convert_mail_date()` → `email.utils.mktime_tz()` →
`calendar.timegm()` raises `OverflowError` for years whose epoch seconds overflow int64, and
`datetime.fromtimestamp()` reports `EOVERFLOW` as `OSError` for a sufficiently large timezone
offset. The `date` and `timezone` properties already wrapped the same conversion in
`except Exception`; only the `Received` path was left open.

**Affected range.** Introduced by the date-handling change in `ca2aa6a`, first released in
3.7.0. Reproduced on PyPI 3.7.0, 3.8.0, 3.9.3, 4.0.0, 4.5.0, 4.6.0, 4.6.2 and on `master`
before the fix (Python 3.14). 3.6.0 is not affected.

### Patches

Fixed in **4.6.3**. `receiveds_format()` now also catches `OverflowError` and `OSError` and
records `date_utc = None` for that hop, so the rest of the message still parses:

```python
try:
    j["date_utc"], _ = convert_mail_date(i["date"])
except (TypeError, ValueError, OverflowError, OSError):
    j["date_utc"] = None
```

A sweep of year magnitudes from 10^7 to 10^12 shows only `ValueError`, `OverflowError` and
`OSError` are reachable on this pat

advisories.summary: Next.js: Information disclosure across root params when a 'use cache' function is called through unstable_cache()
advisories.description:
Next.js applications with `'use cache'` can disclose cached data across root params when the same `'use cache'` function is called both directly during rendering and through `unstable_cache()`, and that function reads a root param. Root params are route parameters of the root layout, and applications commonly use them to scope data, for example per locale.

During a cold process start, a cross-request deduplication race allowed an `unstable_cache()` call to join the in-flight fill of a concurrent direct call and receive its result, bypassing the root param check that would normally reject it. `unstable_cache()` then stored that result under a cache key without root params, so subsequent requests for other root param values received the same entry until it is revalidated or evicted. Cached data produced for one root param value is returned to requests for other values.

Exploitation requires the `unstable_cache()` request to arrive while the function's first fill after a process start is still in flight. Outside this race, the nesting already throws an error: `'use cache' inside unstable_cache() is unsupported`, and avoiding it is a complete workaround.

packages.name: next
packages.note: Next.js: Information disclosure across root params when a 'use cache' function is called through unstable_cache()

advisories.summary: Hono: `mount()` and `app.mount()` can forward a path that bypasses middleware scoped inside the mount prefix
advisories.description:
### Summary

`mount()` and `app.mount()` remove the mount prefix from the request path and forward the rest to the mounted application. Two mistakes in that step let a crafted request reach a route of the mounted application that the outer application protects with path-scoped middleware, such as an authentication check on `/app/admin/*`. The outer application routes on the original path, so the middleware does not run.

### Details

1. **Dynamic prefix** (all affected versions): for a mount such as `/api/:tenant/*`, the prefix was removed by the length of the route pattern, not of the matched prefix. A request with a longer or shorter first segment is cut in the middle, so `/api/a/xxxxx/admin/secret` reaches the mounted application as `/admin/secret`.
2. **Re-normalization** (since 4.12.21): the forwarded path was built from the decoded request path and assigned to `url.pathname`, which turns a decoded backslash into `/` and collapses `..`. `/app/public%5C..%5Cadmin/secret` reaches the mounted application as `/admin/secret`.

The fix removes the prefix segment by segment from the raw pathname, using the matched parameter values for its length. Route patterns that cannot be handled safely now throw: duplicate parameter names and a wildcard inside the last segment such as `/assets*`. A trailing slash in an `app.mount()` prefix no longer removes an extra segment.

### Impact

An unauthenticated client can reach a route of a mounted application that the outer application protects with path-scoped middleware.

This affects applications that use `mount()` or `app.mount()` and rely on middleware registered on a sub-path inside the mount prefix for authentication or authorization.

### Workarounds

Register the authentication middleware inside the mounted application.

packages.name: hono
packages.note: Hono: `mount()` and `app.mount()` can forward a path that bypasses middleware scoped inside the mount prefix

advisories.summary: Loofah: Regular expression denial of service in the SVG local-reference check
advisories.description:
## Summary

Loofah's HTML5 sanitizer restricts the `href` and `xlink:href` attributes of SVG reference elements to local references. That check matched the attribute value against `/^\s*[^#\s].*/m`. In Ruby `^` anchors to every line start and `\s` matches newlines, so an all-whitespace value made the engine rescan the value from each of its line starts, taking time quadratic in its length.

Only Ruby 3.1 and earlier are affected. Ruby 3.2 added linear-time regexp matching, which makes the pattern linear.

## Impact

An attacker who supplies HTML to be sanitized can consume CPU out of proportion to the input size, by sending an SVG reference element whose `href` or `xlink:href` is a long run of whitespace.

The default safelist allows the elements in `SVG_ALLOW_LOCAL_HREF`, so no configuration change is required.

## Mitigation

Upgrade to Loofah >= 2.25.3. Applications that cannot upgrade should run Ruby 3.2 or later, which matches the pattern in linear time.

## Credit

Reported by scyoon through the Rails HackerOne program.

packages.name: loofah
packages.note: Loofah: Regular expression denial of service in the SVG local-reference check

advisories.summary: compose-lint: File paths embedded in pull requests can inject CI workflow commands through command-line error messages
advisories.description:
### Impact

0.31.0 fixed GHSA-6f4g-xm8v-pgv6, where text from a Compose file became GitHub Actions workflow commands in compose-lint's output. The fix escapes the command openers in compose-lint's own output, but not in the argument parser's error messages. When a repository path reaches compose-lint's arguments without a `--` before it, the argument parser prints it raw in its error message. That includes a carriage return, which the runner treats as a line break, so a command can also start a new line there.

A pull request can therefore create annotations, fold or hide parts of the job log, or issue other commands the runner accepts, when CI runs compose-lint over it, before anyone reviews it. The pass/fail result is not changed.

Affected setups pass repository paths to compose-lint without a `--` before them: the pre-commit hook when `args:` is set without the documented trailing `--`, or the `compose-lint` package or Docker image called that way in a workflow. The pre-commit hook's default configuration passes `--` and is not affected. The GitHub Action turns command processing off around each compose-lint run, so it is not affected.

Found during an internal pre-1.0 security review. It was first published as part of GHSA-r7j4-crjv-h467, together with four other gaps in the same fix. Each gap now has its own advisory.

**Docker image.** `composelint/compose-lint` tag 0.31.0 and the matching minor tag are affected, as was `latest` while it pointed to 0.31.0.

Releases before 0.31.0 are covered by GHSA-6f4g-xm8v-pgv6.

### Patches

Fixed in 0.32.0. The argument parser's messages go through the same sanitizer as the rest of compose-lint's output.

### Workarounds

- Upgrade to 0.32.0 or later.
- End the pre-commit hook's `args:` with `--`, and put `--` before file paths when calling compose-lint directly.
- On GitHub Actions, use the `tmatens/compose-lint` Action, or bracket the compose-lint step with `::stop-commands::<random token>` and `::<token>::`, as the Action does.

### Reproduction

On compose-lint 0.31.0 on a GitHub-hosted runner (runner 2.337.0), `compose-lint '--##[warning]X/compose.yml'` with no `--` creates an annotation. The same path after `--` creates none. The `composelint/compose-lint:0.31.0` image produces byte-identical output to the package.

packages.name: compose-lint
packages.note: compose-lint: File paths embedded in pull requests can inject CI workflow commands through command-line error messages

advisories.summary: isomorphic-git: Circular symbolic references cause non-terminating resolution (DoS)
advisories.description:
### Summary
A malicious server can advertise circular `symref=` capabilities (e.g. `a → b` and `b → a`). isomorphic-git writes them to disk as loose symrefs, and `GitRefManager.resolve()` follows them with no depth limit and no cycle detection, so any later operation that resolves one of them (`log`, `status`, `checkout`, `branch`, …) **loops forever** — a persistent denial of service from a single clone.

### Details
`src/managers/GitRefManager.js` — `resolve()` only enforces a depth limit when a `depth` argument is passed (`depth = undefined` by default), and has no visited-set:

```js
static async resolve({ fs, gitdir, ref, depth = undefined }) {
  if (depth !== undefined) { depth--; if (depth === -1) return ref }
  …
}
```

`updateRemoteRefs` persists all server-supplied symrefs unconditionally. After clone the client has `refs/remotes/origin/a → ref: refs/remotes/origin/b` and `b → a` on disk; resolving either never terminates. Because the bad refs live on disk, the repo is effectively bricked for the application.

#### Canonical git behavior (divergence)
git caps symref resolution at `SYMREF_MAXDEPTH = 5` (refs.c): `git rev-parse a` returns immediately with `warning: ignoring dangling symref` — no recursion, no hang.

### PoC
`https://github.com/spiceoverflow/av5-circular-symref` — open in a Codespace; clone writes the circular symrefs, then `git.log` on one never returns (the runner stops it after a 20s hang):

```
[AV-5] refs/remotes/origin/a contains: ref: refs/remotes/origin/b
[AV-5] refs/remotes/origin/b contains: ref: refs/remotes/origin/a
[run] *** DoS CONFIRMED: resolving a circular symref never terminates ***
```

### Impact
A persistent denial of service via non-terminating symbolic-ref resolution (CWE-674 / CWE-835). After a single clone from a malicious (or MitM'd) server the circular refs are written to disk, so every later operation that resolves them (`log`, `status`, `checkout`, `branch`, …) hangs forever — the repository becomes effectively unusable for the application.

Impacted: any application that clones from untrusted/compromised remotes with isomorphic-git.

### Suggested fix
Add visited-set cycle detection (and/or a default maximum depth, as git does) in `GitRefManager.resolve()`; optionally validate server-supplied symref targets before persisting.

packages.name: isomorphic-git
packages.note: isomorphic-git: Circular symbolic references cause non-terminating resolution (DoS)

advisories.summary: MCP TypeScript client SDK: HTTP client transports and OAuth requests followed cross-origin redirects and re-sent custom headers and request bodies
advisories.description:
### Summary
In affected versions, the SDK's HTTP client transports and OAuth requests followed redirects to any origin.

If an MCP server or authorization server redirected a request to another origin, that origin received custom request headers (such as an `X-API-Key` set in `requestInit.headers`) and the `mcp-session-id` header. On a `307` or `308` it also received the request body, including OAuth token requests with their `refresh_token` and `client_secret`.

On current runtimes `fetch` already drops the `Authorization` header across origins.

### Am I affected?
Yes, if your application uses `StreamableHTTPClientTransport`, `SSEClientTransport`, or the SDK's OAuth client functions such as `auth()`. stdio clients are not affected.

Affected versions:

- `@modelcontextprotocol/sdk` all versions through 1.31.0
- `@modelcontextprotocol/client` 2.0.0 through 2.2.0

### Fix
Upgrade to:

- 1.x: `@modelcontextprotocol/sdk` 1.32.0 or later
- 2.x: `@modelcontextprotocol/client` 2.3.0 or later

Redirects are now followed only within the same origin, and not at all in browsers. If your MCP server or authorization server redirects to another origin on purpose, configure the final URL instead. Setting `redirectPolicy: 'follow'` on a transport restores the old behaviour and the exposure.

If a redirect may have reached a host you do not control, rotate the API keys and `client_secret` your application held and revoke its tokens.

If you cannot upgrade yet, pass a `fetch` that refuses redirects, for example `(url, init) => fetch(url, { ...init, redirect: 'error' })`.

advisories.summary: Hono: `validator('form')` skips validation for `multipart/form-data` requests with extra parameters
advisories.description:
### Summary

`validator('form')` only recognizes a `multipart/form-data` `Content-Type` that carries nothing but a single `boundary` parameter. A request with another legal parameter, such as `charset`, or with extra whitespace after the `;` is not recognized as a form. The validation callback then receives an empty object, while `c.req.parseBody()` still parses the body as a form.

### Details

The check that decides whether a request body is a form was written as a strict pattern over the whole `Content-Type` value. Any parameter list that does not look exactly like `; boundary=...` fails the check. When it fails, the middleware does not read the body and passes an empty object to the validation callback. If the callback accepts an empty object, the request proceeds to the handler, which can still read all submitted fields through `c.req.parseBody()` or `c.req.formData()`.

`application/x-www-form-urlencoded` is not affected. Only the `multipart/form-data` branch has the strict pattern.

This issue arises when an application relies on `validator('form')` to reject or restrict fields and the validation callback does not fail on an empty object.

### Impact

An unauthenticated client can send form fields that the `form` validator never sees, by adding a legal parameter to the `Content-Type` header.

This may lead to:

- Allow-list or required-field checks in the validator being skipped
- Fields the application intended to reject reaching the handler

This issue affects applications that use `validator('form')` with `multipart/form-data` requests and whose validation callback accepts an empty object.

### Workarounds

Reject an empty object in the `validator('form')` callback, or validate the result of `await c.req.parseBody()` in the handler.

packages.name: hono
packages.note: Hono: `validator('form')` skips validation for `multipart/form-data` requests with extra parameters

advisories.summary: Pillow: Memory DoS in TIFF and EXIF IFD parsing via overlapping tag data
advisories.description:
```
============================================================================
ANT-2026-D7STJUWL  [medium]  CWE-770  dos
Memory DoS in TIFF and EXIF IFD parsing via overlapping tag data
Location: src/PIL/TiffImagePlugin.py:927  in ImageFileDirectory_v2.load()
Commit:   a707c6b21c313880d0771e54965d142dd42358b6
============================================================================
```

A small, crafted image file can make Pillow use thousands of times its own size in memory while the file is only being opened, which lets anyone who can submit an image crash or stall the process handling it. A 144 KB TIFF makes `Image.open()` return normally while holding 1.6 GiB of memory. The largest such standard TIFF, about 786 KB, asks for roughly 48 GiB, which in practice gets the worker killed by the operating system. The file declares a 1×1 image, so the decompression-bomb check never triggers and no warning is raised. There is no memory corruption; the impact is denial of service.

The bug is in `ImageFileDirectory_v2.load()` in `src/PIL/TiffImagePlugin.py` (around line 927). For every directory entry whose value is stored elsewhere in the file, it reads that value into a new `bytes` object with `ImageFile._safe_read(fp, count * unit_size)` and keeps it in `_tagdata`. `_safe_read()` only checks that the bytes exist. Nothing limits the total read across entries, and nothing stops every entry from pointing at the same bytes. An attacker can therefore give each of N distinct private tags an offset and count that covers the whole file, at a cost of 12 bytes per entry. Memory grows as N × file size, which is quadratic in the file size, and BigTIFF removes the 65,535-entry ceiling.

The same loop parses EXIF data, so the problem reaches beyond TIFF:

* A 66 KB JPEG APP1 segment costs about 340 MiB inside `Image.open()` itself, via `_read_dpi_from_exif()`.
* A 96 KB PNG `eXIf` chunk costs 754 MiB on `getexif()` or `ImageOps.exif_transpose()`.
* WebP EXIF and MPO reach the same code.

The attached reproducer builds a 72 KB TIFF and a 72 KB PNG. Using only `Image.open()` and `getexif()`, each causes 412 MiB of tag data to be retained, about 6,000 times the file size. The loop dates to the original PIL 1.1.7 import, so every Pillow release since 1.0 is affected.

advisories.summary: Astro: Reflected XSS via unescaped slot names in @astrojs/solid-js
advisories.description:
## Summary The `@astrojs/solid-js` renderer wraps named slot content passed to Solid components in an `` element, and writes the slot name into its `name` attribute without HTML escaping. A slot name containing `"` could end the attribute and inject arbitrary HTML into the page. For example, a page that takes a slot name from the request: ```astro --- import Tabs from '../components/Tabs.jsx'; const tab = Astro.url.searchParams.get('tab'); ---
…
 ``` rendered with a Solid component that renders a slot by name: ```jsx export default function Tabs(props) { return
{props[props.active]}
; } ``` would output a `tab` value such as `x">` as live HTML. ## Impact Reflected cross-site scripting. An attacker who gets a user to open a crafted link can run JavaScript on the site's origin, but only in applications where all of the following are true: - The page passes request-controlled input (such as a query parameter) as a slot name. - The Solid component is hydrated with a `client:*` directive. For non-hydrated components the slot wrapper is removed from the output, together with its `name` attribute. - The Solid component renders the attacker-chosen slot, which in practice means accessing slot props by a dynamic name. Components that never render the slot only output Astro's already escaped fallback template. This is the `@astrojs/solid-js` counterpart of GHSA-8hv8-536x-4wqp (CVE-2026-50146), which fixed the same issue in `astro` core. ## Affected versions `@astrojs/solid-js` >= 0.2.0, <= 7.1.1. ## Patches Fixed in `@astrojs/solid-js` 7.1.2. Slot names are now HTML-escaped in the server renderer. ## Workarounds Upgrade to `@astrojs/solid-js` 7.1.2 or later. Before upgrading, do not use request-controlled input as a slot name, or map it to a fixed set of known slot names before passing it to a component. ## Credits Reported by @manus-pi.

packages.note: Astro: Reflected XSS via unescaped slot names in @astrojs/solid-js

advisories.summary: Excelize: Unbounded <col max> attribute is loaded with no MaxColumns check and expanded per-column by flatCols(), so any column mutator hangs or OOMs the process
advisories.description:
### Summary

The `max` attribute of a `<col>` element in `xl/worksheets/sheetN.xml` is read verbatim on open with no check against `MaxColumns`, and `flatCols()` then walks `Min..Max` doing a `deepcopy.Copy` and `append` per iteration. Executed: `max="300000"`, only about 18x past the real 16384 limit, cost 46.2 s of CPU and 122 MB on a single `SetColWidth` call, and the growth is linear in `max` up to 2^31-1.

Confirmed at `ae2113b` (HEAD at the time of audit).

### Details

`col.go:547`, `flatCols()`, with the two loops at `:549` and `:564`:

```go
for i := col.Min; i <= col.Max; i++ {
...
for i := column.Min; i <= column.Max; i++ { ... fc = append(fc, deepcopy.Copy(...)) }
```

`column.Min` and `column.Max` are plain int attributes on `xmlWorksheet.go:279-280`, bound straight from the file. `MaxColumns` is 16384 (`templates.go:176`) and nothing in the parse path compares against it.

The contrast that makes this an oversight rather than a design decision is inside the callers themselves. `SetColWidth` validates its own column argument through `parseColRange`, which clamps to `MaxColumns`. But `flatCols` iterates `ws.Cols.Col`, the file-loaded slice, so the caller's validated argument never constrains the loop. The crafted column expands no matter which column the caller touches.

The row axis has the guard this axis is missing: GHSA-h69g-9hx6-f3v4 capped `checkSheet`'s row allocation at `TotalRows`, and GHSA-q5j5-6p94-4gwc capped streaming `Rows.Next`. There is no column-axis equivalent.

Public entry points that flatten the existing columns: `SetColWidth` (`col.go:498` into `:534`), `SetColStyle` (`col.go:431` into `:477`), `SetColVisible` (`col.go:282` into `:313`), `SetColOutlineLevel` (`col.go:376` into `:407`).

### PoC

Executed in-package: crafted a real xlsx, rezipped with an injected `<cols>` block before `<sheetData>`, opened it with `OpenReader`, then called `SetColWidth`.

```xml
<cols><col min="1" max="2147483647" width="9"/></cols>
```

```go
f.SetColWidth("Sheet1", "A", "A", 12)
```

Measured:

- `max="300000"`: 46.2 s CPU, 122 MB allocated, `ws.Cols.Col` grew to 300000 entries, from one call.
- `max="5000000"`: did not complete in 110 s, killed by the test timeout.

Growth is linear in `max`. At `max=2147483647` that is roughly two billion `xlsxCol` allocations, which is hundreds of gigabytes and in practice a permanent hang ending in OOM.

advisories.summary: Astro: Image endpoint in @astrojs/node can read files from a case-variant sibling of the output directory on case-sensitive filesystems
advisories.description:
## Summary

The `/_image` endpoint used by the `@astrojs/node` adapter checks that a requested local image is inside the build output directory before reading it from disk. That check compared paths case-insensitively. On case-sensitive filesystems (such as Linux), a directory whose path differs from the output directory only by letter case is a different directory, but it passed the check.

For example, with the client output directory at `/srv/app/dist/client/`, a request such as:

```text
/_image?href=/../../DIST/client/secret.png&w=32&f=png
```

resolved to `/srv/app/DIST/client/secret.png` and was served, even though that file is outside the output directory.

## Impact

An unauthenticated attacker can read image files from outside the output directory, but only when all of the following are true:

- The site uses on-demand rendering with the `@astrojs/node` adapter.
- The server runs on a case-sensitive filesystem.
- A directory exists whose path matches the output directory except for letter case (for example `DIST/client` next to `dist/client`). Such a layout is unusual, and the attacker cannot create it.

Only files the image service accepts can be read. Raster images are returned after resizing; SVG files are returned unchanged. Other file types fail during processing. Plain path traversal outside the output directory (for example `/../../secret.png`) was already rejected and is not affected.

## Affected versions

`astro` >= 5.14.3, <= 7.4.6, when used with `@astrojs/node` (all versions up to 11.1.11). The vulnerable image endpoint is provided by `astro` and used by the `@astrojs/node` adapter.

## Patches

Fixed in `astro` 7.4.7. The path check now compares paths exactly, and only ignores letter case for Windows drive-letter paths. The fix ships in `astro`, so upgrading `@astrojs/node` alone is not enough.

## Workarounds

Upgrade to `astro` 7.4.7 or later. Before upgrading, make sure no directory next to the build output directory has a path that differs from it only by letter case.

## Credits

Reported by @zachariah-mithani.

advisories.summary: @hono/node-server: Backslash in the request path is parsed as a path separator, bypassing path-based access control at a reverse proxy
advisories.description:
### Summary

`@hono/node-server` passes the raw request-target to the WHATWG URL parser, which treats a backslash in the path as `/` and then resolves `..` segments. A request for `/admin\secret` or `/public\..\admin/secret` reaches the application as `/admin/secret`. A reverse proxy that follows RFC 3986 forwards the backslash unchanged and applies its path-based rules to the original path, so the request reaches a route the proxy is meant to block.

### Details

A raw backslash is not allowed in a request-target (RFC 3986, RFC 9112 Section 3.2.1), and RFC 9112 Section 3.2 says a recipient should reject such a request rather than correct it. Proxies such as nginx on Linux, HAProxy and Envoy keep the backslash as an ordinary character, so they and the application see different paths.

The fix responds with `400 Bad Request` to a request whose path contains a raw backslash, for HTTP/1.1, HTTP/2, absolute-form request-targets and WebSocket upgrades. A percent-encoded backslash and a backslash in the query string are still accepted.

### Impact

An unauthenticated client can reach a route that a reverse proxy, load balancer or WAF in front of the application blocks by path.

This affects applications served by `@hono/node-server` behind a front component that makes path-based decisions and forwards a backslash unchanged. Access control inside the Hono application, such as middleware on `/admin/*`, runs on the rewritten path and is not affected.

advisories.summary: Loofah: SVG `<textPath>` and `<mpath>` bypass local-reference restriction
advisories.description:
## Summary

Loofah restricts `href` and `xlink:href` on certain SVG elements to same-document references. Two elements escaped the restriction:

- `<textPath>`: `SVG_ALLOW_LOCAL_HREF` listed it in lowercase as `textpath`, but the HTML5 parser names the element `textPath` inside `<svg>`, so the check never matched on the HTML5 path.
- `<mpath>`: absent from `SVG_ALLOW_LOCAL_HREF`, so its references were never restricted on either path.

`rails-html-sanitizer` reuses this safelist in its `PermitScrubber`, so it is affected too.

## Impact

An external `href` or `xlink:href` on `<textPath>` or `<mpath>` survives sanitization. Firefox fetches the URL when rendering the content, which leaks the viewer's IP address, user agent, and referrer, and can reach hosts routable only from the viewer's network. Chrome and WebKit do not fetch external references on these elements. The impact is a network request to an attacker-chosen URL, not script execution.

Applications that sanitize user-supplied SVG, directly or inside HTML, with Loofah's default allowlist or with `rails-html-sanitizer` with SVG elements permitted are affected.

## Mitigation

Upgrade to Loofah >= 2.25.3.

advisories.summary: jackson-databind: InetSocketAddress deserialization triggers eager DNS resolution (SSRF)
advisories.description:
## Summary
`JDKFromStringDeserializer` constructed `InetSocketAddress` with `new InetSocketAddress(host, port)`, which performs eager DNS name resolution for hostname inputs at deserialization time. An application that binds untrusted JSON into a type containing an `InetSocketAddress` field issues an attacker-chosen DNS query during `readValue`, before any application-level validation or connect logic. The fix uses `InetSocketAddress.createUnresolved(host, port)`, deferring DNS to an explicit connect.

## Impact
An attacker controlling JSON deserialized into an `InetSocketAddress`-bearing type can force outbound DNS lookups for attacker-chosen hostnames at deserialization time (SSRF / DNS-based out-of-band interaction / internal-resolver probing), purely from binding.

## Affected / Patched (verified via `git tag --contains` on `1f5a103`)
- 2.18 line: `>= 2.18.0, < 2.18.8` -> fixed in **2.18.8**
- 2.19-2.21 line: `>= 2.19.0, < 2.21.4` -> fixed in **2.21.4**
- 3.x line: `>= 3.0.0, < 3.1.4` -> fixed in **3.1.4**

## Severity / CWE
Maintainer: minor. Reporter: LOW. CWE-918 (SSRF).

## Upstream fix
FasterXML/jackson-databind#5951 ("Improve InetSocketAddress deserialization"). Released 2026-06-04 in 2.18.8 / 2.21.4 / 3.1.4.

## Credits
Omkhar Arasaratnam (@omkhar) - finder.

advisories.summary: mail-parser: Uncaught exceptions and silent header loss in mail-parser on attacker-controlled input
advisories.description:
### Impact

Two effects, sharing the root cause of Advisory 1 — header names chosen by the sender were
resolved through Python attribute lookup and rewritten before lookup.

**Uncaught exceptions.** A crafted message raises an exception that is *outside* the
`MailParser*` hierarchy, so a caller catching only mail-parser exceptions does not catch it
and the worker dies.

*Header named after a method* (CWE-248, reported by @iam-niranjan). Python resolves real
class attributes before `__getattr__`, so a header named after a method put a bound method
object into the parsed mail dict. A 12-byte email is sufficient. Nine colliding names were
confirmed: `Parse`, `Message`, `Write_Attachments`, `From_File`, `From_File_Obj`,
`From_File_Msg`, `From_String`, `From_Bytes`, `Get_Server_Ipaddress`. Also reproducible from
the CLI (`mail-parser -f evil.eml -j`).

```python
import mailparser
mailparser.parse_from_string("Parse: x\r\n\r\n").mail_json
# 4.6.1 -> TypeError: Object of type method is not JSON serializable
# 4.6.2 -> {"parse": "x", "has_defects": false}
```

*Header carrying 8-bit bytes* (CWE-248). For a header containing raw 8-bit bytes, Python's
`compat32` policy returns an `email.header.Header` rather than a `str`, which the `_raw`
accessor passed straight to `json.dumps`. This fires on entirely benign non-ASCII mail via
`parse_from_bytes()`, the normal entry point for mail off the wire.

```python
import mailparser
mailparser.parse_from_bytes(b"Subject: caf\xe9\r\n\r\nbody\r\n").subject_raw
# 4.6.1 -> TypeError: Object of type Header is not JSON serializable
# 4.6.2 -> '["caf�"]'
```

**Silent loss of message content** (CWE-436). A sender can make a header's value vanish from
every output surface, or be replaced by a different header's value, with `has_defects`
remaining `false`. This is an evasion primitive: the tool's output diverges from the bytes
actually in the message, and a pipeline scanning parsed output for indicators sees nothing
and no failure signal.

Header names were normalised before lookup — underscores folded to dashes, and `_json` /
`_raw` suffixes interpreted — so a header genuinely named `Subject_json` was reported with
the value of `Subject` and its own value discarded, and any header whose name contains an
underscore resolved to nothing.

```python
import mailparser

raw = ("From: Real Sender <real@good.example>\r\n"
       "Subject: innocuous\r\n"
       "Subject_json: MALWARE-C2 http://evil.example/payload.exe\r\n"
       "X_Spam_Flag

advisories.summary: OpenTelemetry JavaScript: Insertion of Sensitive Information into Log File and Exposure of Sensitive Information to an Unauthorized Actor in @opentelemetry/instrumentation-http
advisories.description:
### Summary

`@opentelemetry/instrumentation-http` redacts sensitive URL query parameters on **outgoing (client) spans** but not on **incoming (server) spans**. The server-span path writes the raw query string verbatim into the `url.query` attribute, so credentials embedded in inbound request URLs — AWS presigned-URL signatures, Azure SAS tokens (`sig`), GCS signed-URL signatures — are exported in plaintext to the configured tracing backend.

Configuring the `redactedQueryParams` option **does not change this**, as this applies only to outgoing (client) spans.

### Impact

**Information disclosure / credential leakage** (CWE-200; CWE-532, insertion of sensitive information into telemetry data).

**Who is impacted:** any Node.js service instrumented with `@opentelemetry/instrumentation-http` — directly or transitively via `@opentelemetry/auto-instrumentations-node` — that receives inbound requests carrying credentials in the query string. Common cases: services fronting presigned S3/GCS downloads, Azure SAS-token URLs, and signature-authenticated webhooks.

**Consequence:** clients' still-valid credentials are written into server spans and stored by the tracing backend, readable by anyone with span-read access — observability vendor infrastructure, dashboard users, and internal audiences far broader than the credential's intended scope. Presigned-URL signatures typically remain valid for minutes to days after capture, so this is not merely historical exposure.

**Severity:** Moderate. Exploitation requires read access to the telemetry backend, and inbound URLs must actually carry signed credentials. However, the gap is a documented mitigation that silently fails to apply, which defeats the mitigation operators would reach for.

### Patches

This vulnerability has been patched in `@opentelemetry/instrumentation-http` version `0.222.0`.
Known sensitive query string values (as defined by Semantic Conventions) are redacted by default from span data for incoming spans.
The `redactedQueryParamsServer` configuration option was added for customization.

advisories.summary: Eclipse hawkBit DDI has Privilege Escalation that allows Tenant-Isolated Firmware Exfiltration
advisories.description:
## **Description**
A privilege escalation vulnerability has been identified in the Direct Device Integration (DDI) Controller of **Eclipse hawkBit** (versions 1.0.3 and prior).

This vulnerability allows an authenticated device to escalate its permissions and bypass the strict boundaries of its assigned updates. Under normal operation, a device should be restricted **strictly to the specific firmware artifacts explicitly assigned to it**. However, this flaw enables any authenticated device to bypass this restriction and download any firmware artifact **within the same tenant**.

This is **not** an authentication bypass; the requesting device must possess valid credentials for its respective tenant. Instead, the issue stems from a flaw in object-level authorization validation.

A related, lower-severity helper issue exists in the listing software modules artifacts metadata endpoint. This endpoint does not enforce assignment checks, enabling an authenticated device to list and enumerate available firmware artifacts, which can facilitate targeted exfiltration using the main download authorization bypass.

---

## **Impact**
* **Severity:** Moderate
* **Scope:** Tenant-isolated. An attacker must be an authenticated device within the target tenant to exploit this vulnerability.
* **Confidentiality Impact:** **Low**. While firmware binaries can be retrieved, the impact is mitigated because access is restricted strictly to the scope of the pre-authenticated tenant, and no administrative or cross-tenant data is exposed. Additionally, production firmware binaries are by design not expected to contain highly sensitive or confidential data (such as hardcoded credentials or private keys), further supporting the Low confidentiality rating.

---

## **Affected Products and Versions**
* **Product:** `eclipse-hawkbit/hawkbit`
* **Affected Component:** `hawkbit-ddi/hawkbit-ddi-resource`, as well as the compiled binaries and Docker images that contain this component.
* **Affected Versions:** `1.0.3` and prior versions.
* **Patched Version:** `1.0.4`

---

## **Remediation**
Upgrade to version **1.0.4** or later. 

**Fix details:** The download authorization logic has been corrected to ensure that assignment-based verification is executed on every artifact download request. Additionally, the software module metadata endpoint has been updated to enforce proper authorization, restricting access exclusively to software modules and artifacts that are explicitly assigned to or al

advisories.summary: Hono: RegExpRouter skips wildcard middleware for some route sets and for paths with an encoded line terminator
advisories.description:
### Summary

RegExpRouter, which the default `SmartRouter` selects for most applications, skipped wildcard middleware in three cases, so a route handler ran without the middleware registered for it:

1. Middleware whose parameter is written with the explicit default pattern, such as `/api/:tenant{[^/]+}/admin/*`, was not applied to a route written as `/api/:tenant/admin/:id`. (since 4.13.0)
2. Middleware on `/admin/*` was not applied to a route registered on `/admin*` for paths under `/admin/`. (since 4.1.4)
3. For a path with an encoded line terminator (`%0A`, `%0D`, `%E2%80%A8`, `%E2%80%A9`), no wildcard pattern matched, so the request reached the not-found handler without any wildcard middleware. (since 4.4.0)

TrieRouter, LinearRouter and PatternRouter apply the middleware in all three cases.

### Details

RegExpRouter decides at registration time which wildcard middleware covers which route. In cases 1 and 2 it treated patterns that match the same requests as different ones. In case 3 the compiled wildcard did not match line terminators.

The fix derives the coverage from the structure of the registered paths and lets wildcards match line terminators. It also corrects other differences from the other routers (a wildcard in the middle of a path with parameters, duplicate middleware, middleware on static routes), and rejects custom patterns that can match the empty string, such as `{[0-9]*}`, with `UnsupportedPathError`. `PreparedRegExpRouter` data must be regenerated.

### Impact

An unauthenticated client can reach a route handler, or the not-found handler, without the authentication or authorization middleware registered on a wildcard path.

This affects applications that use RegExpRouter, directly or through the default `SmartRouter`, and rely on wildcard middleware for authentication or authorization.

### Workarounds

Use `new Hono({ router: new TrieRouter() })`.

advisories.summary: Nuxt Content: Unauthenticated SQLite Function DoS via Content Query API
advisories.description:
### Summary

The `POST /__nuxt_content/:collection/query` endpoint in `@nuxt/content` accepts an attacker-controlled `sql` field from the HTTP request body and executes it against a local SQLite database after passing it through an insufficient validator (`assertSafeQuery`). The validator only blocks a small set of SQL command keywords and does not reject expensive SQLite built-in functions such as `randomblob()`, `zeroblob()`, `hex()`, or `length()`. An unauthenticated remote attacker can craft a single request that forces SQLite to allocate hundreds of megabytes of memory and perform CPU-intensive work, causing server-wide denial of service. This endpoint is enabled by default for every collection and requires no authentication.

The vulnerability spans three source files:

**Route registration — `src/module.ts:207-208`**

The Nuxt Content module registers a public HTTP POST handler for each configured collection at startup:

```ts
// src/module.ts:207-208
addServerHandler({
  route: `/__nuxt_content/${collection.name}/query`,
  handler: resolver.resolve('./runtime/api/query.post'),
})
```

No authentication middleware is attached; the route is reachable by any client.

**Source (attacker input) — `src/runtime/api/query.post.ts:7-9`**

```ts
// src/runtime/api/query.post.ts
const { sql } = await readBody(event)          // line 8  — attacker-controlled

return loadDatabaseAdapter(conf).all(sql)      // line 18 — raw sql passed to sink

  if (noString.match(SQL_COMMANDS)) {          // /SELECT|INSERT|UPDATE|DELETE|DROP|ALTER|\$/i
    throw new Error('Invalid query: WHERE clause contains unsafe SQL commands')
  }
  // No rejection of function calls (randomblob, zeroblob, hex, length, …)
}

```ts

  return db.prepare(sql).all(...params)        // executes the unmodified attacker sql
}
```

advisories.summary: Moleculer: Unauthenticated Denial of Service via negative length field in the TCP transporter packet parser
advisories.description:
### Summary

The TCP transporter's packet parser (`src/transporters/tcp/parser.js`) reads the packet length field with `Buffer.prototype.readInt32BE`, a signed read. A crafted packet whose length field has the sign bit set yields a negative `length`. The parser then advances past the parsed message with `packet = packet.slice(length)`, but `Buffer.prototype.slice` clamps an out-of-range negative start index to `0`, so the buffer is returned unchanged. The `while (packet.length > 0)` loop condition therefore never becomes false, producing an infinite synchronous loop that blocks the Node.js event loop indefinitely.

### Impact

Any Moleculer node using the TCP transporter can be rendered completely unresponsive by an unauthenticated remote peer sending a single ~10-byte crafted TCP packet, before any protocol handshake or authentication takes place. `TcpReader.onTcpClientConnected` pipes each accepted socket's bytes straight into a fresh `Parser` instance (`socket.pipe(parser)`) with no handshake, so the code path is reachable by any peer able to reach the transporter's listening port. Because Node.js is single-threaded, the hang blocks the entire event loop of the process, taking down every service hosted in it until it is forcibly restarted. TCP transporter endpoints are frequently auto-discovered via UDP broadcast, so any host on the same network segment can reach the port.

Neither the CRC check nor `maxPacketSize` mitigate the issue: the CRC bytes are fully attacker-computable, and `maxPacketSize` bounds the received buffer size, not the value of the length field.

### Affected component

`Parser._write` in `src/transporters/tcp/parser.js`.

### Patch

The fix validates that the decoded length is at least the 6-byte header size before processing, rejecting negative and undersized values (which would otherwise fail to shrink the buffer) with an error on the write callback instead of looping.

### Credit

Reported by xor4xor via the Tidelift security program.

advisories.description:
### Summary

The URL validation regex `^(https?:/)?/.*` added to emissary's `NavAction.java` allows protocol-relative URLs (`//evil.com/...`) and single-slash scheme variants (`http:/evil.com`) to bypass validation, enabling SSRF and open redirect attacks.

### Affected Package

- **Ecosystem:** Maven
- **Package:** NationalSecurityAgency/emissary
- **Affected versions:** < e2078417464b
- **Patched versions:** >= e2078417464b

### Severity

Medium

### CWE

CWE-918 — Server-Side Request Forgery (SSRF)

### Details

The fix in `NavAction.java` (line 47) introduces a `VALID_LINK` pattern:

```java
Pattern.compile("^(https?:/)?/.*")
```

This regex is intended to restrict navigation links to relative paths and HTTP/HTTPS URLs. However, it has multiple bypass vectors.

Protocol-relative URLs (`//evil.com/...`): The group `(https?:/)?` is optional, so the pattern reduces to `//.*` when the group is absent. This matches `//evil.com/steal?c=SESSION`, which browsers resolve to the current page's protocol plus the attacker's host.

Single-slash scheme (`http:/evil.com`): The regex group captures `http:/` as a valid match, and browsers normalize `http:/evil.com` to `http://evil.com`, creating an open redirect to the attacker's server.

Protocol-relative to cloud metadata (`//169.254.169.254/...`): This enables SSRF to cloud instance metadata endpoints, which is particularly dangerous in AWS/GCP environments where IAM credentials can be retrieved.

The pre-fix code had no validation at all, accepting any URL. The fix blocks `javascript:`, `ftp:`, and `data:` URIs, but the protocol-relative and single-slash bypasses remain exploitable.

advisories.summary: mail-parser: One hostile attachment aborts `write_attachments()` and silently drops the rest of the batch
advisories.description:
### Impact

`write_attachments()` called `_safe_attachment_filename()` and `write_sample()` inside its loop
with no guard, so a single crafted attachment raised out of the whole save. Every attachment
**after** the malicious one was silently never written, with no error surfaced to a caller that
catches only `MailParserError`.

That is an evasion primitive as much as an availability bug: a sender puts one poisoned part
first and the real payload second, and the payload never reaches the extraction directory that
a downstream scanner or sandbox reads — while it still reaches the recipient's mail client
intact. The tool's output diverges from the bytes actually in the message, which is the same
failure mode as the filename-sanitizing bypass in
[GHSA-fr3h-cpq2-9496](https://github.com/SpamScope/mail-parser/security/advisories/GHSA-fr3h-cpq2-9496).

Three shapes were reachable, all from attacker-controlled MIME metadata:

- **NUL smuggled through RFC 2231** — `filename*=us-ascii''evil%00.bin` decodes to a NUL in the
  filename during parsing and raised `ValueError` out of the name check;
- **overlong basename** — a filename longer than `NAME_MAX` (e.g. 300 characters) raised
  `OSError: File name too long` from `open()`, *after* creating a zero-byte stub on disk;
- **undecodable payload** — a body that is not valid base64 raised `binascii.Error` (a
  `ValueError` subclass) from the decode performed inside the `open()` block.

```python
import tempfile, mailparser

raw = ("Content-Type: multipart/mixed; boundary=b\r\n\r\n"
       "--b\r\nContent-Type: application/octet-stream\r\n"
       "Content-Disposition: attachment; filename*=us-ascii''evil%00.bin\r\n\r\nxx\r\n"
       "--b\r\nContent-Type: application/octet-stream\r\n"
       "Content-Disposition: attachment; filename=good.bin\r\n\r\nyy\r\n"
       "--b--\r\n")

mp = mailparser.parse_from_string(raw)     # parse itself is fine; safe_filename is None
mp.write_attachments(tempfile.mkdtemp())
# 4.6.0 - 4.6.2 -> ValueError, and good.bin is never written
# 4.6.3         -> logs "Skipped attachment with invalid filename: 'evil\x00.bin'";
#                  good.bin is written
```

`parse()` itself was never affected — it catches the `ValueError` — so only the write path was
unguarded. The reject-paths that made this reachable were introduced with the filename
sanitizing in 4.6.0 (PR #165).

### Patches

Fixed in **4.6.3**. `write_attachments()` now logs and skips a single unusable attachment
instead of aborting

advisories.summary: ag-psd can exhaust memory when parsing crafted PSD dimensions
advisories.description:
### Summary
readPsd() commits the image/layer buffers from the declared header geometry (width x height x channels x depth, and per-layer rectangles) before validating those values against the actual data. A tiny crafted PSD declaring huge geometry forces a multi-gigabyte allocation.

### Impact
On ag-psd 30.2.0, Node 24, a 52-byte PSD makes readPsd(buf) commit ~3.17 GB (measured peak RSS) in ~0.45 s before throwing a catchable RangeError ("Offset is outside the bounds of the DataView") — about 61,000,000x amplification. Because the buffer is committed before validation, the allocation OOM-kills the process before the error on essentially any host (uncatchable), and concurrent requests exhaust memory. Any service reading untrusted PSDs with ag-psd is exposed to a remote DoS.

This is distinct from #39 and #206, which involve genuinely large PSDs (memory proportional to real data). Here the input is 52 bytes: the file declares enormous geometry that is never present, so the allocation is driven by an unvalidated header field, not by actual content, an uncontrolled-allocation denial-of-service vulnerability, not proportional memory use.

### Steps to reproduce
The PoC is a 52-byte PSD (sha256 a1146a6fabdfef289472f99a56851249e7a46e8d19d4d8bf85fe833e2f0158b6). Reconstruct with:

    base64 -d > poc.psd <<'EOF'
    OEJQUwABAAAAAAAAAA0AADcuAAA58wAgAAMAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAdEgNZv+i9bc9ygd2A==
    EOF

Then (commits ~3.17 GB before throwing a catchable RangeError):

    const { readPsd } = require('ag-psd');
    const buf = require('fs').readFileSync('poc.psd');
    readPsd(buf.buffer.slice(buf.byteOffset, buf.byteOffset + buf.byteLength));

### Root cause
psdReader.js sizes the off-heap typed-array buffers from the declared header dimensions (and per-layer rectangles, a second independent lever) before validating against the available bytes.

### Suggested fix
Validate the declared dimensions, channel count, depth, and per-layer rectangles against the actual input length (and a sane maximum) before allocating.
