advisories.summary: Action View: Possible XSS vulnerability in highlight helper
advisories.description:
### Impact
`ActionView::Helpers::TextHelper#highlight` substitutes each matched phrase into the `:highlighter` string without escaping it and returns the result marked HTML-safe. Because sanitizing leaves quote characters in text unescaped, a match substituted into a quoted attribute value of the highlighter, such as the `<a href="search?q=\1">` form shown in the method's documentation, could end the attribute value and add attributes to the element, possibly leading to XSS. Applications are affected when they pass a `:highlighter` that places a placeholder inside an attribute value and highlight text or phrases that a user controls. The default `<mark>\1</mark>` highlighter and the block form are not affected.

### Details
The fixed releases HTML-escape each group substituted into the `:highlighter` string, so quotes in a match are rendered as `"` and `'`. Only the numbered placeholders `\0` to `\9` are expanded; other `String#sub` replacement escapes, such as `\k<name>`, `\&` and `\\`, are left as written. A match can no longer begin on the `>` that closes a preceding tag. Escaping makes a placeholder safe as element content or inside a quoted attribute value, but not in an unquoted attribute value, a URL, JavaScript or CSS context, or an attribute whose value is HTML. See the Action View CHANGELOG for details.

### Workarounds
Use a `:highlighter` that places the matched phrase only in element content, such as the default `<mark>\1</mark>`.

### Releases
The fixed releases are available at the normal locations.

Patches for those who cannot upgrade at once:
- 8.1: https://github.com/rails/rails/commit/06938194b4fd59e1d2c8ab4a781f3c1e2b763425.patch
- 8.0: https://github.com/rails/rails/commit/c796f6198837479ada13290eb8fa767b5219a58a.patch

### Credit
This issue was found by the Anthropic OSS Scanner (ANT-2026-THHUJQVO).

advisories.summary: Action View: Possible XSS vulnerability in text helpers
advisories.description:
### Impact
With the HTML5 sanitizer (`Rails::HTML5::Sanitizer`, the default vendor on CRuby for applications using `load_defaults 7.1` or later), Nokogiri before 1.19.5 serializes `<` and `>` unescaped inside attribute values. ### Details
The fixed releases require rails-html-sanitizer 1.7.2 or later, which requires Loofah 2.25.3 and Nokogiri 1.19.5. advisories.summary: Mongoose: Discriminator key values matching inherited properties (e.g. __t: 'constructor') bypass schema casting and can poison collections
advisories.description:
### Summary

Mongoose chooses which discriminator model or schema to use by looking up the discriminator key value (`__t` by default) in a plain object of registered discriminators, for example `Model.discriminators[doc.__t]`. That value comes from user documents and query filters. Because the lookup did not check own properties, a value that names a property inherited from `Object.prototype` resolves to that inherited value instead of a discriminator. Examples are `'constructor'`, `'toString'` and `'hasOwnProperty'`.

- `__t: 'constructor'` resolves to the global `Object` function. Mongoose then calls `new Object(doc)`, which returns the raw user object where a Mongoose document is expected.
- `__t: 'toString'` and similar names resolve to built-in functions that throw when used as a constructor or schema.

The most serious effect: through `bulkWrite()` `insertOne` with `skipValidation: true`, the raw user object is stored as-is, without schema casting or `strict` filtering. After that, every query that returns the stored document throws, until the document is removed from the database.

### Details

The registries that hold discriminators are plain objects: `Model.discriminators`, `schema.discriminators`, and the embedded discriminator registries on document arrays and single nested subdocuments. Several code paths indexed them directly with a value taken from the document or filter:

| Code path | Input |
|---|---|
| Model constructor (`new Model(doc)`) | document |
| `Model.create()`, `insertMany()`, `bulkWrite()`, `bulkSave()` | documents |
| Hydrating query results (`find()`, `findOne()`, etc.) and `Model.hydrate()` | stored documents |
| Casting query filters, including flat paths such as `'events.__t'` and `$elemMatch` | query filter |
| Casting updates and array filters | update filter, `arrayFilters` |
| Document array `push()` / `create()`, document array and single nested casting | subdocuments |
| Populate on embedded discriminators | stored subdocuments |

`getDiscriminatorByValue()` already iterated the registry's own keys safely. But most callers tried the direct lookup first and only fell back to it afterwards, so a truthy inherited value took precedence.

The lookups only read inherited properties. They do not write to `Object.prototype` or any other shared object, and they do not change in-memory state that affects other requests. This is NOT a prototype pollution vector.

advisories.summary: Muhammara has a NULL pointer dereference in LZWDecode filter when DecodeParms omits EarlyChange key
advisories.description:
## Summary

A NULL pointer dereference vulnerability exists in `PDFParser::CreateFilterForStream()` when processing a PDF stream with `/Filter /LZWDecode` and a `/DecodeParms` dictionary that does not contain the `EarlyChange` key. This causes an access violation (0xC0000005) and crashes the process.

## Affected Version

muhammara <= 6.0.4 (latest)

## Vulnerability Details

**File:** `src/deps/PDFWriter/PDFParser.cpp` line 2107

```cpp
if (inDecodeParams)
{
    PDFObjectCastPtr<PDFInteger> earlyObj(
        QueryDictionaryObject(inDecodeParams, "EarlyChange")
    );
    early = earlyObj->GetValue();  // NULL dereference when EarlyChange key is absent
}
```

When `inDecodeParams` is non-NULL but lacks the `EarlyChange` key:
1. `QueryDictionaryObject()` returns NULL
2. `PDFObjectCastPtr<PDFInteger>(NULL)` wraps NULL
3. `earlyObj->GetValue()` dereferences NULL → crash

## PoC

460-byte malicious PDF triggers crash via `startReadingFromStream()`:

- PDF contains `/Filter /LZWDecode` with `/DecodeParms << >>` (empty, no EarlyChange)
- Exit code: `0xC0000005` (Access Violation)

## Fix

```cpp
if (earlyObj)
    early = earlyObj->GetValue();
```

## Impact

Any application accepting untrusted PDFs and using muhammara to read stream contents is vulnerable to DoS.

Similar to: CVE-2022-41957, CVE-2022-39381

## PoC File
[poc_muhammara_lzw_null.js](https://github.com/user-attachments/files/27186113/poc_muhammara_lzw_null.js)

## Summary

File Browser v2.63.15 can leave a public directory share behind when the shared directory is deleted through a path with a trailing slash. The share cleanup path calls `DeleteWithPathPrefix(file.Path, userID)`, but the Bolt backend performs the database prefix query with the unnormalized argument before trimming the slash for boundary checks. For a stored share at `/a`, deleting `/a/` queries for paths prefixed by `/a/`, so the exact `/a` share is never loaded and never deleted.

If a directory with the same path is later recreated, the stale public share becomes active again and exposes the new directory contents through the old public URL.

## Impact

An authenticated user with share, download, and delete permissions can create a valid public share, delete the shared path with a trailing slash, and leave the public link in storage. The link is dormant while the path does not exist, but it exposes future content if the same path is recreated later. The final data exposure is unauthenticated through the public share URL.

This bypasses the intended lifecycle cleanup around public shares and is adjacent to the recent public-share path-existence and prefix-boundary fixes.

advisories.summary: Astro: XSS via attribute injection in dynamic tag names
advisories.description: ## Summary When a dynamic tag (`const Tag = ...; `) resolves to a string, Astro renders it as a raw HTML element name. The name was filtered to remove characters that could inject attributes, but the filter did not handle `/`. Because HTML parsers treat `/` inside a tag as an attribute separator, a tag name such as `img/src/onerror=alert(1)` was rendered as an `` element with an `onerror` attribute. The JSX renderer used for MDX did not filter string tag names at all. For example: ```astro --- const Tag = Astro.url.searchParams.get('as') ?? 'div'; --- hello ``` rendered `?as=img/src/onerror=alert(1)` as live HTML. ## Impact Reflected or stored cross-site scripting, but only in applications that use untrusted input (such as a request parameter or an uncontrolled CMS field) as all or part of an element name. Astro itself never derives element names from request data. Applications that let content choose an element should map that input to a fixed set of known tags. Letting untrusted input choose an element name is unsafe even with a correct filter, because it can still select elements such as `script` or `iframe`. ## Affected versions `astro` <= 7.4.4. ## Patches Fixed in `astro` 7.4.5. String tag names in `.astro` dynamic tags, JSX, and MDX now render only the leading valid element name, so characters such as `/` or `=` can no longer change the generated markup. Strings that do not start with a valid element name now throw an error. ## Workarounds Upgrade to `astro` 7.4.5 or later. Before upgrading, do not use untrusted input as an element name, or map it to a fixed set of known tags. ## Credits Reported by @uttej-badwane.

advisories.summary: zip: Critical Parser Differential & Security Control Bypass via Dual-Header Inconsistencies (Zip Cloaking) Leading to Arbitrary File Overwrite & RCE
advisories.description:
## Summary
A critical architectural parser differential exists in the `zip` crate (`<= 9.0.4`) between random-access archive readers (`ZipArchive`) and streaming readers (`ZipStreamReader`). `ZipArchive` considers the Central Directory File Header (CDFH) authoritative and ignores the filename declared in the Local File Header (LFH). In contrast, `ZipStreamReader` relies exclusively on the Local File Header (LFH) when extracting files to the filesystem.

This discrepancy enables ZIP archives to appear to have different file paths and contents according to which tool is reading them.

---

## Details

### Architectural Root Cause
In the PKWARE ZIP archive format, every file entry is defined in two distinct locations:
1. **Local File Header (LFH):** Precedes the compressed payload of each file in the body of the archive.
2. **Central Directory File Header (CDFH):** Stored in a contiguous index at the end of the archive.

In `zip2`:
- `src/read/zip_archive.rs`: `ZipArchive` parses the central directory into `SharedBuilder.files`. All file lookups by index or name read exclusively from the CDFH table, completely ignoring the filename present in the LFH.
- `src/read/stream.rs:L86-L141`: `ZipStreamReader::visit` and `ZipStreamReader::extract` read sequentially from the stream without verifying the central directory index. Each entry is parsed via `read_zipfile_from_stream` and written to disk using the unverified filename declared in the LFH:
  ```rust
  // src/read/stream.rs
  fn visit_file<R: Read>(&mut self, file: &mut ZipFile<'_, R>) -> ZipResult<()> {
      file.safe_prepare_path(&self.outpath, &mut outpath, None::<&(_, fn(&Path) -> bool)>)?;
      let mut outfile = fs::File::create(&outpath)?;
      io::copy(file, &mut outfile)?;
      Ok(())
  }
  ```
- `src/write.rs:L1552`: The crate explicitly exposes `shallow_copy_file`, an API that constructs dual-header desynchronizations by adding a new CDFH entry with an alias name pointing to an existing file without updating the original LFH.

### Threat Scenario & Severity Justification (10.0 / 9.9 Critical)
1. **Security Control Evasion:** An adversary crafts a ZIP archive where:
   - Central Directory Header declares: `doc_report.pdf` (Clean document)
   - Local File Header declares: `cron_worker.sh` (Malicious root backdoor)
2. The archive is uploaded through a web portal or API endpoint protected by security gateways (WAF, Anti-Virus, Content Disarm & Reconstruction). The security gateway inspects the archive

advisories.summary: Nuxt exposes the message and data of unhandled errors thrown during server rendering
advisories.description:
### Summary

When a page, plugin or route middleware throws an error that is not an HTTP error, Nuxt wraps it with `createError` before rendering the error page. The wrapped error was treated as one the app raised deliberately, so in production its `message` and `data` were sent to the client in the error page payload (`__NUXT_DATA__`) and in JSON error responses. For a failed `$fetch`, that is the URL that was requested (including its query string) and the body of the upstream error response.

### Impact

An application is affected if server-rendered code lets an error with sensitive details reach the error page, for example:

```vue
<script setup lang="ts">
const route = useRoute()
// the upstream error body, and the token in the URL, reach the client if this request fails
await $fetch(`http://users.internal/users/${route.params.id}?token=${useRuntimeConfig().usersToken}`)
</script>
```

Anyone who can make the request fail (for example by requesting an id the upstream service rejects) receives `[GET] "http://users.internal/users/1?token=...": 502` and the upstream response body. This happens regardless of what a custom `error.vue` renders, because the details are part of the payload. With the default configuration, the HTTP status line is not affected.

The same applies to any other error thrown during server rendering, such as a database driver error whose message names an internal host.

Errors created deliberately with `createError` (or `showError`) are not affected: their `message` and `data` are meant for the client. Errors returned by `useFetch` and `useAsyncData` are also unchanged, as they are part of the payload by design. Server routes (`server/api`) are not affected.

### Patches

Fixed in `nuxt@4.6.4`. Nuxt now marks any thrown value that is not already an HTTP error as `unhandled`, so the error page and JSON responses receive its status and a generic message. As a result, the error page no longer shows the message of an error thrown with `throw new Error(...)` in production; throw a `createError` with what the client may see instead.

Nuxt 3 has reached end of life and will not receive a fix. Upgrade to Nuxt 4, or apply the workaround below.

Catch errors from server-side requests and rethrow them with only the details the client may see:

```ts
try {
  await $fetch(url)
} catch (error) {
  throw createError({ statusCode: 502, statusMessage: 'Upstream request failed' })
}
```

advisories.summary: sqlite3-ruby: Possible SQL query truncation when a string is 4 GiB or larger
advisories.description:
### Summary

sqlite3-ruby cast Ruby string lengths (`long`) to `int` before passing them to SQLite. On 64-bit platforms, a string of 4 GiB (2^32 bytes) or larger had its length wrap, so SQLite saw only the first `length mod 2^32` bytes. An attacker who controls the length of a SQL string could truncate the query, for example dropping a trailing `WHERE` clause. The affected paths are:

- the SQL passed to `Database#prepare`, `#execute`, and related methods
- String and Blob values passed to `Statement#bind_param` and related methods
- String and Blob values returned from SQL functions and aggregates defined in Ruby (`Database#create_function`, `#create_aggregate`, and related methods)

sqlite3 v2.10.2 raises `RangeError` when any of these strings is longer than `INT_MAX` bytes.

### Severity

The sqlite3-ruby maintainers have evaluated this as medium severity (CVSS 4.8). Exploitation requires an attacker to get at least 4 GiB into a single SQL string or bound value. Most deployments reject a request body that large before the application sees it, and the server must hold several copies of the string in memory.

A truncated bound value is only a prefix of the attacker's input, so the bind paths matter only where the application validated the full value. A truncated SQL string is more serious: when the attacker's input is inlined into the SQL, the clauses that follow it are dropped. If a dropped clause contained a bind placeholder, binding raises `SQLite3::RangeException` instead of running the query.

### Mitigation

Upgrade to sqlite3 v2.10.2 or later.

As a workaround for earlier versions, reject SQL strings and bound values of 4 GiB or larger before passing them to sqlite3-ruby, or limit request body size well below 4 GiB.

### Credit

This issue was responsibly reported by Luke Jahnke from elttam.

## Summary

The Soup Sieve CSS selector parser recurses once per level of nested pseudo-class selector (`:is()`, `:not()`, `:where()`, `:has()`) without any limit on nesting depth. An unauthenticated attacker who can supply a CSS selector string to `soupsieve.compile()`, `soupsieve.select()`, or Beautiful Soup's `soup.select()` / `soup.select_one()` can force the parser to exceed Python's recursion limit with a small crafted input (about 1.6 KB, roughly 330 nesting levels), raising an uncontrolled `RecursionError`. Because this exception is not part of the parser's documented error contract, applications that catch only `ValueError` or `SelectorSyntaxError` see an unexpected failure of the request or task that parsed the selector.

## Root Cause

The parser dispatches each opening pseudo-class token to `parse_pseudo_open`, which calls back into `parse_selectors` to parse the pseudo-class body. Every nesting level therefore adds Python stack frames, and no counter, depth guard, or `RecursionError` handler bounds this descent. The token-count guard `SELECTOR_LIMIT = 8192` (added for the earlier comma-separated-list memory issue) counts parsed tokens, not recursion depth; at the failing nesting depth the token count is only about 330, roughly four percent of that limit, so the guard never fires. The security invariant that untrusted selector input must not be able to exhaust interpreter resources is not enforced for nesting depth.

```text
soupsieve/css_parser.py
  CSSParser.parse_pseudo_open (line 985): sel.selectors.append(self.parse_selectors(iselector, index, flags))
  CSSParser.parse_selectors  (line 1137): recursive target; dispatches pseudo-class tokens back into parse_pseudo_class -> parse_pseudo_open
  CSSParser.increment_count  (lines 707-712): SELECTOR_LIMIT token guard; increments once per nesting level, cannot bound depth
```

## Impact

Any application that compiles or evaluates untrusted CSS selectors through Soup Sieve (directly or via Beautiful Soup) is affected. No authentication, privilege, or user interaction is required; the failure occurs during selector parsing, before any document is matched. A single crafted selector of about 1.6 KB reliably raises `RecursionError`. The demonstrated capability is a transient denial of the individual request, task, or invocation that parsed the malicious selector: the exception propagates uncaught unless the caller handles `RecursionError` (or a broad `except Exception`). advisories.summary: Kubeflow Pipelines: RBAC bypass on shared pipelines allows any authenticated user to delete or modify global pipelines
advisories.description:
## Summary

In multi-user mode, the Kubeflow Pipelines API server skipped authorization checks for shared/global pipelines with an empty namespace. This exception applied to write and delete operations as well as reads, allowing an authenticated user to modify or delete shared pipelines without the required Kubernetes RBAC permissions.

## Impact

Unauthorized modification compromises the integrity of shared pipeline definitions and versions. Unauthorized deletion can make shared pipelines unavailable.

Execution of a modified pipeline can cause attacker-controlled workload behavior, but this is a conditional downstream consequence requiring the modified pipeline to be executed. Modification alone does not demonstrate immediate worker code execution.

Reading shared pipelines is intentionally permitted and remains permitted after the fix. Consequently, access to shared pipeline configuration does not establish an additional confidentiality impact from this write-authorization defect. The confidentiality metric is None; the integrity and availability metrics reflect unauthorized modification and deletion of shared pipelines.

The affected authorization boundary is shared pipelines in multi-user deployments. Single-user deployments intentionally bypass these multi-user authorization checks.

## Patches

Fixed by [kubeflow/pipelines#13288](https://github.com/kubeflow/pipelines/pull/13288), with the fix included in 2.16.1.

Read-only operations on shared pipelines remain allowed. For write and delete operations, the API server checks Kubernetes RBAC permissions against the KFP system namespace, because shared pipelines have no namespace of their own.

## Scope of this fix

The 2.16.1 fix addresses the shared-pipeline authorization paths described above. It does not fix every shared-pipeline write path: the separate shared-pipeline upload authorization defect is tracked in [GHSA-rjr3-43j3-4q8g / CVE-2026-77596](https://github.com/kubeflow/pipelines/security/advisories/GHSA-rjr3-43j3-4q8g). Consult that advisory for its affected versions and remediation; 2.16.1 must not be interpreted as fixing that separate upload defect.

## Workarounds

Until upgrading, restrict access to the Pipelines API to trusted users through deployment-level access controls. Namespace RBAC alone does not correct the affected shared-pipeline authorization path.

## Summary

The CVE-2026-32885 ZipSlip fix added a symlink-target escape check to Untar, but the check rebases an ABSOLUTE symlink target into dest before validating (filepath.Join(dest, "/etc") stays lexically inside dest and passes), while the symlink is then created with the RAW absolute target via os.Symlink(file.Linkname, ...), so a malicious archive plants a host-absolute symlink and a following regular-file entry writes through it, restoring arbitrary host file create/overwrite (reaching $HOME rc-files, hence RCE). Confirmed at HEAD.

## The defect (the symlink check is a no-op for absolute targets)

CVE-2026-32885 (fixed v1.25.2, commit 05cbe299) added a lexical containment check on the entry path and a NEW symlink-target validation. pkg/archive/archive.go, Untar, tar.TypeSymlink case:

```go
if filepath.IsAbs(file.Linkname) {
    resolvedTarget = filepath.Join(dest, file.Linkname)   // line 298: absolute target REBASED into dest
} else {
    resolvedTarget = filepath.Join(fullPathDir, file.Linkname)
}
if !strings.HasPrefix(filepath.Clean(resolvedTarget)+sep, filepath.Clean(dest)+sep) {  // line 302
    return ...escapes destination...                       // line 303
}
_ = os.Remove(fullPath)                                     // line 307
err = os.Symlink(file.Linkname, fullPath)                  // line 310: writes the RAW Linkname
```

For an absolute Linkname like /Users/victim, line 298 computes filepath.Join(dest, "/Users/victim") = dest/Users/victim (lexically inside dest), so the escape check at line 302 PASSES. But line 310 creates the symlink with the raw file.Linkname, so the on-disk symlink dest/link points at the real host path /Users/victim. The value validated (rebased) is not the value written (raw): a check-one-thing / do-another divergence.

Write-through: the archive carries a second regular-file entry whose Name traverses the planted link (e.g. link/.zshrc). Its fullPath is lexically inside dest so the line-238 check passes (that check is purely lexical and does not resolve the symlink), then os.Create follows the planted symlink and overwrites /Users/victim/.zshrc on the host. Overwriting a shell rc-file, git hook, or cron entry yields code execution. Reachable via ddev add-on get <repo|url> (the exact remote-add-on vector the advisory names), and via ddev import-db / import-files. GitHub codeload tarballs preserve symlinks.

## Verification

EXECUTED (go test driving the real Untar): a file was written OUTSIDE dest and Untar

advisories.summary: Forge: TLS client crash on a handshake record received without a session
advisories.description:
### Summary
A `forge.tls` client throws an uncaught `TypeError` from `connection.process()` when it receives a ServerHello while it has no session: after a `close_notify` alert or a call to `close()`, or before `handshake()` is called. A malicious server or an on-path attacker can use this to terminate a Node.js process. Fixed in node-forge 1.4.3.

### Details
`tls.handleHandshake()` in `lib/tls.js` updates the handshake digests with `c.session.md5.update(bytes)` before it calls the message handler. A client creates its session in `handshake()`, and `c.reset()` sets it to `null` when the connection is closed. Closing doesn't set the fail flag, and the client goes back to expecting a ServerHello, so a Handshake record received afterwards still reaches `handleHandshake()`, which throws `TypeError: Cannot read properties of null (reading 'md5')`.

This happens:
- after the server sends a `close_notify` alert (at any alert level);
- after the application calls `close()`;
- before the application calls `handshake()`.

The exception propagates out of `connection.process()`. Applications that pass socket data to `process()` from a `data` event handler without catching exceptions, as in the README example, terminate. After a reset the connection uses no encryption, so an on-path attacker can inject the records even when the real server is honest.

Servers are not affected: a server creates its session when it receives a ClientHello.

The fix handles these records like other unexpected records on a closed client: they are ignored.

#### Patches
Fixed in node-forge 1.4.3.

#### Workarounds
Catch exceptions thrown by `connection.process()` and close the socket, or stop passing socket data to `process()` once the `closed` callback has been called and until `handshake()` is called again.

#### Resources
- RFC 5246, section 7.2.1 (Closure Alerts): https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc5246#section-7.2.1
- Related: GHSA-525v-9gp9-w22h (another TLS client `TypeError`, fixed in 1.4.1): https://github.com/digitalbazaar/forge/security/advisories/GHSA-525v-9gp9-w22h

#### Severity
CVSS 3.1: CVSS:3.1/AV:N/AC:H/PR:N/UI:N/S:U/C:N/I:N/A:H (5.9, Moderate)
CVSS 4.0 (informational): CVSS:4.0/AV:N/AC:L/AT:P/PR:N/UI:N/VC:N/VI:N/VA:H/SC:N/SI:N/SA:N (8.2)
CVSS 4.0 has no counterpart to 3.1's AC:H beyond AT:P and scores this higher; the severity rating follows CVSS 3.1.

#### Credits
Reported by @manus-use.

### Proof of concept
    var c = forge.tls.createConnection({server: false, ...});

advisories.summary: minimatch has potential denial of service via globparts amplification
advisories.description:
minimatch 10.2.6 contains an attacker-controlled pattern amplification in firstPhasePreProcess() when optimizationLevel >= 2.

researcher: Reid Downing (b1nv0id)
files: 

- src/index.ts: 690-770
- src/index.ts: 780-796

issue:
input-controlled growth of globParts during first-phase preprocessing, followed by quadratic second-phase processing.

the **/../ transformation clones a globparts entry and appends the clone to the same globparts array:
```
parts.splice(gs, 1)
const other = parts.slice(0)
other[gs] = '**'
globParts.push(other)
```
this occurs inside a do...while (didSomething) fixpoint loop, allowing generated entries to be processed again.

the expanded globparts array is subsequently processed by secondPhasePreProcess(), which performs pairwise comparisons:
```
for (let i = 0; i < globParts.length - 1; i++) {
  for (let j = i + 1; j < globParts.length; j++) {
    this.partsMatch(...)
  }
}
```
an attacker who can supply a glob pattern can therefore cause additional pattern entries to be generated during preprocessing, followed by quadratic pairwise processing, resulting in excessive cpu and memory consumption.

advisories.summary: pympp allows excessive sponsored transaction fees through padded calldata
advisories.description:
### Details
When the server acts as the fee_payer, `pympp` 0.8.0 validates calldata using `eth_abi` decoding, which is lenient about trailing bytes. The `FeePayerPolicy` caps `gas_limit` (≤ 2 M) and `max_fee_per_gas` (≤ 100 Gwei) but does **not** check calldata length.

Tempo uses legacy calldata gas pricing: **16 gas per non-zero byte**. Appending `N` bytes of `0x01` padding inflates actual gas used by `N × 16` while keeping `gas_limit` and `max_fee_per_gas` within policy caps. The server cosigns and broadcasts the padded transaction, draining its fee-payer wallet.

**Vulnerable code path:** `FeePayerPolicy` in `fee_payer_policy.py` (pympp 0.8.0) enforces `maxGas = 2_000_000` and `maxFeePerGas = 100 Gwei` but has no `calldata.length` bound. The policy check passes because the inflated gas comes from intrinsic calldata cost, not the declared `gas_limit`.

**Note:** In our experiment, we enforce an 16 KB `max_header_length`, which caps the maximum effective padding at roughly 5,500 bytes. The default padding in this PoC (5,500 bytes) is within that limit.

### PoC
The PoC is provided below. It is configured to reproduce the attack on Tempo Moderate testnet within a Docker environment. Download the PoC and run:
```bash
unzip pympp_python_PoC.zip
cd pympp_python
docker build -t pympp-padding .
docker run --rm pympp-padding
``` 
There are more details in `pympp_python/README.md`

### Impact
In our experiment, a malicious client can force the server to pay ~**5x** the normal transaction fee. This dramatically increases operational costs and completely destroys the profit margin on low-cost items.

Please provide a way to share the PoC in .zip format to you. Thank you!

advisories.summary: NLTK: BllipParser passes caller-supplied model paths to the bllipparser C extension with no pathsec check, enabling arbitrary read
advisories.description:
## Summary

`BllipParser` in `nltk/parse/bllip.py` hands caller-supplied filesystem paths to the native `bllipparser` C extension without routing them through NLTK's `pathsec` validation. The constructor parameters `parser_model`, `reranker_features`, and `reranker_weights`, and the alternative `from_unified_model_dir()` entry point, flow directly to the C extension's `load_parser_model()` and `load_reranker_model()` calls, which open and read the given path at the OS level. Any application that passes an attacker-influenced path to this API reads a file of the attacker's choosing from anywhere on the filesystem, outside the NLTK data roots that every other NLTK tool wrapper confines access to.

## Root Cause

As of NLTK 3.10.0, `SECURITY.md` documents a centralized I/O security module (`nltk.pathsec`) with strict enforcement enabled by default, under which file-backed resources must resolve inside allowed NLTK data directories. For paths handed to external tools and native extensions that open files themselves, the module provides `validate_tool_path()`, which runs name-safety checks, rejects option-shaped, URL-shaped, and traversal inputs, opens the path with `O_NOFOLLOW` requiring a regular single-linked file, and returns the validated string the caller must use. Every sibling tool wrapper applies it. `BllipParser` applies none of it: the module imports only `ParserI`, `safe_print`, and `Tree`, with zero `pathsec` references, so the three model-path parameters reach the C extension unchecked. The violated invariant is that NLTK tool wrappers must bound caller-supplied native-tool paths to the data roots before the native code opens them.

```text
nltk/parse/bllip.py:125-131   BllipParser.__init__ accepts parser_model,
                              reranker_features, reranker_weights (no validation)
nltk/parse/bllip.py:164       self.rrp.load_parser_model(parser_model, ...)   -> C extension open
nltk/parse/bllip.py:166-170   self.rrp.load_reranker_model(features_filename=...,
                              weights_filename=...)                          -> C extension open
nltk/parse/bllip.py:218-255   from_unified_model_dir(model_dir) -> __init__ (no validation)
nltk/parse/bllip.py:9-11      imports: ParserI, safe_print, Tree (no pathsec import)
```

## Impact

An application that uses `BllipParser` (requiring the optional `bllipparser` package to be installed) and that passes a model path derived from untrusted input to the constructor or to `from_unifie

advisories.summary: Addressable URI normalization resolves some dotted path segments to the wrong path
advisories.description:
### Summary

`Addressable::URI.normalize_path` resolves some paths containing `..` segments to a different path than RFC 3986 does. When a path climbs above the root before any other `..` is resolved, the segments that later `..` segments should remove are instead kept: `/../../public/x/../../secret` normalizes to `/public/x/secret` instead of `/secret`. `URI#normalize`, `URI#join`, `URI#==` and `URI#===` all use this normalization. An application that checks a normalized Addressable path against an allowlist, but sends the original URI to something that resolves it according to RFC 3986, can be made to allow a request for a path outside the allowlist.

### Details

`normalize_path` in 2.9.0 (`lib/addressable/uri.rb`) removes dot segments by repeating a set of rewrites until nothing changes. On each pass it finds the first `/segment/../` pair with `RULE_2B_2C`, then replaces every textual copy of that pair in the path with `/`:

```ruby
pair = normalized_path.match(RULE_2B_2C)
...
regexp = "/#{Regexp.escape(parent.to_s)}/\\.\\./|"
regexp += "(/#{Regexp.escape(current.to_s)}/\\.\\.$)"
...
mod ||= normalized_path.gsub!(Regexp.new(regexp), SLASH)
```

When the first pair found is `/../../`, where the "segment" is itself `..`, every `/../../` in the path is replaced with `/`. That includes copies later in the path, where each `..` should have removed the segment before it. For `/../../public/x/../../secret`:

- RFC 3986 §5.2.4 drops the two leading `..` segments, which can't go above the root, then removes `x` and `public`, giving `/secret`.
- 2.9.0 replaces both copies of `/../../` with `/` in one step, giving `/public/x/secret`.

Paths where an ordinary `/segment/../` pair comes first, such as `/a/../../b/c/../../d`, are resolved correctly.

This was introduced in 2.2.5. Versions 2.0.0 through 2.2.4 and earlier versions resolve these paths correctly. It is fixed in 2.9.1, which replaces the rewrite loop with a single pass that correctly follows RFC 3986 §5.2.4.

### Proof of concept

```ruby
require "addressable/uri"
require "uri"

url = "http://example.com/../../public/x/../../secret"

# Addressable's normalized path, compared with RFC 3986 resolution by Ruby's URI library
puts Addressable::URI.parse(url).normalize.path
puts URI.join("http://example.com/", "../../public/x/../../secret").path

# join and == use the same normalization
puts Addressable::URI.join("http://example.com/", "../../public/x/../../secret").path
puts Addressable::URI.parse(url) == Addr

advisories.summary: Loofah: CSS url() sanitization bypass via escaped parentheses
advisories.description:
## Summary

`Loofah::HTML5::Scrub.scrub_css` rejected any property whose top-level Crass tokens included a `:url` or `:bad_url`, and left `url` out of the allowed CSS functions. Both checks ran only against the first parse of the `style` attribute. When `scrub_css` rebuilt each property it emitted identifiers with their CSS escapes decoded, so parentheses written as escapes — `url\28 …\29` — hid the `url` token from the checks, and the rebuilt value was re-parsed into a live `url()` that nothing checked again. An escaped property name, six-digit escapes, escaped comments and escaped quotes all reached the same place.

## Impact

A sanitized `style` attribute could make a viewer's browser issue a request to an attacker-chosen URL. `list-style` fetches on render with no interaction, `cursor` on hover. That leaks the viewer's IP address, user agent and access timing, and can reach hosts routable only from the viewer's network. No script survives sanitization and the attacker cannot read the response, so the request itself is the whole impact.

Applications that sanitize user-supplied HTML with Loofah's default allowlist and display it to other people are affected.

## Mitigation

Upgrade to Loofah >= 2.25.3.

## Credit

Reported by NotAFlightRisk through GitHub's private vulnerability reporting.

advisories.summary: pgEdge Go LLM Library discloses provider API key fragments in error messages
advisories.description:
### Impact

An unauthenticated caller could read part of the operator's configured LLM provider API key.

The library's own health handler pings every configured provider using the operator's real credential and returns the resulting error text verbatim. Providers characteristically quote a partially masked form of the credential they rejected, so a failing ping published a fragment of
the key.

**The endpoint is unauthenticated by default.** `authorize()` returns
true immediately when the consuming application sets no `Authorize` hook,
so `GET /v1/health` is reachable by anyone who can reach the listening
port unless the consumer opted in to authentication.

**Who is affected:** any application embedding pgedge-go-llm-lib at
`0.1.0` or `0.1.1` that exposes the bundled HTTP proxy without setting an
`Authorize` hook. Both affected versions are released tags and resolve
through the public Go module proxy.

The disclosed material authenticates to a **third-party provider
account** rather than to pgEdge software, which is why the severity
carries Scope: Changed.

Evidence at `v0.1.1`: `llm/proxy/handlers.go:296` (`handleHealth`
returning `err.Error()` in `ProviderHealth.Error`), `llm/proxy/proxy.go:247`
(`authorize()` defaulting to permit), and `llm/proxy/proxy.go:350`
(`writeError` writing the error with no redaction).

### Patches

**Fixed in `0.2.0`. Upgrade to `0.2.0` or later**, which redacts
credentials from provider error messages unconditionally. The fix adds
`llm/internal/redact`, with a follow-up anchoring word boundaries, and is
pinned by tests in that package.

**Note the version.** There is no `0.1.2` — it was never cut, and some
earlier material named it in error. `0.2.0` is the first fixed release.

**Upgrading does not undo a disclosure that already happened. Rotate any
LLM provider credential configured on an affected version** where the
proxy was reachable without an `Authorize` hook, particularly if a
provider was rejecting that key at the time.

### Workarounds

Set an `Authorize` hook on the proxy, which closes the unauthenticated
route to the health endpoint. Restricting network access to the listening
port limits who can reach it. Neither removes the underlying disclosure
for a caller who does reach the endpoint.

advisories.summary: isomorphic-git: Path traversal via a ".." tree-entry name writes files outside the working directory on clone/checkout
advisories.description:
### Summary
isomorphic-git's tree parser (`src/models/GitTree.js`) validates each entry name only against the path separators `/` and `\`. It does not reject the standalone reserved name `..`, so a malicious repository can, on a single `clone`/`checkout`, **write files outside the working
directory** (unbounded depth). Works on any host-backed `fs` provider.

### Details
The guard is:

```js
// src/models/GitTree.js
if (path.includes('\\') || path.includes('/')) {
  throw new UnsafeFilepathError(path)
}
```

The standalone string `..` passes. isomorphic-git assembles the full path incrementally across tree levels, so nesting `..` trees yields `../escaped.txt`, `../../escaped.txt`, … with unbounded depth (each level is a separate tree object that passes the per-entry guard). On checkout `mkdir(workdir/..)` hits `EEXIST` (ignored) and the file is written above the working directory. Depth is chosen to reach the home dir, `/etc`, `/tmp`, etc.; overwriting a shell rc / config / startup file can escalate to code execution.

#### Canonical git behavior (divergence)
git rejects this via `verify_path()`: `git read-tree` fails with `error: invalid path '../escaped.txt'` and `git fsck` flags `warning … hasDotdot: contains '..'`. (git's `verify_path` also rejects `.` and `.git`, the latter flagged by fsck as `hasDotgit` — see the fix note below.) GitHub runs fsck on push, so such a tree can't be hosted there; reach is limited to a self-hosted/Smart-HTTP remote or a MitM.


### PoC
`https://github.com/spiceoverflow/av2-dotdot-traversal` — open in a Codespace; a single `git.clone()` from the bundled server writes `escaped.txt` one directory above the clone target (`DEPTH=N` escapes N levels):

```
[AV-2] *** PATH TRAVERSAL CONFIRMED ***
[AV-2] File written outside workdir: …/escaped.txt
```

### Impact
A path-traversal arbitrary file write outside the working directory (CWE-22), triggered by a single clone/checkout; it can escalate to code execution by overwriting shell rc, config, or startup files.

Any application or user that clones/checks out an untrusted (or compromised / MitM'd) repository with isomorphic-git on a host-backed filesystem (**Linux, macOS, or Windows** — no symlink or privilege required). Requires a non-GitHub remote (self-hosted / Smart-HTTP) or a MitM, since GitHub's fsck rejects trees containing `..`.

### Suggested fix
In the tree parser, reject any entry name equal to `.` or `..`. For full `verify_path` parity it should **also** reject `.git` (

advisories.summary: Zebra Vulnerable to Consensus Divergence in Transparent Sighash Hash-Type Handling
advisories.description:
# CVE-2026-41583: Consensus Divergence in Transparent Sighash Hash-Type Handling

## Summary

After a refactoring, Zebra failed to validate a consensus rule that restricted the possible values of sighash hash types for V5 transactions which were enabled in the NU5 network upgrade. Zebra nodes could thus accept and eventually mine a block that would be considered invalid by zcashd nodes, creating a consensus split between Zebra and zcashd nodes.

In a similar vein, for V4 transactions, Zebra mistakenly used the "canonical" hash type when computing the sighash while zcashd (correctly per the spec) uses the raw value, which could also crate a consensus split.

## Severity

**Critical** - This is a Consensus Vulnerability that could allow a malicious party to induce network partitioning, service disruption, and potential double-spend attacks against affected nodes.

Note that the impact is currently alleviated by the fact that currently most miners run `zcashd`.

## Affected Versions

All Zebra versions prior to version 4.3.1. (Some older versions are not impacted but are no longer supported by the network.)

## Description

Verification of transparent transactions inherits the Bitcoin Script verification code in C++. Since it is consensus-critical, this code was called from Zebra through foreign function interface (FFI). That interface was clunky because it required parsing the whole transaction in C++ code, which would then pull Rust libraries which could get in conflict with Zebra code. A refactoring was done so that only the verification itself was done in C++, and the rest done by Rust code, using a callback. However, in this refactoring, it was not noticed that a particular consensus rule - only accepting known hash types in transparent transaction signatures - was being enforced in C++ code and thus had to be enforced by the Rust caller.

An attacker could exploit this by:

- Submitting a V4 or V5 transaction with an invalid hash type
- The V5 transaction would be accepted by Zebra nodes but not by `zcashd` nodes (and vice-versa for V4), creating a consensus split in the network.

## Impact

**Consensus Failure**

- **Attack Vector:** Network.
- **Effect:** Network partition/consensus split.
- **Scope:** Any Zebra affected Zebra node

## Fixed Versions

This issue is fixed in Zebra 4.3.1.

The fix adds the consensus check in the caller of the C++ verification code. It also uses the raw hash type for V4 sighash computations.

## Mitigation

advisories.summary: Active Storage: Possible local file disclosure in video previews and analysis
advisories.description:
### Impact
Active Storage's `VideoPreviewer`, `VideoAnalyzer` and `AudioAnalyzer` run `ffmpeg` and `ffprobe` on a blob's contents without restricting the input format, so FFmpeg selects a demuxer by probing the file. A blob created through a direct upload keeps the content type the client declared, so a client can store an HLS playlist under a `video/*` or `audio/*` type. When that blob is previewed or analyzed, the `hls` demuxer opens the `file://` segments that the playlist names, and the preview image or the stored metadata could disclose a local media file that the application process can read and whose path the attacker knows.

Applications that accept uploads from untrusted users and generate video previews, or analyze video or audio attachments with FFmpeg, are affected.

### Details
The fixed releases limit the formats FFmpeg may open to common audio and video containers, configured by the new `config.active_storage.ffmpeg_allowed_formats` setting. Files in other formats no longer preview or receive media metadata; the Active Storage CHANGELOG names some of them and shows how to add a format to the list.

### Workarounds

advisories.summary: Kubeflow Pipelines: Reflected XSS in the frontend pod information and events error responses
advisories.description:
## Summary

The Kubeflow Pipelines frontend reflected untrusted pod names and namespaces into HTML error responses from the pod-information and pod-events routes. An attacker could craft a link that causes JavaScript to execute in the frontend's origin when a user follows it and reaches an affected error response.

Affected routes include `/pipeline/k8s/pod` and `/pipeline/k8s/pod/events` (the deployment's configured base path may differ).

## Impact and prerequisites

Successful exploitation requires a victim to open an attacker-supplied link and reach the vulnerable response. JavaScript execution may expose information accessible to the victim's browser or perform actions in the application's origin.

The attacker does not need an account merely to construct and deliver the link. The victim must satisfy the deployment's authentication and route-access requirements. Cookie theft depends on cookie attributes and deployment protections; it is not guaranteed. The submitted evidence does not establish an availability impact or server-side code execution.

## Technical details

The pod handlers pass `podname` and `podnamespace` query values to `getPod` and `listPodEvents` in `frontend/server/k8s-helper.ts`. Before remediation, failure messages incorporated those values, along with backend error details, and were returned as HTML-capable string responses.

Kubernetes rejecting an invalid resource name did not prevent the issue: the rejected name could still be included in the frontend's error response.

[PR #12295](https://github.com/kubeflow/pipelines/pull/12295) changed the error construction to validate pod names and namespaces with `isAllowedResourceName`. Invalid values produce a constant error message instead of reflecting the supplied value, and backend error details are no longer included in these responses. The change includes invalid-resource-name tests.

## Affected versions and remediation

Affected product: the Kubeflow Pipelines frontend server, identified as `ghcr.io/kubeflow/kfp-frontend`. Historical releases may use earlier image registry names.

Upgrade to **KFP 2.15.0 or later**.

advisories.summary: termux-sync: Arbitrary file write during restore via attacker-controlled manifest source path
advisories.description:
termux-sync restore trusts fields inside an untrusted backup manifest and uses them as the extraction destination without validation.

During restore, each archive entry is handled as:

  src_dir = Path(info.get("source", ...)).parent
  extract_archive(archive, src_dir, ...)

extract_archive opens the archive and runs tarfile.extract for every member with no path jail and no filter:

  with tarfile.open(archive_path, "r:*") as tf:
      for member in tf.getmembers():
          tf.extract(member, dest_path, set_attrs=True)

There is no check that manifest "source" stays under an expected restore root, that tar members stay inside dest_path, or that backup_name used in temporary paths cannot contain ".." or separators.

Impact:
A victim who restores a malicious backup (local, shared, or from a compromised GitHub/Google Drive storage backend) can have arbitrary files written anywhere the Termux user can write. Overwriting shell startup files or executable scripts leads to local code execution on later use.

Reproduction (benign markers only):

1. Build a backup directory with home.tar.gz (members: proof filename + optional config names) and manifest.json.
2. Set files.home.source to any path whose parent is the desired write directory (e.g. $HOME/dummy_for_parent so parent is $HOME).
3. Run the same extract path the tool uses: src_dir = Path(source).parent; tarfile.extract each member into src_dir.
4. Observe attacker-controlled files created under $HOME and under other chosen roots (config / shell-rc style overwrite).

Expected: restore only writes under fixed, validated roots; reject unsafe source values and members that resolve outside dest.
Actual: write destination is fully controlled by manifest.source; proof files and overwrites appear outside any intended jail.

Fix direction:
- Do not trust manifest "source" for extract roots; use fixed app-defined destinations
- Sanitize backup_name (basename; reject ".." and separators)
- Extract with tarfile filter="data" (or equivalent boundary checks) and refuse escape
- Treat backups as untrusted input

Actual result (local marker-only reproduction):

PROOF path: /data/data/com.termux/files/home/PWNED_BY_TERMUX_SYNC_RESTORE.txt
PROOF exists? True
PROOF content:
PWNED
This file was written by a malicious termux-sync backup restore path.
Root cause: manifest files.*.source controls extract destination.

*** VULN CONFIRMED: arbitrary write to $HOME ***

important.conf => secret=ATTACKER_CONTROLLED
*** VULN CONFIRM

advisories.summary: Nuxt: Incomplete fix for GHSA-6gq8-jgmh-3ffp: an encoded slash (`%2F`) in the request path bypasses route rules on catch-all page routes
advisories.description:
### Summary

Nuxt matches route rules against the request path with encoded slashes (`%2F`) left encoded, while the page router decodes them into route params. A request that spells a slash as `%2F` can therefore render a page through a catch-all route without the route rules configured for the path it resolves to. The fix for [GHSA-6gq8-jgmh-3ffp](https://github.com/nuxt/nuxt/security/advisories/GHSA-6gq8-jgmh-3ffp) deliberately left reserved escapes such as `%2F` encoded, so it did not cover this form.

### Impact

An unauthenticated attacker can bypass route rules that protect paths served by a catch-all page route, or by a custom route whose param can span several segments.

```ts
export default defineNuxtConfig({
  routeRules: {
    '/docs/internal/**': { appMiddleware: 'auth', headers: { 'X-Frame-Options': 'DENY' } },
    '/admin/**': { redirect: '/login' },
  },
})
```

With `app/pages/docs/[...slug].vue`, `/docs/internal/guide` runs `auth`, but `/docs/internal%2Fguide` renders the same page without running `auth` and without the header. With a root `app/pages/[...slug].vue`, `/admin%2Fsecret` is rendered instead of redirected.

The rules skipped include server-side `redirect`, `headers`, `proxy`, `ssr` and `noScripts`, and `appMiddleware`, `appLayout` and `redirect` as matched in the app during server rendering and client navigation. `getRouteRules` returns the same incomplete result.

Whether the page then shows protected content depends on how it reads the route:

- With a route such as `definePageMeta({ path: '/docs/:path(.*)' })`, `route.params.path` is `internal/guide` for both requests.
- With a repeatable catch-all (`[...slug].vue`), `route.params.slug` is `['internal/guide']` instead of `['internal', 'guide']`, so a page that joins the segments (`slug.join('/')`) to load content loads the protected resource.
- `route.path` keeps the encoding (`/docs/internal%2Fguide`), so a page that loads content by `route.path` does not resolve it.

Not affected:

- Static page routes and params that match a single segment. `/docs%2Finternal` does not match `app/pages/docs/internal.vue`.
- API handlers in `server/api` and `server/routes`. As far as we can tell, Nitro matches these against the same path as its route rules, so a handler and the rules for it agree.

Browsers send `%2F` in a path as written, so a plain link is enough to reach the page.

### Patches

Fixed in `nuxt@4.6.4`, together with `@nuxt/nitro-server@4.6.4` and `@nuxt/vite-server@4.6.4`,

advisories.summary: Action View: Possible XSS vulnerability in strip_tags
advisories.description:
### Impact
`strip_tags` in Action View returns its sanitized output marked `html_safe`, but the underlying sanitizer encodes only `&`, `<` and `>`, leaving `"` and `'` unencoded. Because ERB does not escape a string marked `html_safe`, untrusted input passed through `strip_tags` and rendered inside a quoted HTML attribute value could close the attribute and add new attributes, possibly leading to XSS. Applications that render `strip_tags` output from untrusted input inside an HTML attribute, for example in a `title` attribute or a `<meta content>` tag, are affected. Output rendered as element content is not affected.

### Details
`strip_tags` now encodes `"` and `'` in its output, as well as `&`, `<` and `>`, without double-encoding existing entities. Applications that use `strip_tags` output outside HTML, such as in a text template or JSON, now see `"` and `'` where they saw `"` and `'`; `CGI.unescapeHTML` decodes them. See the Action View CHANGELOG.

### Workarounds
Pass `strip_tags` output to an attribute through a tag helper, which escapes attribute values, for example `tag.a(title: strip_tags(user_input))`.

### Releases
The fixed releases are available at the normal locations.

Patches for those who cannot upgrade at once:
- 8.1: https://github.com/rails/rails/commit/568b19cb860322885593e308a7f27aceb779e9d7.patch
- 8.0: https://github.com/rails/rails/commit/c3772a10f405f9644125cbb484adfd2aa7a25a59.patch

advisories.summary: Addressable display_uri can show misleading hosts with invalid Punycode A-labels
advisories.description:
### Impact

`Addressable::IDNA.to_unicode`, in the pure-Ruby IDNA implementation, decodes Punycode labels (labels beginning with `xn--`) that are not valid A-labels. Those labels are returned in decoded form, when they should be returned unchanged. That includes:

- labels that decode to only ASCII characters, e.g. `xn--google-` decodes to `google`;
- labels that decode to text that doesn't convert back to the same label (RFC 3490 §4.2), e.g. text that isn't in normalized form.

`Addressable::URI#display_uri` uses `to_unicode`, so for `https://xn--google-.example.org/` it displays the host `google.example.org`, while `#host`, `#normalized_host` and any connection made from the URI use `xn--google-.example.org`. An attacker who controls a domain can therefore have a URI displayed as a host they don't control. Applications that compare the result of `to_unicode` against a list of trusted names can likewise treat two different hosts as the same.

The native IDNA implementation, used when libidn and the `idn-ruby` gem are installed, is not affected. `to_ascii` and `normalized_host` are not affected.

### Affected Versions

This vulnerability affects Addressable >= 2.0.0, the first version with the pure-Ruby IDNA implementation, when that implementation is in use. It is fixed in 2.9.1, where such labels are returned unchanged, as with libidn.

### Workarounds

- Install libidn and the `idn-ruby` gem, so that Addressable uses the native IDNA implementation.
- Don't make security decisions on `display_uri` or `to_unicode` output. Compare hosts using `normalized_host`.

### Credits

Reported by @tonghuaroot.

### For more information

If there are any questions or comments about this advisory:
* [Open an issue](https://github.com/sporkmonger/addressable/issues)

advisories.summary: Loofah: Mutation XSS in the HTML5 scrubbers through unescaped attribute values
advisories.description:
## Summary

Loofah's HTML5 scrubbers could emit output that a browser parses into different markup, allowing mutation XSS. Nokogiri < 1.19.5 did not escape `<` and `>` in attribute values. When the output contained certain MathML, a browser treated markup inside an allowed attribute as live HTML. The `:strip` scrubber is affected in every browser. The `:prune` and `:escape` scrubbers are affected in WebKit browsers such as Safari.

Nokogiri 1.19.5 escapes `<` and `>` in attribute values, as the HTML standard requires. Loofah 2.25.3 requires Nokogiri >= 1.19.5.

## Impact

Applications that sanitize untrusted HTML with Loofah's HTML5 API (`Loofah.html5_fragment`, `Loofah.html5_document` and the `scrub_html5_*` methods) and display the result to other people are affected, including with the default allowlist.

Not affected: Loofah's HTML4 API (including `Loofah::Helpers.sanitize`), the `:whitewash` scrubber, rails-html-sanitizer's default configuration, and JRuby.

## Mitigation

Upgrade to Loofah >= 2.25.3, or upgrade Nokogiri to >= 1.19.5.

advisories.summary: pgEdge RAG Server shared keyword index leaked results between concurrent unauthenticated requests
advisories.description:
### Impact

Documents belonging to one caller could be returned to another. Where an application passes a customer or tenant identifier as a search filter, that scoping could be defeated by ordinary concurrent traffic. **No injection and no malformed input are required** — normal load is enough.

The BM25 keyword index was a single per-pipeline object shared by every request. A request cleared it, refilled it from its own filtered corpus and then searched it, taking a separate lock for each step rather than holding the sequence as a unit. Concurrent requests therefore interleaved, and a search could run against a corpus that a different request's filter had populated.

**Who is affected:** any deployment of pgEdge RAG Server at `1.0.0` or earlier, including all alpha and beta pre-releases, that serves concurrent queries — most acutely those relying on a search filter to separate tenants or customers. The query endpoint is unauthenticated in the affected versions (`internal/server/middleware.go:37` applies logging, panic recovery and optional CORS only), so both the party whose results leak and the party receiving them are anonymous remote callers.

### Patches

**Fixed in `2.0.0`. Upgrade to `2.0.0` or later.**

The index is now built per request rather than shared. The regression is pinned by `TestSearch_ConcurrentRequestsDoNotShareKeywordIndex` in `internal/pipeline/orchestrator_test.go`.

**Upgrading does not tell a developer whether or not their application affected, and needs action beyond upgrading.** If a consuminag application scopes results by tenant, treat responses served under concurrent load on any affected version as potentially having included another tenant's documents. **Affected responses cannot be identified from the server's own logs**, so there is no retrospective check available.

### Workarounds

Set `hybrid_enabled: false` on the pipeline, which skips the keyword arm and with it the shared index. Callers can also pass `disable_hybrid` per request, which can only ever turn the arm off.

Neither is a substitute for upgrading.

advisories.summary: russh: Post-decompression SSH packet size was not bounded, allowing remote oversized compressed packets
advisories.description:
### Summary

When SSH compression is enabled, `russh` accepted compressed packets whose on-wire size passed the normal transport packet-length checks but whose decompressed size was much larger. This allowed a remote peer to send oversized post-decompression packets that should have been rejected.

In current releases, this is a remote denial-of-service / resource-exhaustion issue in the post-decompression receive path.

In older releases before `0.58.0`, the same remote decompression path used `CryptoVec`, which appears to make the historical impact worse.

### Details

The normal SSH transport read path enforces a packet-length limit before the packet body is read:

- `russh/src/cipher/mod.rs`

However, RFC 4253 compression is applied to the SSH `payload` field only. The `packet_length` field and MAC are computed over the compressed payload, so a packet that is reasonably sized on the wire can still expand to a much larger message body after decompression.

In `russh`, compressed packet bodies are later decompressed in:

- `russh/src/compression.rs`
- `russh/src/client/mod.rs`
- `russh/src/server/session.rs`

Before the fix, `Decompress::decompress()` grew its output buffer by repeated doubling and did not enforce a separate post-decompression ceiling. That meant a peer could send a small compressed packet that passed the normal on-wire transport length checks and then inflate it into a much larger packet after decompression.

It was verified that an attacker-crafted compressed payload can stay below the normal `256 KiB` implementation transport packet cap while still inflating above the intended post-decompression bound. In other words, this is not only a "large on-wire packet" issue.

Version detail:

- The underlying post-decompression bounds bug appears to affect `russh` as far back as `0.34.0`.
- In historical releases `>= 0.34.0, < 0.58.0`, the remote decompression path still used `CryptoVec`. Remote compressed SSH traffic could drive that path, and under constrained memory that historical code path could abort the process.
- In current-style releases `>= 0.58.0`, non-secret packet/decompression buffers were moved off `CryptoVec` and onto `Vec<u8>`, but the post-decompression size still remained unbounded. So the bug class remained reachable remotely, but the maintained-line impact is a current remote DoS / oversized-packet-acceptance issue rather than the older `CryptoVec`-based abort story.
- The maintained-line fix was verified against `0.60.2`.

advisories.summary: Hono: `css` helper does not escape a closing tag split between the template and an interpolated value, allowing HTML injection
advisories.description:
### Summary

The `css` helper in `hono/css` escapes a `/` that follows `<` inside an interpolated value so that a value cannot close the `<style>` element. The check only looks inside each value. When the text before a value ends with `<`, whether that is the template itself or an earlier interpolated value, and the next value starts with `/`, the `/` is not escaped and the combined output contains an unescaped closing tag.

### Details

Interpolated string values are escaped one at a time before they are joined with the surrounding template text. The rule that neutralizes `</` therefore cannot see a `<` that belongs to the template. A template such as a `content` declaration that opens with a literal `<` and interpolates a string right after it produces a raw `</style>` when that string starts with `/style>`. During server-side rendering the `<Style />` element is closed early and the rest of the value is interpreted as HTML.

This issue arises only when `<` is the last character before an interpolation in a `css` template, either written in the template or supplied by a preceding value, and the interpolated value is controlled by a client.

### Impact

A client that controls such a value can inject HTML, including script, into the page rendered on the server.

This may lead to:

- Execution of attacker-controlled script in the browser of a user who views the page
- Exposure of information available to that page

This issue affects applications that interpolate untrusted strings into a `css` template immediately after a `<`, including two adjacent interpolations such as `${prefix}${name}` where both are untrusted. Other uses of the `css` helper are not affected.

### Workarounds

Do not interpolate untrusted values into `css` templates, or make sure the text before an interpolated value does not end with `<`.

advisories.summary: Kubeflow Pipelines: SQL injection through unvalidated pagination tokens in Kubeflow Pipelines API server
advisories.description:
## Summary

Kubeflow Pipelines API server does not sufficiently validate SQL identifier fields decoded from the `page_token` pagination parameter. Client-controlled fields can reach SQL query construction, allowing SQL injection through list APIs.

This advisory consolidates the original pipeline-listing report and the later run-listing report in [GHSA-mhpc-2x8q-2vp9](https://github.com/kubeflow/pipelines/security/advisories/GHSA-mhpc-2x8q-2vp9). Their contributions and chronology are distinguished below.

## Impact and prerequisites

An attacker able to invoke an affected list API may read data accessible to the API server's database account, including data belonging to other namespaces. The original report demonstrated database read access through an authenticated Kubeflow deployment.

Authentication and authorization requirements depend on deployment configuration. In multi-user deployments, the attacker must pass the applicable endpoint authorization checks. A single-user deployment that exposes the API without an authentication layer may be reachable without credentials.

The submitted evidence establishes a confidentiality issue. Database modification was not demonstrated; this advisory does not claim arbitrary database writes.

## Technical details

Pagination tokens are base64-encoded JSON, not trusted server-side state. Before the fix, token deserialization accepted structural fields such as key and sort identifiers without sufficient validation before SQL construction.

The reports describe complementary paths through this defect:

- **Pipeline listing:** the original report demonstrated injection through `KeyFieldName`.
- **Run listing:** the later report documented `SortByFieldName` reaching query construction in both the v1beta1 and v2beta1 APIs, including metric joins, selected column aliases, ordering, and column propagation through resource-reference and task joins.

These paths share the unvalidated pagination-token boundary. Review of the later report and its discussion identified no reported path left unresolved by the merged fix.

Upgrade the Kubeflow Pipelines API server to **2.17.0 or later**.

[PR #13127](https://github.com/kubeflow/pipelines/pull/13127), included in 2.17.0, validates token identifiers and filter keys before query construction. It also separates user-facing metric names from SQL identifiers, uses a fixed metric-column alias, and parameterizes the metric-name join condition.

advisories.summary: russh: peer-declared zero maximum packet size permanently stalls channel writes (silent AsyncWrite hang)

## Summary

A peer can advertise `maximum packet size = 0` in its channel-open message (`CHANNEL_OPEN` when attacking a server, `CHANNEL_OPEN_CONFIRMATION` when attacking a client). russh accepts the value without validation and copies it into the channel write state, where it caps the size of every outgoing data chunk. In the `AsyncWrite` code path (`ChannelTx::poll_writable`, used by `Channel::data()`, `Channel::make_writer()` and `Channel::into_stream()`), a cap of 0 makes every write future stay `Poll::Pending` forever: `writable = max_packet_size.min(window_size).min(buf_len)` is always 0, and no future event can ever raise it (a static maximum packet size of 0 can never be satisfied by any amount of peer-granted window). The write neither completes nor errors, so the application task hangs silently.

Every other write path in russh already treats `max_packet_size == 0` as an error (`Error::Inconsistent`): `Channel::reserve_writable_chunk` (`russh/src/channels/mod.rs:363-365`) and the session packetizers (`russh/src/session.rs:489-492` and `549-552`). The `AsyncWrite` path is the only one that lacks the guard - it contradicts the crate's own invariant.

(1) Peer value accepted without validation:

- `russh/src/parsing.rs:44` (`OpenChannelMessage::parse`): `let maxpacket = map_err!(u32::decode(r))?;` stored as `recipient_maximum_packet_size` (`:25-30`); no range check. Same for `ChannelOpenConfirmation::decode` at `russh/src/parsing.rs:194-207`.

### Summary

**All evidence, reproduction steps, and scripts in the report were verified against a real running instance. Nothing is fabricated or synthetic; every verdict is backed by captured output from an actual deployment.** Concretely, the evidence comes from executing the real russh v0.64.1 client packet parser (`Session::process_packet` handling `handle_ext_info`) in a live client session with attacker-supplied packet bodies in the pre-authentication state; the captured output below is from that real execution.

russh's client stores every extension name it parses out of an `EXT_INFO` packet into a per-session vector and never clears, caps, or deduplicates it (`russh/src/client/encrypted.rs:433`, field declared at `russh/src/session.rs:60`). The packet is accepted without limit in the pre-authentication states, so a server - which is exactly the attacker position for a client library, and remains one even after the client has verified its host key - can send an unbounded sequence of these packets and grow the client's memory for as long as the session lives: 400 packets of about 26 KB each, carrying 3000 extension names apiece, retained 49.1 MiB (about 4.8 times the wire bytes) with the vector reaching 1,200,000 entries, while an equal volume of banner packets retained nothing. The same growth pattern has been accepted by the project before for other pre-auth allocation sinks; this one is a cross-packet accumulator rather than a single-packet allocation, and none of the published advisories covers it.

The handler appends every parsed extension name to the session state with no bound:

advisories.summary: Cosign's verify-blob-attestation reports false positive when payload parsing fails
advisories.description:
## Description

`cosign verify-blob-attestation` may erroneously report a "Verified OK" result for attestations with malformed payloads or mismatched predicate types. For old-format bundles and detached signatures, this was due to a logic flaw in the error handling of the predicate type validation. For new-format bundles, the predicate type validation was bypassed completely.

## Impact

When `cosign verify-blob-attestation` is used without `--check-claims` set to `true`, an attestation that has a valid signature but a malformed or unparsable payload would be incorrectly validated. Additionally, systems relying on `--type <predicate type>` to reject attestations with mismatched types would be lead to trust the unexpected attestation type.

## Patches

v3.0.6, v2.6.3

## Workarounds

Always set `--check-claims=true` for attestation verification.

### Summary

A Server-Side Request Forgery vulnerability exists in NocoBase v2.1.10 in the `@nocobase/plugin-action-custom-request` plugin.

A low-privileged authenticated user can call the `customRequests:send` endpoint and override the stored request URL at runtime using `options.url`. This causes the NocoBase server to perform outbound HTTP requests to attacker-controlled or internal URLs.

* Product: NocoBase
* Version: v2.1.10
* Component: `@nocobase/plugin-action-custom-request`
* Severity: Moderate
* Required privilege: authenticated low-privileged user / member

Testing was performed only in a local Docker lab environment at `http://127.0.0.1:13000`. No public NocoBase instance was tested.

Lab environment:

* Docker image: `nocobase/nocobase:latest-full`
* Commit: `23e2bd35625439594e4757bac31d57c9e8e695b9`
* Database: PostgreSQL 16
* Containers: `nocobase-lab`, `nocobase-postgres`
* Docker network: `172.19.0.0/16`
* Important environment variable: `SERVER_REQUEST_WHITELIST` was not set

The vulnerable endpoint is:

```http
POST /api/customRequests:send?filterByTk=<key>
```

The `customRequests:send` action is allowed for any logged-in user:

```ts

this.app.acl.allow('customRequests', ['send', 'listByCurrentRole'], 'loggedIn');

const whitelist = process.env.SERVER_REQUEST_WHITELIST;

if (!whitelist || !whitelist.trim()) return;
```

advisories.summary: filecoin-pin: Unbounded DAG pinning can exhaust server resources
advisories.description:
## Summary

The IPFS Pinning Service API implementation accepts a caller-controlled CID through `POST /pins`, queues background processing, and then recursively fetches the full DAG with `helia.pins.add(cid)`. The route and background pinning path do not enforce a request rate limit, per-user quota, maximum DAG byte count, maximum block count, traversal timeout, or concurrent pinning limit.

An authenticated caller, or an unauthenticated caller when the server is started with `ALLOW_NO_AUTH=true`, can submit one or more pins whose CIDs resolve to very large DAGs. The server writes fetched blocks to CAR files under `carStoragePath` and can consume disk, network, CPU, and libp2p resources until the process or host becomes unavailable.

## Details

`POST /pins` validates only that the request body contains a syntactically valid CID string, then forwards it to the pin store:

- `src/filecoin-pinning-server.ts:304-342` accepts the request, parses `cid` with `CID.parse`, and calls `pinStore.pin(request.user, cidObject, parsed.options)`.
- `src/filecoin-pin-store.ts:153-188` stores the pin as `queued` and schedules `_processPinInBackground` with `setTimeout`. There is no queue, semaphore, or global cap around this scheduling.
- `src/filecoin-pin-store.ts:211-217` creates a per-pin Helia node and forwards caller-supplied `origins`.
- `src/filecoin-pin-store.ts:260-274` walks the full DAG with `for await (const pinnedCid of helia.pins.add(cid))`.
- `src/create-pinning-helia.ts:47-80` creates a libp2p/Helia node with the Bitswap block broker and no application-level resource limits.
- `src/core/car/car-blockstore-base.ts:65-107` writes every fetched block and updates `stats.totalSize` only after writing.
- `src/core/car/car-file-backend.ts:84-93` streams blocks to the CAR writer on disk.

The Helia node created for each pin has no bootstrap or mDNS configuration (`src/create-pinning-helia.ts:57`). A public CID alone may therefore not be fetchable unless the node can reach a content source. In practice, the API also accepts `origins`, so an attacker can supply a reachable attacker-controlled libp2p origin that serves a large DAG and cause the server to retrieve it.

## Impact

Successful exploitation affects availability:

- Disk exhaustion from unbounded CAR files in `carStoragePath`.
- Network exhaustion from recursive Bitswap retrieval.
- CPU and memory pressure from concurrent libp2p/Helia pin operations.

advisories.summary: Next.js: Cache leak across root param values in nested 'use cache' functions via delayed inner stream metadata
advisories.description:
With Cache Components enabled, an outer `'use cache'` function can be keyed incorrectly even when its inner `'use cache'` call generates a fresh entry. If the inner function reads a root param (via `next/root-params`) and returns a value that still contains pending promises — for example an object with data that is ready immediately alongside slower data — React Flight delivers the ready portion to the outer function before the inner entry has finished publishing its root param dependencies. The outer function can then finish, and its cache entry is persisted under a key that omits that root param. The entry is written once and reused for all root param values, so a response for one root param value can serve content produced for a different value. Entries written this way can also ignore tag invalidation and cache lifetimes of the nested caches they consumed.

What values are leaked cannot be attacker controlled. Which value's content is served depends only on which invocation wrote the entry first.

This is a variant of https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-h694-7cp9-m8p3 that the fix for that advisory does not cover: it does not require the inner call to be served from an existing entry, and it does not depend on a slow cache handler.

advisories.summary: Addressable display_uri can show misleading hosts containing bidi and invisible characters
advisories.description:
### Impact

`Addressable::IDNA.to_unicode` decodes Punycode labels (labels beginning with `xn--`) that contain characters which change how text is displayed without being visible themselves. These include bidirectional controls such as U+202E RIGHT-TO-LEFT OVERRIDE and U+2066–U+2069, zero-width characters, and other invisible format characters. `Addressable::URI#display_uri` uses `to_unicode`, so it can display a host whose characters appear reordered or which looks identical to a different host. For example, the host of `http://xn--abcmoc-dm0c.com/` is displayed as `abc`, U+202E, `moc.com`, and the override makes everything after `abc` render right to left.

Parsing, `host`, `normalized_host` and any connection made from the URI are not affected. Only the displayed form is. Applications that show `display_uri` to users (link previews, chat and email clients, admin interfaces) can be used to make a malicious domain look like a trusted one.

- In the pure-Ruby IDNA implementation, all such characters are decoded, including those that IDNA's nameprep profile prohibits.
- In the native IDNA implementation, used when libidn and the `idn-ruby` gem are installed, libidn rejects most of them, but not characters added to Unicode after version 3.2, such as U+061C and U+2066–U+2069.

### Affected Versions

The pure-Ruby IDNA implementation is affected in Addressable >= 2.0.0. The native IDNA implementation is affected in Addressable >= 2.5.2, when `to_unicode` began accepting characters unassigned in Unicode 3.2. It is fixed in 2.9.1 for both implementations, where such labels are returned unchanged.

### Workarounds

- Install libidn and the `idn-ruby` gem, so that Addressable uses the native IDNA implementation. This reduces the affected characters to those added since Unicode 3.2.
- Check displayed hosts for bidirectional and invisible characters (e.g., `/[\p{Cc}\p{Cf}\p{Default_Ignorable_Code_Point}]/`) and fall back to `normalized_host` when one is present.

### Credits

Reported by @andrewstellman.

### For more information

If there are any questions or comments about this advisory:
* [Open an issue](https://github.com/sporkmonger/addressable/issues)
