advisories.summary: Action View: Possible XSS vulnerability in tag helpers
advisories.description:
### Impact
The fix for [CVE-2026-33168](https://github.com/rails/rails/security/advisories/GHSA-v55j-83pf-r9cq) skips blank HTML attribute names in Action View tag helpers, but it tests the name before converting it to a string. A Symbol name made only of whitespace, such as `:" "`, is not blank, because `Symbol#blank?` is `Symbol#empty?`, so it reaches the attribute escaping, which emits an attribute with no name and produces malformed HTML. The asset tag helpers, such as `image_tag`, `video_tag` and `audio_tag`, symbolize their options, so a whitespace String name passed to them takes the same path. A carefully crafted attribute value could then be misinterpreted by the browser as a separate attribute name, possibly leading to XSS. Applications that allow users to specify custom HTML attribute names are affected.

### Releases
The fixed releases are available at the normal locations.

Patches for those who cannot upgrade at once:
- 8.1: https://github.com/rails/rails/commit/9190210606ffe52f92fdc75637f8ff69404f22c8.patch
- 8.0: https://github.com/rails/rails/commit/f47452533e1f28d847c63181b9d5f8b7243ef9a4.patch

The `sql()` VQL plugin runs a caller-supplied database driver and connection string with no permission check (`vql/parsers/sql/sql.go:93`, `SQLPlugin.Call`). Every sibling network plugin (`http_client`, `netcat`, `s3`, `rsyslog`) calls `CheckAccess(acls.NETWORK)` in its own body; `sql()` calls nothing.

The built-in `analyst` role holds `ANY_QUERY` but not `FILESYSTEM_READ` or `NETWORK` (`acls/roles.go:222`), and reaches this sink through the notebook query API.

- Stock install, default Basic authenticator, any built-in `analyst`, `investigator`, or `api` role (all hold `ANY_QUERY`, none holds `FILESYSTEM_READ` or `NETWORK`).

against an agent driving `kubeshark mcp --allow-destructive`) can inject
arbitrary `--set` Helm value overrides — notably `tap.docker.registry` /
`tap.docker.tag` — redirecting the deployed worker/hub/front images to an
attacker-controlled registry. The worker DaemonSet runs privileged with
`hostNetwork` and the host filesystem mounted, so an attacker image yields node
and cluster-admin compromise.

(#1832)", 2026-02-06 — first released in **v53.1.0** (`v53.1.0~23`). The
`pod_regex` argument has been appended as a bare positional since the tool's
introduction; there is no regression window, every MCP-capable release is
affected.

In `callStartKubeshark` (`cmd/mcpRunner.go`), the command was built as

and there was no `--` guard, so `pod_regex="--set=tap.docker.registry=…,tap.docker.tag=…"`
became a real `--set`. The tool is only registered when
`kubeshark mcp --allow-destructive` is set.

attacker image. The image ran as root inside the privileged worker container and
read the host's cluster-admin kubeconfigs
(`/etc/kubernetes/super-admin.conf`, `admin.conf`, `pki/`) — i.e. cluster-admin
takeover from a single `pod_regex` value.

advisories.summary: rails-html-sanitizer: Possible XSS via shared scrubber state in concurrent calls
advisories.description:
## Summary

`Rails::HTML::SafeListSanitizer` (both the HTML4 and HTML5 variants) shares one `Rails::HTML::PermitScrubber` across every `sanitize` call on the same instance, assigning its `tags` and `attributes` on each call without synchronization. Two concurrent `sanitize` calls with different `tags:` or `attributes:` options can interleave, so one call is scrubbed with the other call's allowlist.

- Versions affected: `< 1.7.2`
- Not affected: none
- Fixed versions: `1.7.2`

## Impact

Action View memoizes a single `SafeListSanitizer` per helper module and uses it for every `sanitize` call in the process, so in a multi-threaded server (for example Puma) all requests share the same `PermitScrubber`. If any code path calls `sanitize` with a more permissive allowlist, an attacker who can trigger that path concurrently with another request can cause the other request to be sanitized with the permissive allowlist. If the permissive allowlist admits `script` or an event-handler attribute, the strict call emits it unchanged, which is a cross-site scripting vector when the strict output is stored or rendered to other users.

Applications are affected only if they run more than one thread per process and some `sanitize` call passes `tags:` or `attributes:` options that differ from another call's, including a call that passes no options and so uses the defaults. Applications that use a single configuration everywhere, pass their own `scrubber:`, or run single-threaded are not affected.

## Workarounds

Use the same allowlist for every `sanitize` call, or pass a `scrubber:` built per call (`Rails::HTML::PermitScrubber.new` with `tags=` and `attributes=` set) instead of `tags:` and `attributes:` options.

## Credit

Reported by hiumee via HackerOne.

advisories.summary: ezBookkeeping: Source-IP allowlist (MCP & API token) is bypassable via a spoofed `X-Forwarded-For` header
advisories.description:
### Summary
A remote attacker from any IP address defeats the operator-configured source-IP allowlist (`mcp_allowed_remote_ips` / `api_token_allowed_remote_ips`) by sending a single `X-Forwarded-For: <allowlisted-ip>` header. The router is created with `gin.New()` and never calls `SetTrustedProxies`, so gin trusts every proxy by default and `c.ClientIP()` returns the attacker-supplied header verbatim. The same forged value is also written to `Transaction.CreatedIp` and the access log, so the attacker's real IP never appears in any record.

`cmd/webserver.go:104` builds the router with `gin.New()`. A grep of `cmd/` and `pkg/` confirms `SetTrustedProxies` is never called, leaving gin's default trusted-proxy range of `0.0.0.0/0` and `::/0`. `WebContext` (`pkg/core/context_web.go:39`) embeds `*gin.Context` and does not override `ClientIP()`.

```go
// pkg/middlewares/mcp_server_ip_limit.go:19
if config.MCPAllowedRemoteIPs[i].Match(c.ClientIP()) { c.Next(); return }
```

The identical `c.ClientIP()` is consumed by the audit trail at `pkg/api/transactions.go:1078` (`createNewTransactionModel(..., c.ClientIP())` → `CreatedIp`) and the access log (`pkg/middlewares/request_log.go:28`), so one header both bypasses the gate and forges attribution.

```

```

Output:
```

gate status = 200 | created_ip that would be persisted = "10.0.0.1"
```

advisories.summary: Remark42: Rate limit bypass via unconditional trust of X-Forwarded-For/X-Real-IP headers in direct-internet deployment
advisories.description:
### Summary
Remark42 applied chi's `middleware.RealIP` globally, trusting `True-Client-IP` / `X-Real-IP` / `X-Forwarded-For` headers without verifying the request came from a trusted proxy. The per-IP rate limiters key on the overwritten `r.RemoteAddr`, so any client can bypass every per-IP rate limiter by rotating spoofed IP headers. The same spoofed IP also drives other per-IP controls (stored comment IP, anonymous identity derivation, and `--votes-ip` vote de-duplication). This affects deployments reachable directly from the internet (Remark42's built-in HTTP, static TLS, and ACME modes are all documented and supported), as well as any proxied deployment where the proxy forwards an attacker-controlled recognised header.

### Details
The router applies `middleware.RealIP` globally, ahead of the per-route limiters, without any check that the server is behind a trusted proxy (in v1.16.1, `backend/app/rest/api/rest.go:207`).

The `rateLimiter` function (v1.16.1, `backend/app/rest/api/rest.go:769-779`) builds a tollbooth limiter with `IPLookup{Name: "RemoteAddr"}`, which reads `r.RemoteAddr`. Since chi's `middleware.RealIP` (v1.16.1, `backend/vendor/github.com/go-chi/chi/v5/middleware/realip.go:42-55`) unconditionally overwrites `r.RemoteAddr` from `True-Client-IP > X-Real-IP > first X-Forwarded-For` (accepting any syntactically valid IP), any client can set its apparent IP to an arbitrary value.

This bypasses every per-IP rate limiter that runs after `RealIP`: `/auth` (2/s), avatars (100/s), the image proxy (10/s), open / protected / admin route groups (10/s), root routes (50/s), and `/web/*` (20/s). Comment and vote creation go through the update limiter, whose server default is `UPDATE_LIMIT=0.5`/s (burst 1), not 10/s. The global 1,000 concurrent-request throttle still applies, so this is a per-IP-limit bypass rather than truly unlimited throughput. chi's own documentation warns that `middleware.RealIP` should be used only behind a trusted proxy.

# Comment creation is limited to UPDATE_LIMIT (default 0.5/s, burst 1) per IP.

for i in $(seq 1 100); do
  curl -s -o /dev/null -w '%{http_code}\n' \
    -H "X-Real-IP: 192.0.2.$i" \
    -X POST 'https://remark42.example.com/api/v1/comment?site=site1' \
    -H 'Authorization: Bearer YOUR

advisories.summary: nimiq-block has skip block quorum bypass via out-of-range BitSet indices & u16 truncation
advisories.description:
### Impact
`SkipBlockProof::verify` computes its quorum check using `BitSet.len()`, then iterates `BitSet` indices and casts each `usize` index to `u16` (`slot as u16`) for slot lookup. If an attacker can get a `SkipBlockProof` verified where `MultiSignature.signers` contains out-of-range indices spaced by 65536, these indices inflate `len()` but collide onto the same in-range `u16` slot during aggregation.

This makes it possible for a malicious validator with far fewer than `2f+1` real signer slots to pass skip block proof verification by multiplying a single BLS signature by the same factor.

### Patches
[The patch for this vulnerability](https://github.com/nimiq/core-rs-albatross/pull/3657) is included as part of [v1.3.0](https://github.com/nimiq/core-rs-albatross/releases/tag/v1.3.0).

### Workarounds
No known workarounds.

advisories.summary: Forge: Ed25519 signature verification accepts small-order public keys
advisories.description:
### Summary
`ed25519.verify()` does not reject public keys of small order, such as the identity point. Under such a key, a signature with `S = 0` and a small-order `R` verifies for many messages, or for every message with the identity key, without any private key. Fixed in node-forge 1.4.3.

### Details
`crypto_sign_open()` in `lib/ed25519.js` decodes the public key `A` with `unpackneg()`, which only checks that the point is on the curve, and then checks `R == [S]B - [k]A` with `k = SHA-512(R || A || M)`. Nothing rejects public keys of small order: the identity point, the other 7 points of order 2, 4 or 8, and their non-canonical encodings with `y >= p`.

With `S = 0`, the check becomes `R == [k](-A)`. For a small-order `A`, `[k](-A)` is one of at most 8 small-order points, so an attacker can make a valid signature by trying the small-order values of `R`. For the identity key (`01 00 … 00`), `R = identity` and `S = 0` verifies for every message. For the other small-order keys, a given message can be forged with high probability. No private key is involved. The `S < L` check added for CVE-2026-33895 (GHSA-q67f-28xg-22rw) doesn't apply, because `S = 0` is canonical.

Keys produced by Ed25519 key generation (`ed25519.generateKeyPair()` or any RFC 8032 implementation) are never small-order, so signatures under them cannot be forged this way. Applications are affected when they verify signatures against a public key an attacker can choose (for example a key included with the signed data, a self-registered key, or a key in an attacker-controlled document) and rely on the signature being bound to the message: proof of possession, attribution, non-repudiation or deduplication.

RFC 8032 doesn't require rejecting small-order public keys, and implementations differ. libsodium rejects them, and Node.js `crypto.verify()` (OpenSSL) rejects these signatures.

The fix rejects a public key `A` when `[8]A` is the identity point. This covers all small-order points and their non-canonical encodings.

#### Patches
Fixed in node-forge 1.4.3. `ed25519.verify()` returns `false` for small-order public keys.

#### Workarounds
Before calling `ed25519.verify()` with a public key from untrusted input, reject keys whose 32-byte encoding is one of the small-order points (the identity `01 00 … 00` and the other encodings that libsodium blocks), or only verify against keys you generated or have otherwise validated.

#### Resources
- RFC 8032, Section 5.1.7 (Ed25519 verification): https:/

The password reset flow did not revoke existing refresh tokens, allowing an attacker with a previously stolen refresh token to continue minting valid JWTs after the victim resets their password.

`passwordReset()` in `users.service.ts` updated `token_version` (invalidating JWTs) but did not call `UserRefreshToken.deleteAllUserToken()`. The `refreshToken()` method only checked token existence, not `token_version`. Both `passwordChange()` and `signOut()` correctly deleted all refresh tokens.

### Impact
An attacker who previously obtained a refresh token retains access after password reset until the token expires.

advisories.summary: mail-parser: Sender IP address spoofing in get_server_ipaddress()
advisories.description:
### Patches

Fixed in **4.6.2**. Upgrade with `pip install --upgrade mail-parser`.

Candidate addresses are now selected by position, not by appearance — a bracketed address
the sender wrote is byte-identical to one the MTA wrote, so no amount of pattern matching
can tell them apart:

- the first token of the `from` clause is the HELO name, whatever its shape, and is never a
  candidate;
- an explicit HELO marker inside a comment group is sender text and is excluded;
- a candidate must sit inside a `(` / `[` group;
- IPv4 and IPv6 matches are merged positionally, never family-first;
- the walk stops at the first trusted hop naming no address, rather than continuing into
  sender-written headers.

The IPv6 pattern was corrected to skip the `IPv6:` tag and to prefer the longest valid form.

**Behaviour change.** `get_server_ipaddress()` now returns `None` rather than an unreliable
value in two cases that previously returned an address: a `from` clause consisting of a bare
address with no HELO marker (indistinguishable from `EHLO <that address>`), and a trusted hop
naming no address at all. Callers must handle `None`.

### Workarounds

None within mail-parser. Callers who cannot upgrade should not treat the return value of
`get_server_ipaddress()` as trustworthy, and should derive sender attribution from an
authenticated signal instead — the MTA's own logs, or SPF/DKIM/DMARC results computed
outside this library.

advisories.summary: Kubeflow Pipelines — API server fetches a caller-supplied pipelineURL without host validation
advisories.description:
## Summary

The Kubeflow Pipelines API server fetched caller-supplied pipeline package URLs without restricting the destination. A caller authorized to create a pipeline or pipeline version could cause requests to originate from the API server's network position, including to internal services that the caller could not otherwise reach.

## Impact

The reported evidence demonstrates blind server-side request forgery and a limited status-code oracle. The fetched response is processed as a pipeline package; the report does not demonstrate arbitrary response-body disclosure or credential theft. A request to a cloud metadata endpoint returned HTTP 403, which does not establish access to metadata contents or tokens.

The confidentiality metric is Low to reflect the limited information obtainable through the status-code oracle. High confidentiality impact and integrity or availability impact are not established by the submitted evidence. Impact depends on the API server's network reachability and the deployment's trust boundaries.

## Patches

Fixed by [kubeflow/pipelines#12750](https://github.com/kubeflow/pipelines/pull/12750), first released in 2.17.0. The fix validates URL schemes, ports, allowed domains, and resolved IP addresses; validates redirects; and enforces IP restrictions at connection time. The HTTP client also applies timeouts and disables environment proxy use so connections pass through the validated dialer.

Operators should keep pipeline URL validation enabled and limit additional allowed domains to trusted pipeline sources.

## Workarounds

Until upgrading, restrict API-server egress to required destinations through deployment-specific network controls. Account for required Kubernetes and storage connectivity when applying these restrictions.

## Related reports

This is the canonical advisory for the API-server pipeline URL SSRF family. [GHSA-wg4h-pp3x-hxhv](https://github.com/kubeflow/pipelines/security/advisories/GHSA-wg4h-pp3x-hxhv) is tracked as a duplicate submission. advisories.summary: Kubeshark: MCP `download_file` writes fetched bytes to an unvalidated destination path
advisories.description:
**Ecosystem / package:** Go — `github.com/kubeshark/kubeshark` (the `kubeshark`
CLI, `kubeshark mcp` subcommand)
**Affected component:** `cmd/mcpRunner.go`, MCP tool `download_file`
**Affected versions:** `>= v53.1.0`, `< v53.4.0` (the flaw shipped with the
tool's first release; v53.3.0 was the last affected release)
**Patched version:** `v53.4.0`
**Credit:** novice-22 (Urim), via private coordinated disclosure.

## Summary
The `download_file` MCP tool fetches a caller-supplied `path` from the Kubeshark
Hub API and writes the response body to a caller-supplied `dest` on the local
filesystem with no validation of `dest`. An attacker who can influence the MCP
tool arguments — e.g. via indirect prompt injection against an AI agent driving
`kubeshark mcp` — can write attacker-controlled bytes to an arbitrary path
writable by the user running the MCP server (e.g. `~/.ssh/authorized_keys`,
`~/.kube/config`, `~/.bashrc`), and can request arbitrary Hub API endpoints.
`download_file` is registered unconditionally (available in the default,
non-`--allow-destructive` posture).

Commit `eb7dc42b` — "Add get_file_url and download_file MCP tools (#1853)",
2026-03-04 — first released in **v53.1.0** (`v53.1.0~1`). An earlier attempt
(`dbfd17d9`) was reverted (`a46f05c4`) before any release, so no tag before
v53.1.0 is affected.

In `callDownloadFile` (`cmd/mcpRunner.go`), both `path` and `dest` come straight

- `path` was concatenated onto the Hub API base URL with no allowlist, so any
  Hub endpoint (including captured-traffic exports) is reachable.

The tool originally issued the fetch with no authentication. The authentication
gap was addressed by the gated-Hub authentication refactor: the download now

rejects auth-required responses instead of writing a login page to disk. **But**

`kubeshark tap` the Hub API answers without authentication and captured traffic
(credentials/tokens/PII) can still be read and exfiltrated end-to-end. Enforcing

### Summary

LightSaml 5.0.0 (latest release; also confirmed on 4.6.1) validates an inbound `samlp:Response` by collecting its direct-child `saml:Assertion` elements and validating each one's `ds:Signature` via robrichards/xmlseclibs. `Response::deserialize` collects assertions with `manyElementsFromXml`, whose relative XPath `saml:Assertion` matches only direct children of the `Response`. https://github.com/litesaml/lightsaml/blob/5.0.0/src/Model/AbstractSamlModel.php#L93
https://github.com/litesaml/lightsaml/blob/5.0.0/src/Action/Assertion/Inbound/AssertionSignatureValidatorAction.php#L28

The check delegates to xmlseclibs `XMLSecurityDSig::validateReference()`, which first removes the signature node being validated from the shared document (enveloped-signature removal):

advisories.summary: NLTK dot2img runs Graphviz 'dot' without the trusted-exec chokepoint, enabling local code execution via a writable PATH element
advisories.description:
## Summary

`nltk.parse.dependencygraph.dot2img` invokes the Graphviz `dot` executable without the trusted-execution guarantees that NLTK applies to its other native-tool wrappers. The function resolves `dot` by bare name and then runs the resolved absolute path with a raw `subprocess.run`, omitting the ownership/writability check and the loader-environment scrub that `nltk.pathsec.spawn_trusted` provides. On a POSIX host, a local, unprivileged actor who can write to any group/world-writable directory that appears on the victim's `PATH` can plant a trojan `dot`; when the victim later renders a `DependencyGraph` (for example in a Jupyter notebook, which auto-invokes `_repr_svg_`) or calls `dot2img` directly, the planted binary executes as the victim. The advisory GHSA-6hwm-xvph-95vm (CVE-2026-78680) addressed the same untrusted-search-path class for the Graphviz `dot` invoker in `nltk/translate/api.py`, but `dot2img` received only part of that remediation and remains exploitable.

## Root Cause

Layer 1 rejects only non-absolute matches, so an absolute path returned by the `which` search stage survives even when the file lives in a writable directory. Because `dot2img` never calls `spawn_trusted`, the ownership check and environment scrub never run.

nltk/parse/dependencygraph.py:631   subprocess.run([dot_binary, "-T%s" % t], ...)   # no trust check, no env=
nltk/parse/dependencygraph.py:638   subprocess.run([dot_binary, "-T%s" % t], ...)   # binary-format branch, same gap
nltk/internals.py:1034              if searching_bare_name and not os.path.isabs(path): continue  # skips only relative matches
nltk/translate/api.py:145           process = spawn_trusted(dot_bi

advisories.summary: rfc3161-client has insufficient verification for timestamp response signatures
advisories.description:
### Impact

`rfc3161-client` 1.0.2 and earlier contain a flaw in their timestamp response signature verification logic. In particular, it performs chain verification against the TSR's embedded certificates up to the trusted root(s), but fails to verify the TSR's own signature against the timestamping leaf certificates. Consequently, vulnerable versions perform insufficient signature validation to properly consider a TSR verified, as the attacker can introduce _any_ TSR signature so long as the embedded leaf chains up to some root TSA.

### Patches

Users should immediately upgrade to `rfc3161-client` 1.0.3 or later.

### Workarounds

There is no workaround possible. Users should immediately upgrade to a fixed version.

advisories.summary: Hono: `csrf()` does not check requests sent by hyperlink auditing (`text/ping`)
advisories.description:
### Summary

`csrf()` validates a request only when its `Content-Type` is one of the three types an HTML form can send. Chromium's hyperlink auditing (`<a ping>`) sends a cross-origin POST with the user's cookies and the content type `text/ping`, which is not in that list. The middleware does not look at `Origin` or `Sec-Fetch-Site` for such a request, so it is passed to the handler.

### Details

The middleware skips the origin check when the content type is not one that a form submission produces. The assumption was that any other content type requires a CORS preflight and therefore cannot be sent cross-origin with credentials. Hyperlink auditing is an exception: Chrome and Edge send the ping as a credentialed POST without a preflight, with a fixed body and `Content-Type: text/ping`.

A page on another origin can therefore trigger a POST to any URL of the application. The `csrf()` options for `origin` and `secFetchSite` do not change the outcome, because neither header is evaluated for the request.

The request body is fixed, so only actions whose effect does not depend on the body can be triggered. Firefox does not send pings by default. As with any CSRF, the user's cookie must be sent with the request, which with the default `SameSite=Lax` means a same-site origin or a cookie set with `SameSite=None`.

### Impact

A user who visits a malicious page in Chrome or Edge while logged in to an application protected by `csrf()` can be made to send a state-changing request to that application, such as logging out, deleting a resource, or toggling a setting that is selected by the path or query string.

This issue affects applications that rely on `csrf()` as their CSRF protection and expose state-changing endpoints whose effect does not depend on the request body.

### Workarounds

Reject requests with a `Content-Type` of `text/ping` in a middleware registered before `csrf()`, or set session cookies with `SameSite=Strict`.

### Summary

Terragrunt's `terragrunt catalog` command clones each repository referenced in your catalog configuration into a temporary working directory. In affected versions, the clone path it derived was deterministic and sat under the shared system temporary directory, in the form `<tmp>/catalog-<base64 sha1 of the repo URL>`. Because that path was predictable and Terragrunt followed a symlink already present there instead of rejecting it, a local attacker could plant a symlink at that path and cause Terragrunt to delete a directory and re-clone into it outside the intended temporary root.

### Impact

This affected users who ran `terragrunt catalog` on a host they shared with other local users or processes they did not fully trust, such as a multi-user server or a shared CI runner. The attack required a local attacker: a separate local user or process able to write to the shared system temporary directory. It was not remotely exploitable, and the victim had to run `terragrunt catalog` while the attacker's symlink was already in place.

Because the predictable path depended only on the repository URL being cataloged and the location of the system temporary directory, the attacker could compute it in advance and plant a symlink there before the victim ran the command. When the victim ran `terragrunt catalog`, Terragrunt followed the symlink out of the intended temporary root, deleted an existing `<repoName>` directory under the attacker-chosen parent, and repopulated that path with the cloned repository contents. The attacker controlled the parent directory the symlink pointed to, but not the leaf name: the leaf was fixed to `<repoName>`, derived from the repository URL the victim cataloged. This vulnerability has been resolved in Terragrunt version `v1.1.1`.

If you cannot upgrade immediately, ensure that you do not allow untrusted parties to control the values of `TMPDIR`, `TMP`, and `TEMP` in environments where you run `terragrunt catalog`.

advisories.summary: Forge: X.509 pathLenConstraint not enforced by verifyCertificateChain() for CA certificates without keyUsage
advisories.description:
### Summary
`forge.pki.verifyCertificateChain()` enforces the `pathLenConstraint` of a CA certificate's `basicConstraints` extension only when that certificate also has a `keyUsage` extension. For a CA certificate with a `pathLenConstraint` and no `keyUsage`, chains with more intermediate CA certificates below it than the constraint allows are accepted. Fixed in node-forge 1.4.1.

### Details
In `pki.verifyCertificateChain()` (`lib/x509.js`), the path length check for a CA certificate was guarded by `keyUsageExt !== null && 'pathLenConstraint' in bcExt`. The `keyUsage` test was originally a proxy for "a basicConstraints extension exists". Since node-forge 1.4.0 (GHSA-2328-f5f3-gj25), basicConstraints is required for every certificate that reaches this check, so the only remaining effect of the guard is to skip `pathLenConstraint` enforcement for CA certificates without `keyUsage`.

RFC 5280 permits CA certificates without `keyUsage`, and path length processing in section 6.1.4 (l)-(m) does not depend on `keyUsage`; section 4.2.1.9 defines `pathLenConstraint` as part of basicConstraints only. For example, with a trusted root, an intermediate CA with `pathLenConstraint=0` and no `keyUsage`, a sub-CA issued by that intermediate, and a leaf issued by the sub-CA, node-forge accepts the chain. It correctly rejects the same chain when the intermediate has `keyUsage`.

The fix checks `pathLenConstraint` whenever the basicConstraints extension is present, regardless of `keyUsage` (based on PR #1142).

#### Patches
Fixed in node-forge 1.4.1. `pathLenConstraint` is now enforced for CA certificates without a `keyUsage` extension.

#### Workarounds
None in node-forge itself. Applications that pass an `options.verify` callback to `pki.verifyCertificateChain()` (or `verify` to `forge.tls.createConnection()`) can reject chains in which a CA certificate at `depth` d has `basicConstraints.pathLenConstraint < d - 1`. Re-issuing constrained CA certificates with a `keyUsage` extension that includes `keyCertSign` also restores enforcement.

#### References
- RFC 5280, sections 4.2.1.9 and 6.1.4: https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc5280#section-6.1.4
- Related: GHSA-2328-f5f3-gj25 / CVE-2026-33896 (basicConstraints bypass, fixed in 1.4.0)
- https://github.com/digitalbazaar/forge/pull/1142

#### Severity
CVSS 3.1: CVSS:3.1/AV:N/AC:H/PR:N/UI:N/S:U/C:N/I:H/A:N (5.9, Moderate)
CVSS 4.0 (informational): CVSS:4.0/AV:N/AC:L/AT:P/PR:N/UI:N/VC:N/VI:H/VA:N/SC:N/SI:N/SA:N (8.2)
CVSS 4.0 weig

advisories.summary: Pocket ID: Email verification token remains valid after address change, enabling arbitrary verified-email spoofing
advisories.description:
## Summary

An authenticated Pocket ID user can request an email-verification token while their account uses an address they control, change the account email address, and then redeem the previously issued token. The token is bound only to the user ID, not to the address to which it was sent, and changing the address does not revoke outstanding tokens.

As a result, Pocket ID marks the newly supplied address as verified even though the user never proved control of it. Pocket ID subsequently returns that address with `email_verified: true` in OIDC claims. A relying party that trusts this claim for email-based account linking or provisioning can therefore link the attacker's Pocket ID identity to a victim's existing account, leading to cross-application account takeover.

This was verified against commit `9f559788a44cfea790de360da0a74d4bdf8ca5d5`.

## Preconditions

- The attacker has an ordinary Pocket ID user account.
- Email verification is in use (`emailsVerified=false`, which is the default).
- The user can edit their own account (`allowOwnAccountEdit=true`, which is the default).
- The target address is not already assigned to another Pocket ID user.
- For downstream account takeover, a relying party links or provisions users based on a trusted, verified email address. Applications that rely exclusively on the stable OIDC `sub` claim are not affected by that downstream consequence.

No administrator privilege, victim interaction, or access to the victim's mailbox is required.

## Reproduction through the API

1. Sign in as an ordinary user whose current email address is controlled by the attacker, for example `attacker@example.test`.
2. Call `POST /api/users/me/send-email-verification`.
3. Obtain the token from the message delivered to `attacker@example.test`, but do not redeem it yet.
4. Call `PUT /api/users/me` and change the account email to an address the attacker does not control, for example `victim@example.test`.
5. Observe that the new address is initially stored with `emailVerified: false`.
6. Call `POST /api/users/me/verify-email` with the token delivered to `attacker@example.test`.
7. Call `GET /api/users/me`. The current address is now `victim@example.test` and `emailVerified` is `true`.
8. Complete an OIDC flow with the `email` scope. Pocket ID emits:

```json
{
  "email": "victim@example.test",
  "email_verified": true
}
```

The old token has therefore verified a different address from the one to which it was delivered.

advisories.summary: @grpc/grpc-js: safe_regex incorrectly applies partial string matching for patterns with alternation
advisories.description:
### Summary

The StringMatcher/PathMatcher for `safe_regex` builds its RE2 as `^${regex}$` with no surrounding group. Because alternation has the lowest precedence, a pattern `"a|b|c"` compiles to `/^a|b|c$/` -- "starts with a" OR "contains b" OR "ends with c" instead of a full match of the whole value. Configurations with `safe_regex` matchers that use a regex alternation (a natural way to list methods or service identities) therefore apply partial string matches. This impacts route selection, xDS credentials, and RBAC.

### Details

`src/matcher.ts`: `SafeRegexValueMatcher` and `PathSafeRegexValueMatcher` both do
```ts
this.targetRegexImpl = new RE2(`^${targetRegex}$`, 'u');
```

and `apply()` returns `targetRegexImpl.test(value)`. With a top-level alternation the anchors bind only to the first/last branch.

https://github.com/grpc/grpc-node/blob/e742b11bd8039f3dbea4cd29afdf5d95a8ba6b92/packages/grpc-js-xds/src/matcher.ts#L59

https://github.com/grpc/grpc-node/blob/e742b11bd8039f3dbea4cd29afdf5d95a8ba6b92/packages/grpc-js-xds/src/matcher.ts#L232

`src/route.ts` (`getPredicateForStringMatcher` / `getPredicateForHeaderMatcher`) builds these for every `safe_regex` `StringMatcher`/`HeaderMatcher`, and src/rbac.ts uses them for RBAC `url_path` `permissions`/`principals`, `authenticated.principal_name` (mTLS SAN/CN), `requested_server_name` and `header rules`. So an ALLOW rule written with an alternation grants access to method names, certificate identities or header values that extend an intended one. DENY policies only become broader (fail-safe).

https://github.com/grpc/grpc-node/blob/e742b11bd8039f3dbea4cd29afdf5d95a8ba6b92/packages/grpc-js-xds/src/route.ts#L28

advisories.summary: Kubeflow Pipelines: Cross-tenant execution-cache poisoning / output substitution via a namespace-blind cache key in the cache webhook (multi-user)
advisories.description:
## Summary

The legacy Kubeflow Pipelines V1/raw-Argo execution cache does not separate cached results by Kubernetes namespace. In multi-user deployments where tenants share the cache service, a tenant can receive another tenant's cached outputs or seed outputs that are subsequently substituted into another tenant's step.

This affects the Argo-template cache mutating webhook and its cache-server storage path. Standard KFP V2 component pods bypass this webhook cache; the separate V2 cache implementation is outside this advisory's scope.

## Affected deployments and impact

The issue requires multiple tenant namespaces sharing the legacy cache service, cache-enabled V1/raw-Argo steps, and cache entries that satisfy the configured staleness policy. The standard multi-user configuration watches pods across namespaces.

A tenant able to submit a step with the same cache-relevant template fields as another tenant's step can:

- Read cached step outputs originally produced in another namespace.
- Populate the shared cache before another tenant's matching step runs, causing that step to report the cached outputs instead of executing its intended containers.

Matching refers to the selected template fields used by the cache key, not merely an identical container image. This is an application-level cache-key collision caused by missing tenant scope, not a cryptographic SHA-256 collision. The finding establishes cross-namespace confidentiality and integrity impact; it does not establish arbitrary code execution.

**Medium — CVSS 3.1: 5.4**

- **S:U:** the established impact is disclosure or substitution of output data managed by the same cache service. Crossing tenant namespaces alone does not establish a change in security authority; execution under a separate victim authority has not been established here.

advisories.summary: @nuxt/webpack-builder and @nuxt/rspack-builder dev server serves built source to DNS rebinding pages
advisories.description:
### Summary

When using the webpack or rspack builder, the dev server serves built client chunks to any request whose `Host` header matches its `Origin`/`Referer`, or that carries `Sec-Fetch-Site: same-origin`. After a DNS rebinding attack both headers name the attacker's hostname, so a malicious page opened while `nuxt dev` is running can read `/_nuxt/*.js` and exfiltrate the app's source. This bypasses the same-origin check added for [GHSA-4gf7-ff8x-hq99](https://github.com/nuxt/nuxt/security/advisories/GHSA-4gf7-ff8x-hq99), [GHSA-6m52-m754-pw2g](https://github.com/nuxt/nuxt/security/advisories/GHSA-6m52-m754-pw2g) and [GHSA-x6qj-4h56-5rj5](https://github.com/nuxt/nuxt/security/advisories/GHSA-x6qj-4h56-5rj5).

### Impact

A developer runs `nuxt dev` with `builder: 'webpack'` or `builder: 'rspack'` (the default config is enough; `--host` is not required) and opens a page on an attacker-controlled hostname, for example `http://rebind.attacker.example:3000/`. The attacker then re-points that hostname at `127.0.0.1`. Requests from the page now reach the dev server as same-origin requests:

```bash
curl -H 'Host: rebind.attacker.example:3000' -H 'Sec-Fetch-Site: same-origin' http://127.0.0.1:3000/_nuxt/app.js
# 200, with the compiled modules
```

The page can read the response with `fetch`, which exposes the compiled source and its inline source maps, module identifiers, the developer's local filesystem paths, and any developer-controlled values inlined into the client bundle (for example through a custom `DefinePlugin`). With rspack, the HMR websocket also accepts connections from the rebound hostname. Private `runtimeConfig` is not part of the client bundle.

The attacker needs to know or guess the dev server port and to time the DNS change. Chrome 142+ and other Chromium-based browsers that enforce [Local Network Access restrictions](https://developer.chrome.com/release-notes/142#local_network_access_restrictions) prompt before a public page can reach a loopback address.

The default Vite builder is not affected: Vite rejects unknown `Host` headers through `server.allowedHosts`. Production builds are not affected.

### Patches

Fixed in `@nuxt/webpack-builder` 4.6.4 and `@nuxt/rspack-builder` 4.6.4. The dev middleware now rejects requests whose `Host` header is not `localhost`, `*.localhost`, an IP address, or a hostname allowed by the new `devServer.allowedHosts` option or by `vite.server.allowedHosts`, before any `Sec-Fetch-Site`/`Origin`/`Referer` chec

advisories.summary: Active Storage: Unsigned Content-Type in GCS direct uploads with cache_control
advisories.description:
### Impact
When a GCS service is configured with the `cache_control` option, `ActiveStorage::Service::GCSService#url_for_direct_upload` signs direct-upload URLs with V4, and the V4 signature covers only the `Cache-Control` and `Host` headers. A direct-upload client can therefore send a `Content-Type` of its choosing, and can omit the declared `Content-MD5`, without invalidating the URL. GCS stores the supplied content type as object metadata, which takes precedence over the `response-content-type` that Active Storage sets on download URLs, so an uploaded object could be served as inline HTML under the application's bucket path on `storage.googleapis.com`. Script in such an object runs on the storage origin rather than the application's, but could register a Service Worker scoped to the bucket path and read or replace a victim's later responses for signed URLs in that bucket.

Applications that use the GCS service with `cache_control` configured and accept direct uploads are affected. GCS services without `cache_control` sign with V2 and are not affected.

### Details
The fixed releases sign every GCS direct-upload URL with V2, which binds an empty `Content-Type` and the declared `Content-MD5`. The configured `Cache-Control` is still returned by `headers_for_direct_upload` and sent by the client, but it is no longer part of the signature, and direct-upload URLs for these services are no longer limited to V4's seven-day maximum expiry. See the Active Storage CHANGELOG.

### Workarounds

advisories.summary: Forge: Incomplete PKCS#7 padding validation in AES/DES CBC and ECB decryption
advisories.description:
### Summary
`decipher.finish()` in CBC and ECB mode accepted malformed PKCS#7 padding: only the last byte was checked, against a limit of four blocks, so mismatched padding bytes, a zero count and oversized counts were accepted and up to four blocks of plaintext could be silently removed. Fixed in node-forge 1.4.1.

### Details
`modes.cbc.prototype.unpad()` and `modes.ecb.prototype.unpad()` in `lib/cipherModes.js` read the last decrypted byte as the PKCS#7 padding count, rejected it only if it was larger than `blockSize << 2` (64 for AES, 32 for DES), and then removed that many bytes. They did not reject a count of 0 or a count larger than one block, and did not check that every padding byte equals the count, as PKCS#7 (RFC 5652 section 6.3) requires. On the Wycheproof AES-CBC-PKCS5 test vectors, 69 of 144 invalid vectors decrypted successfully.

CBC and ECB without a MAC do not provide integrity: an attacker who can modify ciphertext can already make the final block decrypt to any padding. The effect of this bug is that malformed ciphertext is accepted as valid and that oversized counts silently truncate up to four blocks of plaintext. The fix does not protect against padding oracle attacks; applications that decrypt untrusted CBC data need to authenticate it (for example with an HMAC) or use AES-GCM.

The fix requires a count from 1 to the block size and checks every padding byte. Data with other padding schemes that only use the last byte as the count (ANSI X.923, ISO 10126, XML Encryption) now fails to decrypt with default unpadding; set `decipher.mode.unpad = false` before `finish()` and remove such padding in application code.

#### Patches
Fixed in node-forge 1.4.1. CBC and ECB decryption requires valid PKCS#7 padding.

#### Workarounds
Authenticate CBC/ECB ciphertext before decrypting it, or use AES-GCM. To check padding on 1.4.0, set `decipher.mode.unpad = false` and validate the padding in application code.

#### References
- https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc5652#section-6.3 (PKCS#7 content-encryption padding)
- https://github.com/C2SP/wycheproof/blob/master/testvectors_v1/aes_cbc_pkcs5_test.json
- https://cwe.mitre.org/data/definitions/354.html (CWE-354: Improper Validation of Integrity Check Value)

#### Severity
CVSS 3.1: CVSS:3.1/AV:N/AC:H/PR:N/UI:N/S:U/C:N/I:L/A:N (3.7, Low)
CVSS 4.0 (informational): CVSS:4.0/AV:N/AC:L/AT:P/PR:N/UI:N/VC:N/VI:L/VA:N/SC:N/SI:N/SA:N (6.3)
CVSS 4.0 rates this Moderate because its integrity weighting is higher;

advisories.summary: Gradle Shadow: Zip Slip path traversal in ShadowCopyAction — no independent entry-name sanitization
advisories.description:
### Summary
ShadowCopyAction in the Shadow plugin does not validate or sanitize ZIP entry names before writing them to the output fat JAR. A malicious upstream dependency containing path traversal sequences (e.g. `../../../../tmp/pwned.txt`) in entry names will have those entries reproduced verbatim in the output shadow JAR.

### Details
The vulnerability exists because Shadow relies entirely on Gradle's ZipFileTree for entry sanitization rather than implementing its own path validation. This means:

1. Users on Gradle < 7.6.2 / 8.x < 8.2.0 are directly exploitable
2. The produced shadow JAR becomes a Zip Slip weapon against any 
downstream consumer using unprotected extraction (raw ZipInputStream, 
older CI tooling, custom Java unpackers)
3. If Shadow ever uses a non-ZipFileTree code path, protection 
disappears silently

Affected file: `src/main/kotlin/com/github/jengelman/gradle/plugins/shadow/internal/ShadowCopyAction.kt`

### PoC
1. Create a malicious JAR with path traversal entry:
```python
import zipfile
with zipfile.ZipFile('evil.jar', 'w') as zf:
    zf.writestr('../../../../tmp/zipslip_proof.txt', 'pwned')
```
2. Add as dependency in a shadow project
3. Run `gradle shadowJar`
4. Run `unzip -l build/libs/*.jar | grep "\.\."`
5. Traversal entry survives in output JAR

### Impact
Any tool extracting the shadow JAR with unprotected extraction is subject to arbitrary file overwrite. Users on older Gradle versions  are directly vulnerable at build time.

advisories.summary: envd: Host file disclosure through requirements path traversal and TOCTOU
advisories.description:
### Summary

envd’s `install.python_packages(requirements=...)` could read files outside the build context on the host. Content interpreted as dependency entries could appear in build logs and build-step metadata.

Commit f576c92, released in v1.3.5, added path containment validation but left a time-of-check/time-of-use (TOCTOU) race between symlink resolution and opening the requirements file. Commit 9d575b3 addresses this race by opening requirements files through a directory-rooted filesystem handle.

### Details

envd reads requirements files on the host to determine whether their contents can be embedded directly into a pip installation build step.

The vulnerable host-side requirements read was introduced in v0.3.38. Version v1.3.5 added containment checks for static path escapes but remained vulnerable to a TOCTOU race. The complete fix is included in v1.3.6.

Before f576c92, this host read lacked a build-context containment check. That commit added frontend path validation and a compile-time check using filepath.EvalSymlinks followed by a containment comparison.

However, symlink resolution returns a pathname rather than a pinned filesystem object. The subsequent os.Open independently resolves that pathname. Concurrent filesystem changes could therefore invalidate the containment check before the file was opened.

The complete fix uses os.OpenRoot and Root.Open to enforce containment during filesystem traversal.

Resources:
- first commit: be783264fdd79ad7262cea0485b7d449ca514f80
- Initial containment fix: f576c92
- TOCTOU fix: 9d575b3

### Proof of concept

The security-relevant condition is a requirements-file pathname whose filesystem resolution changes between validation and opening. The containment check describes the filesystem at validation time, while the later pathname-based open may access a different object.

The fix includes a deterministic regression test for the underlying object-pinning guarantee. It opens a context directory handle, moves that directory, and creates a replacement directory at the original pathname containing different requirements. The rooted reader continues reading the original context; a pathname-based reader reads the replacement.

This regression test demonstrates the distinction between rooted and pathname-based reads. It is not an end-to-end demonstration of host file disclosure.

That hash was computed over `ohash`'s serialization, which does not escape quotes inside strings or delimiters inside keys, so two different prop objects can produce the same hash. A request with crafted props can therefore pass validation for another island's path and render different content at that path. ### Impact For example, these two prop objects serialize identically and share one island path: ```js { html: '', note: '' } { html: '\',note:\'' } ``` This reopens the scenarios described in GHSA-g8wj-3cr3-6w7v: - **`nuxt generate` / prerendering.** Nuxt caches prerendered island responses by path. If the crawler reaches a link to the colliding URL (for example in user-submitted content included in the build) before it renders the page that uses the legitimate props, the colliding response is written into the generated page. - **Path-keyed shared caches.** A CDN or reverse proxy that caches `/__nuxt_island/*` by path only, ignoring the query, can be primed with the colliding response. An attacker has to construct props that collide with a specific legitimate tuple, which in practice means at least part of that tuple is a string they control (for example a stored comment or profile field passed as a prop). advisories.summary: pgEdge Control Plane generates pg_hba.conf with trust authentication for local and loopback connections
advisories.description:
### Summary

Every `pg_hba.conf` generated by the pgEdge Control Plane begins with a hard-coded block of `trust` entries covering Unix-socket and loopback connections. Any operating-system account that can reach the Postgres socket or the loopback interface on a database host can authenticate as any Postgres role, including the superuser, without presenting a credential.

### Details

The generated file opens with the following six entries:

```
local   all         all                     trust
host    all         all     127.0.0.1/32    trust
host    all         all     ::1/128         trust
local   replication all                     trust
host    replication all     127.0.0.1/32    trust
host    replication all     ::1/128         trust
```

Postgres evaluates `pg_hba.conf` top-down and stops at the first matching rule. Because these entries are emitted at the top of the file, they also pre-empt every rule below them — including entries supplied by an operator through the `pg_hba_conf` field of a database node specification, which are appended lower in the file and are therefore never reached for local or loopback connections.

Both supported orchestrators emit these entries, but exposure differs by deployment model:

* **systemd** — the database runs on a shared multi-user host. Any local account
  on that host can connect as the Postgres superuser. This is the
  higher-severity case and the one the CVSS score below reflects.
* **Docker Swarm** — the Unix socket and the loopback interface belong to the
  Postgres container, so reaching these entries requires code execution inside
  that container. Publishing the Postgres port to the host does not change this:
  such connections are not seen by Postgres as originating from `127.0.0.1` or
  `::1`, so they do not match the entries above. The practical exposure is
  correspondingly narrower.

An operator who verifies their own deployment can confirm the issue by inspecting the generated `pg_hba.conf` on a database node for the entries above.

### Impact

An unprivileged local operating-system account on an affected database host obtains full control of every Postgres database on that host: read of all data, modification or destruction of all data, and any action available to a Postgres superuser. Under the systemd orchestrator this converts any local account into a database superuser with no additional prerequisites.

### Affected versions

pgEdge Control Plane v0.1.0 through v0.10.1, inclusive.

advisories.summary: Cocos AI Intra-handshake attested TLS implementation is vulnerable to TOCTOU Attacks
advisories.description:
### Summary
An attacker who can modify the attested workload’s code, memory-backed state, or configuration after the initial attestation — but without necessarily terminating the existing TLS connection — can cause the peer to continue trusting the connection as if the originally attested state were still running.

### Details
Once attestation is successfully appraised and connection is established, there is a window of vulnerability from the establishment of connection to the termination of connection where an attacker can modify the state of the workload and platform at runtime on the TLS endpoint acting as the Attester. Workload state includes code, data, and configuration. Other examples of state changes at the workload level include cases where a new device (such as a GPU) is connected, or where a connected device is disconnected, since the connection establishment.

In Cocos AI, there is no mechanism for the peer to know that some state has changed in the Attester after the connection establishment. The vulnerability is particularly concerning for long-lived connections.

In short, this vulnerability was possible because Cocos AI performs attestation only once in the lifetime of the connection (at connection establishment time) and the verifying peer continues to believe that the state is the same as in initial Evidence throughout, whereas it could be stale at some point in time.

This vulnerability for Cocos AI was found and demonstrated by Muhammad Usama Sardar via formal analysis. Formal analysis was performed in the state-of-the-art tool, ProVerif.

### Workarounds
The proposed workaround is to allow re-attestation of the workload after periodic or user-defined intervals using post-handshake attestation.

### Background and General Technical Details
For background and general (not specific to Cocos AI) technical details on this vulnerability, please see `G-RA2: Freshness of Evidence` in Sec. 5.1.1 of [Identity Crisis in Confidential Computing: Formal Analysis of Attested TLS](https://doi.org/10.1145/3779208.3785387). Also, see the corresponding [formal analysis](https://github.com/CCC-Attestation/formal-spec-id-crisis).

### Credits
This vulnerability for Cocos AI was found and _responsibly_ disclosed by Muhammad Usama Sardar (TU Dresden, Germany).

advisories.summary: russh's SSH agent server is susceptible to unbound allocations via repeated SSH_AGENT_CONSTRAIN_CONFIRM messages
advisories.description:
### Summary

**All evidence, reproduction steps, and scripts in the report were verified against a real running instance. Nothing is fabricated or synthetic; every verdict is backed by captured output from an actual deployment.**

The SSH agent server that ships with russh (`russh::keys::agent::server::serve`) parses client key-addition requests and, for each `SSH_AGENT_CONSTRAIN_CONFIRM` (0x02) record it finds, pushes one `Constraint::Confirm` value into a per-key vector inside an unbounded loop, then stores the resulting pair permanently in its keystore (`russh/src/keys/agent/server.rs:296-303`). Neither the constraint vector nor the keystore has a size or count limit: the only boundary is the 256 KiB agent frame cap, and every 1-byte record a client sends becomes a 56-byte enum retained for the life of the process. Any process that can connect to the agent socket - the same trust model the project itself established when fixing a prior advisory about this same request handler - can therefore grow the agent's memory without bound and renew the growth at will: six 256 KiB requests retained 72.4 MiB (about 12.1 MiB per request, a roughly 48-fold amplification) while an equal number of unconstrained key additions retained nothing, measured against the unmodified server through its public API on v0.64.1. The earlier fix for that prior advisory deduplicates only the sibling `SSH_AGENT_CONSTRAIN_LIFETIME` (0x01) record type and leaves this parallel variant untouched, and since constrained keys never expire the retained memory is never reclaimed.

When a client adds a key with constraints, the server walks the constraint section byte by byte and collects typed values with no upper bound on how many it will accept:

```text
    - the (key, timestamp, constraints) triple is inserted into the keystore,
      and keys without a LIFETIME constraint never expire
```

advisories.summary: qbee-agent: Local Privilege Escalation and Arbitrary File Tampering via Symlink Following in createFile helper
advisories.description:
This is a Local Privilege Escalation (LPE) vulnerability stemming from improper symlink handling (CWE-59: Link Following) and improper ownership management (CWE-282) inside the qbee-agent file manager logic.

### Impact

Any managed device running qbee-agent up to the affected versions. The impact manifests in three distinct vectors:

1. **Primary Vector (Full Privilege Escalation to Root - Default Configuration)**: If an unprivileged user's account is managed by the SSH Keys bundle, they can replace or remove their own `~/.ssh` directory and create a symlink pointing to `/root/.ssh`. On the next configuration apply, qbee-agent follows the symlink and writes the user's server-provisioned public key directly into `/root/.ssh/authorized_keys`. Since the symlink resides inside the user's own home directory, kernel protections like `fs.protected_symlinks` do not block this execution. The attacker can then instantly log in as root via SSH.

2. **Secondary Vector (Arbitrary File Overwrite / DoS via RAUC Staging)**: On devices utilizing RAUC download mode, the agent uses a predictable, world-writable staging path (`/tmp/.bundle.raucb.part`). If `fs.protected_symlinks` is disabled `(0)`, an unprivileged user can symlink this path to a vital system file (e.g., `/etc/shadow` or `/etc/pam.d/*`), causing the agent to truncate or overwrite it with server-supplied update data during a RAUC update deployment.

3. **Tertiary Vector (Arbitrary File Re-ownership via File Distribution)**: If an operator configures a file-distribution/template destination under a directory owned by an unprivileged user, the attacker can create a symlink at the partial download path targeting a sensitive system file. The agent will then inadvertently execute `file.Chown()` on the targeted file, handing ownership over to the unprivileged attacker.

### Patches

The vulnerability has been addressed by hardening file creation and directory traversal inside `app/configuration/file_manager.go`. Specifically, the agent now enforces `syscall.O_NOFOLLOW` and proper existence validation flags during privileged operations to prevent link resolution outside intended directories.

Users should upgrade to version 2026.27 (or newer) to fully mitigate these vectors.

### Workarounds

If upgrading immediately is not feasible, administrators can apply the following mitigations:

advisories.summary: Forge: Certificate signature verified with the issuer's RSA signature scheme
advisories.description:
### Summary

When verifying a certificate, node-forge chose the RSA padding scheme (PKCS#1 v1.5 or RSASSA-PSS) and PSS parameters from the issuer certificate's own signature algorithm instead of the certificate being verified. A certificate labeled as signed with RSASSA-PSS could pass `verifyCertificateChain()` with a PKCS#1 v1.5 signature. Fixed in node-forge 1.4.1.

### Details

`certificate.verify(child)` in `lib/x509.js` hashes the child's TBSCertificate with the digest of the child's signature algorithm, then calls `_verifySignature()` with the issuer certificate. `_verifySignature()` selected the padding scheme from that certificate's `signatureOid` and `signatureParameters`, so the child was verified with the issuer's own scheme rather than the one the child declares.

As a result, a child certificate whose signature algorithm says RSASSA-PSS was accepted with a PKCS#1 v1.5 signature when the issuer itself was signed with PKCS#1 v1.5. The outer `signatureAlgorithm` field of a certificate is not covered by the signature, so an existing PKCS#1 v1.5 (SHA-256) certificate can be relabeled as RSASSA-PSS and still pass verification. The signature itself must still be made with the issuer's private key over the certificate's contents; no certificate can be forged.

The same cause made correctly signed chains fail: a PKCS#1 v1.5 certificate issued by an RSASSA-PSS-signed certificate, or the reverse, was rejected.

The fix verifies with the child certificate's signature scheme and parameters and the issuer's public key.

### Patches
Fixed in node-forge 1.4.1. Certificate signatures are verified with the scheme of the certificate's own signature algorithm.

### Workarounds
Applications that make decisions based on a certificate's signature algorithm can verify the signature themselves with that algorithm's scheme and the issuer's public key.

### References
- https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc4055#section-3 (RSASSA-PSS signature algorithm in certificates)
- https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc5280#section-4.1.1.2 (Certificate signatureAlgorithm)
- https://cwe.mitre.org/data/definitions/347.html (CWE-347: Improper Verification of Cryptographic Signature)

### Severity
CVSS 3.1: CVSS:3.1/AV:N/AC:H/PR:N/UI:N/S:U/C:N/I:L/A:N (3.7, Low)
CVSS 4.0 (informational): CVSS:4.0/AV:N/AC:L/AT:P/PR:N/UI:N/VC:N/VI:L/VA:N/SC:N/SI:N/SA:N (6.3)

advisories.summary: libp2p: gossipsub creates a permanent topics-map entry per distinct subscription with no cap in the default config
advisories.description:
### Summary
A single gossipsub peer can grow a node's `topics` map without bound by flooding subscription RPCs, because the default configuration has no global, per-peer, or topic-length cap and peer scoring does not penalise subscription volume. The peer is never greylisted, so the growth continues toward OOM.

### Details
`handleReceivedSubscription` (`packages/gossipsub/src/gossipsub.ts:1028`, line 1036) runs `this.topics.set(topic, new Set())` for every distinct topic string:

```ts
private handleReceivedSubscription (from, topic, subscribe) {
  let topicSet = this.topics.get(topic)
  if (subscribe) {
    if (topicSet == null) {
      topicSet = new Set()
      this.topics.set(topic, topicSet)   // no global cap, no per-peer cap
    }
    topicSet.add(from.toString())
  }
}
```

The only topical gate (`gossipsub.ts:981`, `if (this.allowedTopics != null && !this.allowedTopics.has(topic)) return`) is skipped when `allowedTopics` is null — the default. Subscriptions are unsigned RPC metadata (no signature needed); `decodeRpc`'s per-RPC limit caps count (`maxSubscriptions = 5000`) but not topic-string length or aggregate size; and the peer-scoring components P1–P7 have no subscription-volume term, so the attacker's score stays at 0 (above the `graylistThreshold` of −80) and `acceptFrom` keeps returning true. Verified on js-libp2p commit `a04f5e0`, where `@libp2p/gossipsub` reads `16.0.4`.

### PoC
Full PoC attached (`gossipsub-topics-unbounded-growth-poc.tar.gz`). Build the js-libp2p monorepo at the affected version (`npm install --ignore-scripts && npm run build`), extract the package inside the monorepo root (sibling of `packages/`), then `cd gossipsub-topics-unbounded-growth-poc && node attack.mjs`. Expected (default config):

```
[*] sending 300 RPC frames x 4000 unique ~190-byte topic subscriptions (1,200,000 topics total)
[*]   progress: 88% sent | victim topics=1,032,000 rss=740MB peers=1
[*] victim quiesced: topics=~1,100,000 rss=~870MB peers=1
[!] Vulnerability reproduced: one connected peer grew the victim's gossipsub topics map to ~1.1M entries (RSS +~900MB) with 300 subscription RPCs — no global, per-peer, or topic-length cap in the default config
```

Control run (`ALLOWED_TOPICS=legit-topic`, i.e. `node attack.mjs control`): the identical flood is rejected at the `allowedTopics` gate and the topics map stays at 0 entries — confirming the vulnerable condition is the default `allowedTopics`-unset config. The map grows monotonically with no cap

advisories.summary: libp2p: ASN.1 DER decoder drives an unbounded synchronous loop on attacker-controlled length fields, stalling the Node event loop pre-auth
advisories.description:
### Summary
A remote peer can stall a js-libp2p node's entire event loop for ~4–5 seconds per connection (and transiently allocate ~2 GB) by sending a ~15-byte crafted `publicKey` inside an Identify message. The malformed key reaches the DER decoder before any peer-id/signature check, so the attack is pre-auth and repeatable indefinitely by reconnecting.

### Details
`packages/crypto/src/keys/rsa/der.ts` `readLength()` parses DER long-form lengths with no comparison to `buf.byteLength`, and `readInteger()` then loops over the attacker-claimed length:

```ts
function readInteger (buf, context) {
  const length = readLength(buf, context)   // attacker-controlled, claims up to 2^64
  const end = context.offset + length
  for (let i = context.offset; i < end; i++) // runs far past buf.byteLength
    vals.push(buf[i])                         // pushes `undefined` past the end
}
```

The blob reaches the parser pre-auth: Identify runs on every `connection:open` and calls `publicKeyFromProtobuf(publicKey)` (`packages/protocol-identify/src/identify.ts:85`) before the `connection.remotePeer.equals(id)` check at `identify.ts:88`. The `MAX_RSA_JWK_SIZE` guard in `pkixToRSAPublicKey` only bounds the total blob size, not the inner length field, so a 15-byte payload defeats it; the ECDSA path (`unmarshalECDSAPublicKey`) has no cap at all. The decode runs in a single synchronous tick, so no `AbortSignal` — including Identify's 5 s timeout — can interrupt it. Verified on js-libp2p commit `a04f5e0`, where `@libp2p/crypto` reads `5.1.21`.

### PoC
Full PoC attached (`libp2p-crypto-der-eventloop-dos-poc.tar.gz`). Build the js-libp2p monorepo at the affected version (`npm install --ignore-scripts && npm run build`), extract the package inside the monorepo root (sibling of `packages/`), then `cd libp2p-crypto-der-eventloop-dos-poc && node attack.mjs`. Expected:

advisories.summary: SAML2: Incomplete fix of CVE-2026-49283: unsigned embedded Response bypasses HTTP-Artifact signature verification (no embedded-Issuer binding)
advisories.description:
## Summary
CVE-2026-49283 / GHSA-6929-8p9f-26jx ("HTTP-Artifact TLS validator confusion allows cross-IdP authentication bypass") was fixed so that `HTTPArtifact::receive()` verifies the embedded SAML `Response` using the IdP metadata signing keys. The current implementation (master `31c72c1d`, released **v6.2.3**) reaches that verification **only when the embedded Response is signed**:

```php
// src/Binding/HTTPArtifact.php  (receive())
if (!$samlResponse->isSigned()) {
    return $samlResponse;                         // ← unsigned embedded Response returned UNVERIFIED
}
return $this->verifyMessageSignature($samlResponse, $idpMetadata);   // only runs when signed
```

An attacker who controls one trusted-federation IdP therefore returns a **validly-signed outer `ArtifactResponse`** (signed with their own real key, which passes the mandatory outer check) that **wraps an *unsigned* `<samlp:Response>` whose `<Issuer>` names a *different* IdP**. `isSigned()` is false, so `verifyMessageSignature()` never runs and the forged Response is returned as successfully received. Additionally, even on the signed path `verifyMessageSignature()` verifies against the **artifact issuer's** metadata keys but **never asserts that the embedded Response's `<Issuer>` equals the artifact issuer** — the same cross-IdP confusion the CVE was assigned for is not closed by identity binding.

This is an incomplete implementation of the fix's own stated goal ("verify signatures using IdP metadata signing keys", commit `dac0b4b6` / #419), and a regression introduced by the `#414` refactor (v6.2.2) — the official CVE fix in **v6.2.1 did not contain this short-circuit**.

## Affected component
- `src/Binding/HTTPArtifact.php`
  - `receive()` line **206-207**: `if (!$samlResponse->isSigned()) { return $samlResponse; }` — the bypassed guard.
  - `receive()` line 210: `verifyMessageSignature($samlResponse, $idpMetadata)` — only reached when signed.
  - `verifyMessageSignature()` lines 230-286: verifies against `$idpMetadata` (artifact-issuer keys); **no `getIssuer()` comparison** to bind the embedded Response to the artifact issuer.
  - `verifyArtifactResponseSignature()` line **300-302**: `if ($artifactResponse->isSigned() !== true) throw` — the OUTER response is mandatorily signed; the asymmetry with the embedded `return`-on-unsigned is the defect.
- Regression commit **3b589636** (#414, v6.2.2, "refactor/soap-ssl-validator-openssl"); key-source fix **dac0b4b6** (#419) left the short-circu

advisories.summary: Filament Curator: Cross-tenant media metadata disclosure via Curator picker search
advisories.description:
Summary

  In multitenant Filament panels, an authenticated user could retrieve media metadata belonging to other tenants
  by typing in the Curator media-picker search box. The search query omitted the tenant ownership scope that the
  normal file listing applies.

  Details

  CuratorPanel::updatedSearch() built its Eloquent query independently of getFiles() and did not apply the
  filament()->hasTenancy() && $isTenantAware tenant-ownership where clause. As a result, the search matched media
  across all tenants. A secondary flaw compounded it: the orWhere('title'…) chain was not wrapped in a nested
  group, so the OR conditions also broke out of the isLimitedToDirectory constraint.

  The issue was introduced in v3.2.4, when multitenancy support was added to the media picker.

  Impact

  - Who: any authenticated user with access to a panel that uses the Curator picker.
  - What: disclosure of other tenants' media metadata (name, title, alt, caption, description, path, etc.)
  returned by the search.
  - Conditions: only affects deployments using Filament multitenancy with Curator's tenant awareness enabled.
  Single-tenant installs are not affected.

  Patches

  Fixed in 3.7.8, 4.1.1, and 5.1.1 by applying the tenant scope to the search query and grouping the search terms
  so they cannot escape the directory/tenant constraints. Upgrade to a patched version.

  Workarounds

  None other than upgrading. Disabling tenant awareness does not help (it removes the boundary entirely).

  Credit

  Reported via coordinated disclosure by [Afsana Alijabarova](https://github.com/afa114).

advisories.summary: NLTK: Quadratic CPU exhaustion in LegalitySyllableTokenizer.tokenize via unguarded onset reversal loop
advisories.description:
## Summary

`LegalitySyllableTokenizer.tokenize` in the NLTK tokenizer package contains an unguarded O(n^2) processing loop. When the method is called on a single token that consists of a long run of vowels (for example `"a" * n`), it consumes CPU time proportional to the square of the token length. An attacker who can supply an untrusted token to this public tokenizer API can force a single request to saturate one CPU core for a prolonged period, degrading availability of any service that syllabifies attacker-controlled text. No authentication, special configuration, or user interaction is required.

## Root Cause

The method walks the token in reverse and, on every iteration after the first vowel is seen, evaluates the membership test `char_lower + current_onset[::-1] in self.legal_onsets`. The set `legal_onsets` is built by `onset()`, which returns only the characters up to the first vowel, so every member is vowel-free. For an all-vowel token the first branch can therefore never match, `onset` never becomes `True`, and the reset branch that would clear `current_onset` is never reached. As a result `current_onset` grows by one character on every iteration. Building `current_onset[::-1]` and hashing the resulting string costs O(k) on iteration k, and this is repeated for k from 1 to n, giving total cost O(n^2). The security invariant that is violated is bounded per-token work: there is no length cap on this code path, so untrusted token length translates directly into quadratic CPU consumption.

```text
Affected function: LegalitySyllableTokenizer.tokenize
Source: nltk/tokenize/legality_principle.py (membership-test sink at line 133; loop over token[::-1] beginning at line 126)
Helper establishing the vowel-free onset set: LegalitySyllableTokenizer.onset (nltk/tokenize/legality_principle.py, returns prefix up to first vowel)
```

## Impact

An attacker who controls a token passed to `LegalitySyllableTokenizer.tokenize` can trigger quadratic CPU work. In the reviewed release a token of roughly 64,000 vowel characters takes about 1.8 seconds on a single core, and the cost grows with the square of the length, so a token in the hundreds of kilobytes to megabyte range consumes a core for many seconds to minutes. Memory use is linear. The demonstrated capability is single-core CPU exhaustion leading to denial of service or latency degradation in any network-reachable component that syllabifies untrusted input. There is no confidentiality or integrity impact; t

advisories.summary: Rucio: Unauthenticated administrator impersonation through SSH challenge tokens
advisories.description:
## Summary

SSH challenge tokens are mistakenly accepted as valid credentials during the authentication token validation process.

While an SSH challenge token is intended as a short-lived nonce for use in a subsequent SSH key exchange, the function to validate authentication tokens does not differentiate between these and actual authentication tokens. Because challenge tokens are generated based on an account name provided via headers without requiring prior authentication, an unauthenticated attacker can request a valid "challenge" token for any account (including administrative ones) and use it to authenticate against other API endpoints.

## Proof of Concept

The vulnerability exists because SSH challenge tokens are stored in the same database table as regular authentication tokens and `validate_auth_token` in `lib/rucio/core/authentication.py` accepts these "challenge" tokens. An attacker can obtain a challenge token for an account such as “root” via the REST API and then present it as a valid authentication bearer token:

1. Request a challenge token for an arbitrary account (e.g., "root"):
   `curl -i -H "X-Rucio-Account: root" https://rucio/auth/ssh_challenge_token`
2. The server returns a `200 OK` with the header `X-Rucio-SSH-Challenge-Token`.
3. The attacker can then use this specific token within the ten-second challenge lifetime as an authentication credential in subsequent requests to the Rucio API:
  `curl -H "X-Rucio-Auth-Token: $CHALLENGE_TOKEN"  https://rucio/accounts/whoami`

advisories.summary: Forge: RSA PKCS#1 v1.5 signature forgery via non-canonical DigestInfo encoding
advisories.description:
### Summary
RSASSA-PKCS1-v1_5 signature verification (`publicKey.verify()` with the default scheme, also used by X.509 certificate and PKCS#7 verification) accepted non-canonical BER encodings of the DigestInfo, such as NULL parameters with content and non-minimal lengths. These leave attacker-controlled bytes inside an accepted DigestInfo, which allows signatures to be forged without the private key for RSA keys with a low public exponent (e=3). Fixed in node-forge 1.4.1.

### Details
In `lib/rsa.js`, `key.verify()` with the default `RSASSA-PKCS1-V1_5` scheme removes the padding, parses the recovered DigestInfo with the lenient BER parser `asn1.fromDer()` and checks its structure with `asn1.validate()` against `digestInfoValidator`. Neither requires a canonical DER encoding, so verification accepted, among others:
- NULL parameters with content bytes (e.g. `05 40 <64 bytes>`)
- non-NULL or constructed values in the parameters position
- non-minimal (long form) and indefinite lengths
- non-canonical OID encodings (padded subidentifiers, trailing bytes)

These leave attacker-controlled bytes inside an accepted DigestInfo. For RSA keys with a low public exponent (e=3) this allows signatures to be forged without the private key (BERserk / Bleichenbacher-style forgery, see CVE-2014-1568).

RFC 8017 section 8.2.2 verifies a signature by encoding the expected EMSA-PKCS1-v1_5 message and comparing it with the recovered one; section 9.2 defines the DigestInfo encoding.

The fix adds `_encodeDigestInfo()`, which DER-encodes the expected DigestInfo from the digest algorithm OID and the digest (with and without NULL parameters). Verification now requires the recovered DigestInfo to match one of these encodings byte for byte. The same change fixes GHSA-2g46-22mc-6gwp (CVE-2026-85393).

#### Patches
Fixed in node-forge 1.4.1. Verification now re-encodes the expected DigestInfo and requires a byte-for-byte match (RFC 8017 section 8.2.2).

#### Workarounds
Do not use RSA keys with a low public exponent (e=3) for signature verification.

#### References
- https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc8017#section-8.2.2
- https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc8017#section-9.2
- CVE-2026-85393 / GHSA-2g46-22mc-6gwp (related, same fix)
- CVE-2026-33894 / https://github.com/digitalbazaar/forge/security/advisories/GHSA-ppp5-5v6c-4jwp
- https://www.cve.org/CVERecord?id=CVE-2014-1568 (BERserk)

advisories.description:
# NodeVM `builtin: ['*']` exposes `os` and `dns` — process-wide observability reads AND writes that hijack the host (sibling class of GHSA-9g8x-92q2-p28f)

**CWE**: CWE-200 (Exposure of Sensitive Information to an Unauthorized Actor) chained with CWE-732 (Incorrect Permission Assignment for Critical Resource) and CWE-285 (Improper Authorization) — same class the maintainer codified as Defense Invariant #13 in `lib/builtin.js` and as Category 35 / GHSA-9g8x in `docs/ATTACKS.md`.

**CVSS v3.1**: `CVSS:3.1/AV:N/AC:L/PR:N/UI:N/S:C/C:H/I:H/A:L` → 9.3 (Critical)

(Scope = Changed because the data being read and the state being written both belong to the host process, not the sandbox. Confidentiality = High because `os.userInfo()` returns host UID/GID/username/homedir + `os.networkInterfaces()` returns the full host network topology including container/VM interfaces with IPs and MAC addresses. Integrity = High because `dns.setServers()` is a process-wide write that hijacks every subsequent DNS lookup the host makes — including outbound HTTP, telemetry, npm/registry, and any host code that uses `fetch` or URL-based fs paths. Privileges Required = None because the attacker controls sandbox code, which is the threat model `NodeVM` exists to mitigate.)

## Summary

GHSA-9g8x-92q2-p28f closed the "process-wide observability builtins" class by adding `diagnostics_channel`, `async_hooks`, `perf_hooks`, and `v8` to `DANGEROUS_BUILTINS` in `lib/builtin.js`. The fix's rationale (in the commit message and `docs/ATTACKS.md` Category 35) is general:

> Process-wide observability builtins. Unlike most Node builtins, these expose state of the *entire host process* rather than sandbox-local state — the vm2 boundary cannot usefully contain them because the data they surface […] belongs to the embedder. Even a readonly proxy that forwards every call to the host module is a working host-data exfiltration primitive.

Two builtins satisfying the same description were not added: **`os`** and **`dns`**. Both are reachable today under the documented `builtin: ['*']` configuration; both expose host-process state that the `vm.readonly()` proxy cannot localise; and both have *write* APIs that mutate global host-process state from the sandbox (`os.setPriority()`, `dns.setServers()`, `dns.setDefaultResultOrder()`). `dns.setServers()` in particular turns sandbox code into a process-wide DNS hijack primitive — strictly worse than every read-only leak that GHSA-9g8x added.
